_comment: Art asset registry. Single source of truth for the generation pipeline. See ../guidelines/art-pipeline.md. Every asset is declared here BEFORE it is drawn; status walks slot -> inbox -> art.

world-prop.note: Top-down orthographic. Drawn in the world at `world` px (camera is 1:1). Baked at 4x display like boat parts. MASTER AND BAKE ARE BOTH PER-ASSET OVERRIDABLE (`master`, `bake`), because both are really questions about the SUBJECT, not the class. `master` is how many px of subject the biggest consumer needs — a buoy at world 40 is finished at 1024, the cove cargo ship at world 720 is not — and ingest NEVER upscales a delivered file to meet it. `bake` is oversampling for devicePixelRatio, not display size; the camera is 1:1 and nothing zooms, so 4x is generous everywhere and unaffordable at the top of the size range, where world x 4 would invent every px past the master. Pair a raised `master` with `gen` (batch_generate) when the subject is long: a square frame caps a ship at 8.6 boat lengths and a portrait frame at 12.8, for the same master budget.

terrain.note: Reserved. Islands/shore are procedural today (bakeIslandSprite); this profile exists so the rework has a home.

texture.note: Seamless tiling ground fill — repeated across a land polygon, not placed like a sprite. The camera is 1:1, so the square draws at `tileWorld` px on screen and the 1024 master is a 2x supersample. Opaque and full-bleed, so it takes ingest's static path and NONE of the transparent-corner checks. It must wrap on all four edges and carry no landmark, no light direction and no vignette; per-asset tileWorld overrides the profile.

illustration.note: Venue cards. Bottom fifth stays simple for the name scrim.

portrait.note: Bust crop, centered for circular use, face within central 70%.

ui-icon.note: Test over both the navy shell and bright water.

element.note: Source element for compose.py. NEVER ships on its own — a single penguin is 4-7px at race scale. Lives in art/elements/, not assets/images/.

roles.hazard: Collides or penalizes. Must telegraph before contact and hold the 3:1 contrast floor on Pearl Lagoon AND Glacier Sound.
roles.ambient: Decorative, no collision. MUST NOT be confusable with a hazard at race scale — different silhouette family, not just different color.
roles.landmark: Venue identity, on land or fixed. Never affects play.
roles.traffic: Non-racing boats. MUST NOT be confusable with a competitor at race scale (extends race-view.md 10.2).
roles.nav: Navigation aids the player is meant to read — channel markers, beacons. Canonical buoyage color coding.

anchors.center: Rotation and placement origin at the art's centroid. Floating things.
anchors.waterline: Origin where the object meets the water. Things that stick up out of it.
anchors.trunk-base: Origin at the base of the stem. Trees, reeds.
anchors.footprint: Origin at the center of the ground contact polygon. Buildings, standing birds.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE TREE STANDING ALONE ON DRY GROUND, shot straight down from well above the crown the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. You are looking at the TOP of the whole tree: the crown fills most of the frame, and through the gaps in it you catch the main limbs radiating out from the middle, with the trunk reading as a dark hub at the centre where they meet. The limbs are seen from ABOVE — you see the top of each branch running outward and never its side, and no length of trunk is visible at all. A bald cypress: a spreading, slightly flat-topped crown of clustered feathery needle-mass blobs in olive and yellow-green, each blob one chunky two-tone tuft and never individual needles. The limbs beneath are relatively slender and reach almost horizontally, and at the centre the buttressed base shows as a fluted dark hub, its ridges just readable radiating from the stem. A SCATTER of pale grey-green spanish moss, thin enough that the needle-mass still reads through it. THE SPANISH MOSS MUST OBEY THE CAMERA TOO, and it is where this subject goes wrong: moss hangs straight DOWN under gravity, so from directly overhead you are looking along the strands END-ON and they foreshorten almost to nothing. Draw each beard as a COMPACT PALE TUFT sitting exactly where it is attached — a small rounded clump of grey-green, frayed and a little ragged at its rim, lying ON TOP of the darker leaf-mass and hiding the foliage under it. Where a limb runs outward the moss reads as a broken line of these tufts strung ALONG the limb, densest near the fork and thinning toward the tip. NO LONG STREAKS, no strands trailing off the crown, no soft strokes sweeping one way across the frame: a plan view has no down, so moss that trails in any single direction is proof the camera was at the side. THE OPENINGS ARE PAINTED NEAR-BLACK, and this matters more than it sounds. Where the crown thins you are looking down into deep shade, so paint those gaps almost black — clearly and cleanly darker than the darkest shadowed foliage, with a hard edge rather than a soft gradient into them. Six to ten scattered through the crown, plus two or three notches biting in from the outer edge. They are what lets the limb structure read, and the pipeline keys exactly that dark phase to transparency so that in the game the land itself shows through them — a gap painted mid-green is a gap that will not exist. THE SILHOUETTE IS AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE. Seen from straight above a crown is a round mass; one wider than it is tall means the camera was tilted and the image is wrong. Irregular is right and elongated is not — the lobes and bays are uneven, but the span top-to-bottom matches the span side-to-side. NO WATER ANYWHERE: this one stands on dry ground, so no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — dry land is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the tree is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the bank it stands on
assets.note: WHOLE TREE, one sprite — the land counterpart to the bayou-cypress-trunk + bayou-cypress-canopy pair. The pair exists so a hull can pass under a crown and hit a stem; on land nothing passes under, so one sprite is the honest object and it keeps a single anchor. Prompt rewritten 2026-08-09 from a one-line stub. DELIVERED 2026-08-09. Content fills 90-97% of the 1024 frame, past the 6% safeMargin, so fillTo 0.86 is set — it clears the tripwire and makes `world` mean the crown's width rather than the frame's. Prep was a halo strip only (dilate the alpha core 3px, drop the diffuse glow the file carried inside its own alpha). CHECKED FOR THE MANDALA the arrangement negatives exist to prevent, because a tree drawn from straight above with limbs radiating from a hub is sitting right next to that attractor: measuring rotational self-similarity of the LIMB MASS ALONE at 4/5/6/8/10-fold, all three score NEGATIVE (cypress -0.08, oak -0.28, tupelo -0.09), i.e. the limbs do not self-align under rotation at any order. Whole-sprite correlation is a bad test here and was tried first — a dense round crown self-correlates just by being a disc, which is why tupelo, visibly the least spoked of the three, scored HIGHEST on it (0.38). Measure the limbs, not the blob. MOSS CLAUSE REWRITTEN 2026-08-09. The previous wording asked for the defect: it said the moss should read as 'soft pale streaks trailing off the crown' with 'strands trailing past the outer edge', and TRAILING describes lateral motion across the frame, which is a side view. Spanish moss hangs on the vertical axis, so a true plan view sees it end-on and it collapses to a compact tuft at its attachment point — the same foreshortening the heron's beak and the tree limbs are already required to show. The rewrite states the physics, gives the correct read (tufts strung along a limb, densest at the fork), and names the failure so a generator can refuse it. RE-DELIVERED 2026-08-09 against the rewritten moss clause, and the fix is MEASURED rather than eyeballed. Test: take every elongated pale-moss blob, compute its principal axis, and ask how strongly those axes align with one fixed direction in image space. For randomly oriented marks that figure is 2/pi = 0.64, so 0.64 means direction-neutral and 1.0 means every strand points the same way. The previous delivery scored 0.95 — nearly every strand hanging down the frame, which is side-view moss and exactly what the old wording asked for. This one scores 0.70 (oak) and 0.62 (cypress), i.e. no vertical bias left, with alignment to the LIMB direction rising to 0.71 / 0.68. Careful with the simpler metric: raw blob ELONGATION got WORSE by the numbers (median 2.48 against 3.69, but a longer tail to 23), and that is not a regression — the new clause deliberately asks for tufts strung ALONG a limb, and a chain of touching tufts merges into one long connected component. Elongation cannot tell a correct chain from a wrong streak; only direction can. Both ingest gates now pass for the first time on this family: no NOT ORTHOGRAPHIC warning (aspects 0.97-1.02 against the old 1.24) and no NO REAL OPENINGS warning, the latter because the enclosed gaps were cut with the saturation key rather than dekey's border flood. Tones landed at oak 34, cypress 50, tupelo 17, against a venue band of 16-46. PUNCHHOLES RETUNED 38 -> 16. The threshold is not a constant of the asset, it is a constant of the DELIVERY, and that is the lesson: punch_holes keys everything below a luma into transparency, so it only separates painted openings from real foliage while the gap between them holds. This Gemini batch renders far deeper darks than the batch the old value was set against — crown luma at the 1st percentile is 4 on the tupelo against a threshold of 28 — so the old number was eating leaf, not hole. Measured on this delivery it kept only 83.3% of the crown and punched 11.2% holes, well past the 6% asked for; 16 keeps 100.0% and punches 7.4%, which clears the floor with the least foliage sacrificed. RE-SWEEP THIS ON EVERY NEW DELIVERY: pick the LOWEST luma that still clears minHoles, because every point above that is crown thrown away. The symptom to watch for is a crown that looks eaten or lacy at race scale while the master looks correct. DELIVERED PRE-CUT 2026-08-09 (background remover, real alpha, black under it). Two things follow from that and both matter. FIRST, THE ALPHA IS AUTHORITATIVE and is passed through untouched — no keying, no choke, no threshold — so the silhouette, the coverage and the openings are exactly what was delivered. SECOND, IT STILL NEEDS A COLOUR BLEED, which is the counter-intuitive part: a remover leaves BLACK under the alpha, and ingest downsamples the master with a plain RGBA resize that PIL performs channel-by-channel without premultiplying, so that black is averaged into every edge pixel on the way down and comes out as a dark halo. Correct alpha does not save you from it; the alpha channel has no say in what the RGB resize does. Flooding the subject's own colour under the transparent pixels makes the average foliage-with-foliage and the halo disappears, whatever the water underneath. PUNCHHOLES REMOVED: the cut art already delivers 8.4% see-through against a 6% floor, and the step is inert below luma 17 because the gaps are alpha now rather than dark paint. Keying more would only eat crown. PROCESSING REDUCED TO GEOMETRY ONLY, 2026-08-09, after a pass that punched holes and bled colour left visible artefacts in the crown. The delivery is pre-cut with real alpha, so the correct handling is to change nothing about the pixels: crop to the alpha bbox, pad square because ingest requires it, ingest. No key, no choke, no unmix, no colour bleed, no punchHoles. Every one of those was solving a problem this file does not have. PUNCHHOLES AND MINHOLES DO NOT APPLY TO THIS ASSET AT ALL, which is the thing that was missed for several rounds: the openings floor exists because a CANOPY-plane sprite draws over the fleet, where a painted gap hides a boat as well as a leaf does. All three whole trees are registered on the `surface` plane — they are land trees, nothing sails beneath them — so see-through is worth nothing here and buying it by keying dark pixels out of the crown is pure loss. punchHoles removed; minHoles removed with it, so ingest stops reporting a failure against a requirement this asset does not have. Both belong on the *-canopy halves of the split pairs, which do draw over boats, and the coupling is recorded on the PROP_KINDS entry: anyone re-planing these to `canopy` has to restore the openings requirement first.

The replacement measures 1.04:1, a true plan view. STYLE: the first needed 135 tones to cover 90% of the sprite against a venue band of 16-46 (gator 16, airboat 35, cypress tree 44); the replacement needs 28. Its outline is also properly lobed with deep bays where the first was a near-perfect disc, which is what the subject asks for. Neither is a mandala — limb-mass rotational self-similarity is 0.00 for both. KEYING NOTE, AND IT GENERALISES: this delivery arrived opaque on a PURE WHITE backdrop, and dekey floods only from the BORDER, so every gap enclosed by foliage stayed opaque white — 3.9% of the sprite, which would have drawn white blobs on the water. The delivery is pre-cut with real alpha, so the correct handling is to change nothing about the pixels: crop to the alpha bbox, pad square because ingest requires it, ingest. No key, no choke, no unmix, no colour bleed, no punchHoles. Every one of those was solving a problem this file does not have. PUNCHHOLES AND MINHOLES DO NOT APPLY TO THIS ASSET AT ALL, which is the thing that was missed for several rounds: the openings floor exists because a CANOPY-plane sprite draws over the fleet, where a painted gap hides a boat as well as a leaf does. All three whole trees are registered on the `surface` plane — they are land trees, nothing sails beneath them — so see-through is worth nothing here and buying it by keying dark pixels out of the crown is pure loss. punchHoles removed; minHoles removed with it, so ingest stops reporting a failure against a requirement this asset does not have. Both belong on the *-canopy halves of the split pairs, which do draw over boats, and the coupling is recorded on the PROP_KINDS entry: anyone re-planing these to `canopy` has to restore the openings requirement first.

assets.subject: DERIVED from bayou-cypress by treesplit.py — see that asset for the art.
assets.note: DERIVED 2026-08-09 by treesplit.py from the whole-tree master — this asset is no longer drawn. The pair exists so a hull can pass UNDER a crown and hit a stem, which needs two sprites in two planes; drawing them as two separate generations gave two different trees, and no prompt makes a canopy match a trunk it never grew on. Cutting one accepted tree guarantees they are the same tree and drops the art bill for a species from three masters to one. Same argument split.py already makes for the orca's body and flukes. BOTH HALVES KEEP THE FULL MASTER FRAME and therefore the full tree's `world`, which is the point of the change: place them at one position and they reassemble into exactly the delivered tree. The hand-drawn pair this replaces was world 30 against world 110 and lined up only because a designer put it there carefully. NO fillTo ON A DERIVED PART, ever — it crops to content and rescales to a fixed fraction of the frame, so the small trunk would blow up to fill it and the halves would stop registering. The whole tree keeps its fillTo; the parts must not have one. The cut is RADIAL, not by colour: seen from above a tree's limbs radiate out to ~0.7 of the crown radius, so keying the wood by hue yields a sprite of branches to draw at water level. The alphas are complementary (trunk a*(1-t), canopy a*t) so the seam cannot show. ANCHOR CHANGED from waterline to trunk-base: with both halves on the full frame there is one origin for the pair and it is the stem. The waterline anchor described a hand-drawn buttressed base that no longer exists as separate art.

assets.subject: COMPOSED from bayou-knee — see that element for the art.
assets.note: COMPOSED by compose.py. Repeated instances of one object are generated once and scattered in code; diffusion models return symmetric arrangements when asked for N of something. SEED 13, from the same sweep discipline as bayou-cattails but READ THE OTHER WAY ROUND, which is the point worth recording: with five tufts the failure was a ring with a hollow centre, so a HIGH centre-fill score was what to chase. With THREE knees a ring is not geometrically available and the failure flips to the opposite — the three clumping into one lumpy mass, which throws away the multiplicity that makes a knee cluster read as a cluster. So here the LOW scores are the good ones: 13 (65%) and 19 (66%) hold three distinct knees in an irregular triangle, while 7 (94%), 11 (90%) and 23 (89%) fuse into a single blob. The metric is the same; what counts as a good value depends on the count. 13 over 19 because 19 spreads far enough that the collider circle starts covering open water between the knees.

assets.subject: half-submerged fallen log seen from directly above, lying with its long axis running UP the frame — a barked trunk a little over three times as long as it is wide, splintered open at both ends into pale angular chips, one broken stub branch jutting from one side and two shorter snapped stubs on the other. Down one side the bark is dark and mossy where the log rides wet; down the other it has peeled away to bare sun-bleached and rust-brown heartwood, the two running the whole length in chunky flat facets rather than fine grain
assets.note: THE LONG one — a fallen trunk lying across the channel, which is what 'a stain along its length' is describing. Do not fill this slot with a cut log section: the first candidate offered for it measured 1.52:1, which at world 70 would have been a log 5 m thick — as thick as the boat is long. That art became bayou-deadhead instead, at the size its own proportion could carry. DELIVERED ART measures 3.32:1 and arrives already cut, running up the frame, needing neither dekey nor rotation — the only preparation was square-padding 1000x1600 to 1600 (ingest hard-fails on non-square) and zeroing 150 stray pixels of alpha-1 export dust. That dust mattered: it sat 434px out from the log and would have set the alpha bbox to 902px wide, which is the number BOTH fillTo and the anchorPx seed read, so unclean it would have baked the log at about half its intended size and off centre. SIZING: world 81 with fillTo 0.86 is 70px of visible log = 7.6 m long. MEASURE THE TRUNK BY SCANLINE, NOT BY THE BBOX: the bbox is 3.32:1 only because the stub branch juts out sideways, and reading thickness off it gives 2.3 m — a redwood. The median scanline is 8.4u, so the trunk body is 0.91 m thick over 7.6 m, an 8.3:1 deadfall, which is what a fallen cypress actually looks like and needs no reroll. The same mistake in the other direction is what disqualified the deadhead art from this slot, so it is worth stating the method once: bbox aspect describes the FRAME the art needs, scanline width describes the OBJECT. REPLACED 2026-08-09 at Wes's direction with art measuring 1.82:1, and the slot's own warning above now applies to what it holds: this is the proportion it was written to refuse. Kept at world 81 so the log stays 7.6 m LONG — the thing that makes it 'the long one' rather than a second deadhead — which puts its thickness at 4.15 m against the outgoing art's 2.27 m. The trade is forced, not chosen: at 1.82:1 no world size buys both, and world 44 would restore the 2.26 m thickness only by halving the log to 4.1 m, at which point bayou-deadhead already exists at 3.0 m. The previous 3.33:1 master is in the round-1 backup if this wants reverting.

assets.subject: a short waterlogged log section adrift, seen from directly above — a stubby barked cylinder lying with its long axis running UP the frame, roughly three halves as long as it is wide. The upper half of the log is dry sun-bleached wood in pale tan and grey-brown, cut into chunky flat facets with the split ends of the grain reading as coarse angular chips, never fine texture. The lower half sits wet and near-black where it rides under the surface, the two halves meeting in a hard horizontal line — that line IS the waterline, not a shadow. One broken stub branch juts from the upper end at an angle, snapped off short with a splintered tip. The outline is irregular and knocked about, no end cut square
assets.note: A DEADHEAD: the waterlogged chunk that floats mostly under the surface and is the hazard you do NOT see coming, as against the three tree trunks, which are hazards you can see from a long way off. That is the design job it does for the venue, and it is why it is worth keeping as its own asset rather than forcing it into bayou-driftlog — see that slot's note. SIZING is what separates the two: this art measures 1.52:1, so world 32 with fillTo 0.86 is 27.5x18.1px visible = 3.0 m long x 2.0 m thick, a believable chunk. The same art at driftlog's world 70 would be 5 m thick. fillTo fits the LONG axis, so `world` means the log's length whatever padding the generation leaves. DELIVERED ART WAS ROTATED 90 DEGREES at ingest: the generation came back lying across the frame, and art-pipeline §3 puts the long axis up the frame so heading 0 means the same thing across the library. Rotation is lossless at 90 degrees, so this costs nothing and is not a reroll reason.

assets.subject: COMPOSED from bayou-lilypad — see that element for the art.
assets.note: COMPOSED by compose.py. Repeated instances of one object are generated once and scattered in code; diffusion models return symmetric arrangements when asked for N of something.

assets.subject: COMPOSED from bayou-cattail-tuft — see that element for the art.
assets.note: COMPOSED by compose.py. Repeated instances of one object are generated once and scattered in code; diffusion models return symmetric arrangements when asked for N of something. SEED 3, CHOSEN BY EYE FROM A SWEEP of 3/5/7/11/13/17/19/23 and not by arithmetic, exactly as the arctic-station note prescribes: the manifest's original seed 5 put all five tufts in a RING WITH A HOLLOW CENTRE, which is the rosette this tool exists to avoid — compose's inward bias (r = R*u^0.62) makes that unlikely, not impossible, and minGap 0.58 against spread 0.5 is tight enough for five tufts that a ring is one of the few packings that satisfies it. Measured as the share of the group's alpha falling inside the middle third of its own radius, seed 5 scores 36% and seed 3 scores 81%; 11, 19 and 23 are also ringed (44-53%), 7 and 13 are acceptable (72%, 62%). Seed 3 reads as an irregular clump of reeds with no hole. If the count or minGap ever change, RE-SWEEP — the good seed is a property of those numbers, not of the art.

assets.subject: alligator cruising just under the surface — armored ridged back and tail in olive, snout breaking the water, faint wake V behind, naturalistic not cartoon-eyed
assets.note: The venue is named for this animal, so it is sized as the specimen the name implies rather than the average one: world 70 with fillTo 0.86 is 60px = 6.5 m, against a 4.6 m record for a wild American alligator and a 6.1 m player hull. A DELIBERATE EXAGGERATION at about 1.4x record, recorded here as the scale block asks. At a truthful 4 m it would draw 37px and read as a lizard rather than the thing the venue is named after. AMBIENT/HAZARD SEPARATION CHECKED, because this lands at the same size and aspect as bayou-driftlog (3.48:1 against 3.23:1, both about 70u long) and role ambient promises it can never be mistaken for a hazard: in greyscale the two are unmistakable — a smooth tapered body with a head, four leg bumps and a REGULAR SCUTE GRID against a ragged asymmetric trunk with a stub branch. Different silhouette families, not different colour, which is the form the rule actually takes. COLOUR IS OFF-SPEC and left alone: the slot asks for olive and the hide came back 99% saturated at hue 87deg, where the venue water sits at 49% and a real gator is a dark desaturated olive-grey. It reads well and it is decoration, so it ships; a desaturation pass is a small change if it ever looks too acid next to the weed.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE WADING BIRD, shot straight down from well above it onto shallow water, the way a survey frames a single animal. You are looking at the BIRD'S BACK. WHAT YOU MUST NOT SEE, because this is the way this subject fails: no face, no profile, no eye looking out of the picture, and no side of the head or neck. From straight overhead a heron's head is THE BACK OF A SKULL — a small rounded cap — and the beak is a short spike FORESHORTENED almost to nothing, pointing away from the body and lying flat on the water. If the beak reads as a long blade across the frame, or an eye is visible, the camera was at the side and the image is wrong however beautiful it is. A GREAT BLUE HERON STANDING IN THE SHALLOWS. The shape from above is a smooth slate-blue OVAL of folded wings and back filling most of the frame, drawn in a few chunky flat facets of slate, dusty blue-grey and a paler grey along the folded wing edges — broad feather GROUPS, never individual feathers, and no soft gradients anywhere. Behind it the closed tail narrows to a short blunt wedge. THE NECK IS THE ONE THING THAT MAKES IT A HERON at a glance, so it is drawn folded into a tight flat S lying ON TOP of the shoulders, reading from above as a pale grey-white coil against the slate back — the single lightest shape in the sprite, and the thing to protect if anything has to be simplified. Two thin dark legs trail down into the water below the body as simple straight lines with a small angled foot each, and directly beneath the bird a soft dark SHADOW lies on the shallow bottom, offset slightly from the body so the bird reads as standing above it. A little dark crest plume trails back off the rear of the head cap.
assets.note: PROMPT REWRITTEN 2026-08-09 from a one-line stub, after a delivery came back as a beautiful SIDE PORTRAIT — full profile, visible eye, beak lying at full length across the frame — which is the failure the tree slots were rewritten to prevent and which nothing downstream can fix. The rewrite copies what worked there: lead with the drone framing, then spend a whole clause on WHAT MUST NOT APPEAR, naming the face and the un-foreshortened beak as the specific tell. THIS IS THE HARDEST SUBJECT IN THE VENUE and the reason is geometric: everything that says 'heron' to a person — the long neck, the long legs, the dagger beak — is vertical, and a plan view foreshortens all three to nothing. What survives is a grey oval. So the subject leans the identity onto the ONE feature that stays legible from above, the folded S of the neck lying on the shoulders as a pale coil, and states outright that it is the thing to protect. SIZING raised from 40 to 44, with fillTo 0.86 giving 38px of bird = 4.1 m across the folded wings, against a real great blue heron's ~1.8 m wingspan and a much smaller standing footprint. That is a deliberate exaggeration of roughly 2x, recorded as the scale block asks, and it is the same argument the penguins made: a truthful overhead footprint here is about 10px and cannot carry a silhouette. AMBIENT, so it must never read as a hazard: the venue's small dark hazards (cypress knees 26u, deadhead 32u) are dark lumpy masses, and this is a pale smooth oval with a light coil on it. Check that separation on the contact sheet in greyscale before accepting.

assets.subject: stilt fishing shack from above — rust corrugated roof with a simple ridge line, small dock finger reaching into the water, one moored skiff, weathered board walkway
assets.note: REGENERATED 2026-08-09, replacing a first delivery that was a wide 3/4-view scene; every number here is from the new art and the old note's reasoning no longer applies. WHAT CHANGED, and all three were real defects: it now arrives SQUARE at 1024 (was 1536x1024, needing a pad); it is a TRUE PLAN VIEW (the first was oblique — pilings showing their sides, the hut showing two walls — which mattered more than it first seemed, because the race camera lerps its rotation to the player's heading, so the world turns under the viewer and a non-orthographic sprite is seen at every angle rather than the one it was placed at); and it is COMPACT, a hut with two short dock arms and a moored skiff instead of a hut trailing a long boardwalk. SIZING, calibrated the same way on the moored skiff — the one object in the picture the game already has a length for: world 130 with fillTo 0.86 puts the skiff at 6.1 m against the player's 6.1 m hull, and the whole structure at 12.2 x 7.8 m. That lands back on this slot's ORIGINAL world 130, which the first delivery could not honour at any size. PREP was a halo strip only: the file ships with real alpha, but a glow was retained in it as a partial band brighter than the art itself (luma 104.5 against the core's 94.2), and left in it would have set the bbox 925px wide instead of 851 — the number fillTo and the anchorPx seed both read. Cut by dilating the alpha core 3px rather than thresholding, so the keyline survives. REGENERATED AGAIN 2026-08-09 and RESIZED with it. The new art is a hut beside a long walkway rather than a compact hut with two short arms, so the structure occupies a smaller share of the frame and the slot's own calibration had to be re-run: the moored skiff spans 0.346 of the content, which at world 130 would have drawn it 4.2 m against the player's 6.1 m hull — two thirds of a competitor, beside a fleet it shares the water with. World 189 puts the skiff back on 6.1 m and the whole hut-and-walkway complex at 17.7 m. The number moved because the SUBJECT changed, not because the ruler did.

assets.subject: A SMALL STILT CRAWFISH CAMP standing in shallow bayou water, seen from straight overhead. FROM THIS HEIGHT A STILT SHACK IS ALMOST ENTIRELY ROOF, and that is the test of the camera: you see the roof PLANES and the ridge between them, and you never see a WALL. Not one wall, not a corner, not two sides of the hut meeting — if any wall is visible the camera has tilted. The pilings show only as small dark circles standing in the water around the deck, each one a post seen end-on down its length, never a leaning stick with its side showing. THE BUILDING IS L-SHAPED IN PLAN: a one-room hut with a lower lean-to running off one side, so the footprint makes a clear L rather than a plain rectangle. Both roofs are patched TAR-PAPER in weathered moss-green, streaked and blotched where the damp sits, with a few silvered bare-timber patches and one small rust-brown repair sheet — dark and mossy overall, and never the bright rust-orange corrugated iron of the bigger shack nearby. A plain ridge line runs down each roof and the sheets read as broad flat bands, not fine corrugation. Around two sides of the hut, a narrow open DECK of weathered grey boards, the planking running lengthways, cluttered with a low stack of square wire crawfish traps, a coiled line and an upturned bucket. A short covered BOAT SLIP is cut into the deck on the open side — a roofed notch with dark water showing beneath it. Tied alongside the deck, ONE PIROGUE: a slim flat-bottomed plank skiff in plain weathered wood, empty, lying parallel to the deck edge. No water beyond the immediate pilings and slip, no bank, no cast shadow, no people
assets.note: SECOND SHACK, the humble one — bayou-shack is the rust-roofed camp, this is the mossy L-shaped crawfish camp. DISTINGUISHABLE AT A GLANCE per the arctic-orca-b precedent, and the axis is chosen deliberately: from overhead a stilt shack is nearly all roof, so two shacks that differ only below the eaves are two identical shacks. This differs on roof colour (mossy tar-paper vs rust corrugated), plan shape (L with a lean-to vs plain ridged rectangle) and size (96 vs 130). SIZED BY THE VENUE'S RULER, the same method bayou-shack's note records: it calibrated on a moored skiff at 6.1 m against the player's 6.1 m hull, which fixes the venue at 9.2 units per metre. This one carries a pirogue for the same job — bayou-pirogue is world 62, the same ~6.1 m boat — and world 96 with fillTo 0.86 gives a longest span of 82.6u = 9.0 m against the first shack's 12.2 m. A smaller camp, not a rescaled one. THE ORTHOGRAPHIC FAILURE THIS SLOT ALREADY SUFFERED IS NAMED IN THE SUBJECT: bayou-shack's first delivery came back oblique, with pilings showing their sides and the hut showing two walls, and had to be regenerated. That matters more here than for most props because the race camera lerps its rotation to the player's heading, so the world turns under the viewer and a non-orthographic sprite is seen from every angle rather than the one it was placed at. Hence 'you never see a WALL' as the stated test. REGISTER THE KIND WHEN THE ART LANDS, not before — contactR should be measured off the delivered sprite the way the tree radii were, rather than scaled from bayou-shack's 36. DELIVERED 2026-08-09 and RESIZED on the same ruler: the pirogue spans 0.490 of the content, so world 96 would have drawn it 4.4 m instead of 6.1 m. World 133 fixes the boat and puts the camp at 12.4 m — still the smaller of the two shacks (17.7 m), so the size distinction the slot was written around survives, just at different numbers than specced.

assets.subject: weathered timber dock seen from directly above. THE SILHOUETTE IS A LONG NARROW RECTANGLE RUNNING UP THE FRAME, about four times as long as it is wide: this subject is genuinely oblong, so the usual as-tall-as-it-is-wide test does not apply to it — but it must be TALLER than it is wide and never wider than tall, because that is still the tell that the camera was tipped. A straight plank walkway runs UP the frame from a wider shore platform at the bottom to a squared-off open end at the top. The deck is a run of separate grey-brown boards in two flat tones, several boards clearly paler or darker than their neighbours and one or two missing so the deck line breaks. Round piling heads stud both edges as small dark discs, six to eight of them, unevenly spaced and a few sitting slightly proud of the line so the edge never reads as machined. A single cleat and a loose coil of rope lie near the open end. The whole run is a little out of true, its outer third bending a few degrees off the walkway's axis, and each piling head carries a dark wet tide band around it
assets.note: THE DOCK ALONE, which is what separates it from bayou-shack: the shack is a whole homestead that happens to own a small dock finger, so it can only be placed once per bank before it reads as a copy of itself. This is the piece a designer repeats — a landing on a levee, a pair facing each other across a channel, a berth with bayou-pirogue moored alongside. No boat is drawn on it for exactly that reason; the pirogue is its own prop and can be placed against this one. ROLE HAZARD, NOT LANDMARK, and the role contract is what decides it: a landmark 'never reads as an obstacle in the water', and a dock reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one. It wants contact hard when its PROP_KIND is registered, overridable to none on any single placement the way every other prop trait is. SIZING: world 108 with fillTo 0.86 is 93px of visible deck = 10.1 m at 9.2 px/m, 1.7x the racing hull — long enough to pinch a lane, short enough that sailing past it is a decision rather than a wall. fillTo is not optional on an oblong subject: it fits the LONG axis to 86% of the frame, so `world` means the dock's length however much padding the generation leaves around it, and 0.86 rather than 0.88 clears the profile's 6% safeMargin tripwire instead of landing on it (the arctic-station precedent). At world 108 the default 4x bake is nowhere near the master/bake = 256 upscale ceiling. THE SUBJECT OVERRIDES THE CLASS'S SQUARE-SILHOUETTE TEST, deliberately: the ortho clause asks for a silhouette as tall as it is wide, which is the anti-tilt test for a roughly round subject and simply false for a pier. The cove-cargo-ship answer is the one used here — state the true aspect ratio loudly in the subject, and keep the half of the test that still bites (taller than wide, never wider than tall). Orientation per art-pipeline §3: the OPEN WATER END is the top of the frame, so a placement's heading points the deck out from the bank. ANCHOR: art-pipeline §3 names the L-shaped dock as the case the alpha-bbox centre gets wrong, and an earlier draft of this note told you to pull anchorPx toward the shore platform so the prop would drop ON the bank. THAT DOES NOTHING FOR A PROP. anchorPx is read by contact.py (the crosshair) and ingest.py (seeding) and by nothing in js/ at all: drawProps paints every prop centred on its own frame, and compile centres the contact circle on the same point. So the placement point IS the frame centre whatever this field says. Position a dock by eye with its middle where you want the middle, and treat anchorPx here as a pipeline record only.

assets.subject: flat-bottomed pirogue skiff from directly above — plain wooden hull, no sail and no mast, two thwarts and a push pole lying inside, unmistakably not a racing sailboat
assets.note: TRAFFIC, so the binding contract is never-confusable-with-a-competitor (art-pipeline 2, extending race-view 10.2 off the starting grid), and it was tested against a real racing hull rather than assumed. COLOUR CANNOT CARRY IT: 10 of the 96 competitor hull colours in the roster are golden or tan (#FFE600, #FFD84D, #FFEB3B and friends), so a bare-wood boat shares its hue with about a tenth of the fleet. The separation is entirely in the silhouette and it is decisive — the pirogue is a 3.9:1 double-ender, pointed at BOTH ends, narrow, and OPEN, showing thwarts and a pole across bare floorboards; a racing hull is a 1.8:1 teardrop with a blunt stern, a filled deck and a cockpit, and it is carrying a sail besides. In greyscale at race scale the two are not in the same family. SIZING: world 62 with fillTo 0.86 is 53px = 5.8 m long and 1.5 m in the beam, which is a real pirogue and is deliberately NOT the 6.1 m of the player hull.

assets.subject: A LOUISIANA AIRBOAT — a flat-bottomed swamp boat driven by a big caged fan — seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating level, bow pointing to the TOP of the frame. COMPLETELY FLAT 2D VECTOR-STYLE RENDERING, and this is the thing to get right: every shape is a flat fill seen square from its top, no bevelled edges, no isometric walls on the seat or the engine, no 3D depth anywhere, and the deck is one unbroken flat tone. TRUE PLAN VIEW AT BOTH ENDS: only top surfaces show — no hull side, no curved bow face, no perspective step anywhere. THE PROPORTION IS THE IDENTITY: BROAD, BLUNT AND SLAB-SIDED, about twice as long as it is wide, with a squared-off transom at the stern and a wide shallow bow that is rounded but never pointed. It must read as a raft with a machine on it, never as a hull with a bow. THE FAN IS THE SIGNATURE and it sits at the STERN, at the BOTTOM of the frame: a large upright CIRCULAR GUARD CAGE seen from above as a bold ring roughly a third of the boat's length across, with a small dark hub at its centre, a few straight guard bars crossing the ring, and two or three broad propeller blades reading as flat shapes behind the bars. The ring is the single highest-contrast element in the sprite. Forward of the fan sits an ELEVATED PILOT SEAT, drawn from above as a small squared platform with a headrest; ahead of that, one plain bench across the open deck. The hull is bare weathered aluminium in two flat grey tones with a single faded painted stripe along the gunwale, and a few scuffs. NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO RIGGING, NO SPINNAKER anywhere — this is a motorboat and must be unmistakable from a racing sailboat at a glance.
assets.note: Gatorgrass Bayou's second traffic vessel, and the SILHOUETTE SPACE IS DIVIDED between the two on purpose, per the cove-tugboat precedent where the tug owns short-and-beamy so the cargo ships cannot read as toys. Here bayou-pirogue owns NARROW, DOUBLE-ENDED AND OPEN — 3.9:1, pointed at both ends, showing its thwarts — and the airboat owns BROAD, BLUNT AND MACHINED at about 2:1 with a hard circular fan cage at one end. Nothing else in the venue is a big ring on a rectangle, so this reads at a glance against the pirogue, against the racing fleet, and against the round hazards (knees, deadhead) which are lumps rather than rings. SIZING: world 56 with fillTo 0.86 is 48px = 5.2 m long by about 2.6 m in the beam, a real 16-18ft airboat, and deliberately shorter than the 6.1 m player hull. The fan cage lands near 16px across, which is the floor for a ring to still read as a ring — do not shrink this asset without checking that first. allowSymmetry is TRUE, which is rare here and is the cypress-trunk argument: a fan guard genuinely radiates, and the arrangement negatives would fight the one feature the sprite is built around. The risk they normally guard against does not apply, because the BOAT is strongly asymmetric — the fan sits at one end of an oblong hull, so nothing is going to come back a mandala. TRAFFIC, not hazard: the contract is never-confusable-with-a-competitor, which is why the subject spends a clause banning sails outright rather than trusting the hull shape alone. DELIVERED 2026-08-09, chosen from three candidates on two measured grounds. ORIENTATION: this one arrived with the fan at the STERN (68% down the hull) where the other two put it at the bow (33-35%) and would each have needed a 180-degree rotate — lossless, so not disqualifying, but a free win. DECK FLATNESS decided the rest: high-frequency energy across the mid-deck measures 14.9 here against 19.1 and 21.2, and cove-tugboat names mottling as the specific way a traffic vessel goes wrong (its subject demands one unbroken flat deck tone with no mottling and no pixel texture). A CLAIM CHECKED AND WITHDRAWN, recorded so nobody re-argues it: the other two LOOK as though their fan cages are drawn in perspective, and they are not — measuring the cage mass, all three come back round (w/h 1.10, 0.88, 0.91), so that read was an artefact of interior shading rather than a fault in the silhouette. Delivered 22x48px visible = 2.4 x 5.2 m, fan cage about 16px across, which was the stated floor for a ring to still read as a ring.

assets.subject: GREEN day beacon on a single piling seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD — the sawn top of a weathered timber pile fills the frame as a rough circle of end-grain, growth rings and radial checking cracks in two flat tones of grey-brown, and a single flat rectangular DAYBOARD lies across it, its long axis horizontal, drawn as a clean hard-edged bar with a brighter top face and a darker lower face so it reads as a solid board rather than a painted stripe. The board overhangs the pile at both ends. A dark wet band rings the pile where it meets the water. The board is a strong mid signal green, matched to buoy-channel-green's #268B34 — never teal, never lime, never olive.
assets.note: The bayou's fixed lateral mark, and the FIXED half of the game's nav vocabulary: buoy-channel-red/green are floating drums with a white band and a lantern, this is a board bolted to a pile that does not move. Two different objects doing the same job, and a player can tell them apart from the silhouette alone. PAIRED with bayou-daybeacon-red — same art, board colour only, which follows the precedent buoy-channel-green already sets ('the IDENTICAL buoy to the red one in every respect except colour'). REAL-WORLD BUOYAGE WOULD MAKE THE RED ONE A TRIANGLE (IALA-B pairs a green square with a red triangle) and this pair is two rectangles; recorded as a known divergence rather than fixed, because the game's own shipped lateral pair already differentiates on colour alone and one venue is the wrong place to break that. SIZE IS A DELIBERATE EXAGGERATION, per the scale block's instruction to record them: world 34 with fillTo 0.86 makes the board 3.0 m and the pile 2.25 m across, where a real daymark is well under a metre. At true scale this asset would be 3px. The floating buoys take the same liberty at world 28.

assets.subject: SEVEN EMPEROR penguins crowded together on ice, seen from directly overhead. COMPOSITION IS THE HARD PART — read this first: the group must look like real animals standing around at random, photographed from a drone. Arrange them IRREGULARLY and ASYMMETRICALLY. Absolutely NOT in a circle, ring, radial pattern, rosette, mandala or snowflake, and NOT evenly spaced. The centre of the group must be its DENSEST part, never an empty hole. Some birds should stand closer together than others, a couple should slightly overlap or touch, one or two should sit a little apart from the main mass, and the whole cluster should be lopsided rather than balanced. Headings should be scattered and unrelated to each bird's position — not all turned inward, not all turned outward. Keep the group compact so it fills a roughly circular-but-lumpy footprint. EACH BIRD: a compact teardrop seen from above — a glossy black back and head filling most of the shape, a short beak pointing outward, two dark flippers held slightly away from the body, a sliver of white breast at the front edge, and a vivid orange-yellow ear-and-neck flash. Seven warm yellow flecks scattered through a dark irregular mass is what identifies this species at distance, so keep every flash legible and larger than life. Keep visible dark gaps between most neighbours so the group reads as several distinct animals. Each bird is only about 12 pixels at final size, so give each a clean silhouette, its yellow flash, and nothing else. No ice, no ground, no shadow
assets.note: COMPOSED by compose.py from arctic-penguin-emperor. Two generated huddles came back as rosettes; a PRNG does irregular scatter that a diffusion model will not. Upsized ~50% over strict scale: measured, birds do not resolve below ~70px for a seven-bird group.

assets.subject: a Weddell seal hauled out and resting, seen from directly overhead — a plump elongated torpedo body tapering to paired rear flippers, a small distinctly rounded head set off from the shoulders, and two short fore-flippers held out from the sides. Mottled silver-grey and charcoal in flat hard-edged facets, with a paler belly tone showing along the flanks. CRITICAL: it must read unmistakably as a living animal and never as a rock or a chunk of ice — the head, the neck taper and the fore-flippers are what separate it from a boulder, so keep all three clearly articulated and never let the outline collapse into a plain oval. Naturalistically proportioned, never a cartoon-eyed mascot. No ice, no ground, no shadow

assets.subject: FOUR ADELIE penguins walking in single file on ice, seen from directly overhead. DIRECTION IS CRITICAL: the line of travel runs VERTICALLY up the frame — the last bird near the bottom edge, the leader near the top edge, the others evenly between them on a gently curving track that never departs far from vertical. Every bird faces ALONG the line, i.e. toward the TOP of the frame. Do NOT run the line diagonally or across the frame; the engine rotates this sprite and treats straight up as the direction of travel. VIEWPOINT: from directly above you see the back of each bird's head and its back — no eyes, no face, no chest, with the beak foreshortened and pointing away up the frame. EACH BIRD: a compact teardrop — glossy black back and head filling most of the shape, dark flippers held slightly away from the body, a sliver of white breast at the leading edge only. SPECIES SIGNATURE: Adelies are the PLAIN penguin — solid black head with no yellow anywhere, just a fine white eye ring and a small dull pinkish beak. The absence of warm colour is the identifier; do not add any. Keep spacing close to even but not mechanical, with one bird lagging slightly, and keep every bird clearly separated. Each bird is only about 12 pixels at final size. No ice, no ground, no shadow
assets.note: COMPOSED. Vertical track, so sprite-up is the direction of travel. Upsized ~50% over strict scale: measured, birds do not resolve below ~70px for a seven-bird group.
