assets.subject: a temperate tidal estuary at low water, aerial-oblique, horizon just below the top quarter. THE SAND IS THE DOMINANT COLOR: broad exposed sandbars filling roughly half the picture in confident warm amber-gold, built from bold chunky faceted planes, dry crowns bright and sunlit, wet margins a much darker ochre where the tide has just left, crisp scalloped edges, bold branching drain-runnels cut into them. ONE sinuous channel of DEEP SATURATED SLATE-BLUE water — a rich blue-grey with real blue in it, never neutral grey — winds from the plain empty foreground back toward a distant sea, and it is the eye-path: big angular ripple planes in two clear tones, carrying bright white current streaks and eddy curls that show which way the water is running. A line of leaning rust-red withy markers, bundled sticks, steps irregularly along the channel edge into the distance. The focal element is a small loose group of FOUR SPOON-BILLED SANDPIPERS on the nearest bar — plump little shorebirds with the distinctive flat spatulate spoon-shaped bill tip, warm brown backs and white bellies, bold simplified two-tone shapes rather than feather-by-feather naturalism, one with wings raised, the others feeding head-down. SKY WITH REAL VARIETY: several big rounded blob-stack cumulus of clearly DIFFERENT sizes, each with a single flat shade tone underneath, at different heights, mixed with a few thin horizontal streak clouds — not a uniform band of identical wisps. Green is limited to one thin dark shore line at the horizon and nowhere else. STRICTLY EXCLUDE: neutral grey or desaturated water; muted, washed-out or pastel color; naturalistic wildlife-illustration rendering; long down-curved curlew bills; turquoise or tropical water; flamingos or any pink bird; otters or any mammal; broad green marsh grass; evenly repeated identical clouds; any grass, bird or object in the lower fifth of the frame
assets.note: Regen 4. Pass 1 drifted tropical (marsh/flamingos/otter). Pass 2 specced pewter-pastel, measured 0.185 sat vs set 0.66-0.94 and read unfinished. Pass 3 gold-dominant fixed that but water stayed neutral grey (0.507). Pass 4 cut to 4 large birds; with blue water it reaches 0.693 = in range. This pass: deeper slate blue, varied cumulus, and the spoon-billed sandpipers PINNED BY NAME so they survive regeneration (Wes liked them; the spatulate bill is the charm).

assets.subject: ONE wandering albatross in flight, soaring, seen from directly overhead — enormous slender wings held straight out and locked, not flapping, spanning nearly the full width of the frame and giving the bird a long thin CROSS silhouette unlike anything else. Body and back are white, the upperwing surfaces darken toward the trailing edge and finish in clean black wingtips, and the short wedge tail trails behind. The heavy pale hooked bill leads, pointing to the TOP of the frame. Wings are narrow and stiff with a subtle backward sweep, never broad or rounded. Crisp flat faceted shading, a clean dark contour no heavier than the rest of the set, no glossy speculars, no motion blur. Exactly one bird, alone. No water, no ground, NO SHADOW — the engine draws the shadow that makes it read as airborne
assets.note: AIR-LAYER PROP. Needs two engine pieces that do not exist yet: a draw pass above the boats, and a displaced shadow on the water. The shadow IS the altitude cue — without it a bird seen from directly overhead reads as floating, not flying. `world` folds in three things: true wingspan at 9.2px/m, the ~1.5x recognition exaggeration, and an altitude magnification (a bird at height is closer to the camera, so it is genuinely larger — not a cheat). Sprite carries NO shadow. Solitary by nature, so one bird alone is correct rather than a compromise.

assets.subject: ONE snow petrel in flight, seen from directly overhead, centred and filling the frame, flying toward the TOP. Wings spread and slightly swept back in a shallow M, short wedge tail behind, small head leading. The snow petrel is UNIFORMLY WHITE — body, back, and both wings from shoulder to wingtip, with no dark wingtips, no dark trailing edge and no grey banding. Think of a white dove rather than a gull or an albatross. The only non-white parts are a small black bill and a black eye. Shade the white with the faintest cool grey planes only, just enough to show the wing surfaces turning, and give it a clean thin dark contour so the shape still separates when it passes over pale ice. Crisp flat faceted shading, no glossy speculars, no motion blur. Exactly one bird, alone. No water, no ground, NO SHADOW
assets.note: Element for arctic-snow-petrel-flock. First attempt came back with navy wingtips and trailing edges — 38% dark body, statistically the same bird as the albatross. Root cause was the prompt's own palette clause, which told every arctic prop to commit to steel navy; that clause is now context-only for props. Its unbroken whiteness is why this asset exists: the only bright object in the darkest venue.

assets.subject: COMPOSED from arctic-snow-petrel — see that element for the art.
assets.note: AIR-LAYER PROP. Needs two engine pieces that do not exist yet: a draw pass above the boats, and a displaced shadow on the water. The shadow IS the altitude cue — without it a bird seen from directly overhead reads as floating, not flying. `world` folds in three things: true wingspan at 9.2px/m, the ~1.5x recognition exaggeration, and an altitude magnification (a bird at height is closer to the camera, so it is genuinely larger — not a cheat). Sprite carries NO shadow. Flocks, so the birds share a rough heading — hence the narrow rotate range, unlike a standing huddle.

assets.subject: ONE polar research hut, alone, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD — a prefab field-station module standing on short skids, so nearly all of what shows is its ROOF. A plain rectangular footprint about half again as long as it is wide, with a shallow gabled roof and one crisp RIDGE LINE running the full length of the long axis, straight up the frame. The ridge splits the roof into two flat planes of clearly different lightness — that hard two-tone split is what makes it read as a solid volume instead of a flat rectangle, so it must be unmistakable. CRITICAL: image models want to draw a building in three-quarter view. There must be NO visible wall face, NO end elevation, NO perspective and NO vanishing point — the roof is a flat rectangle seen square-on, exactly as a building looks in a satellite photograph. COLOUR: painted high-visibility international orange-red, warm and saturated across the whole roof — the deliberate safety colour field huts are painted so they can be found in a whiteout, and the one thing that separates a hut from the rock and ice it sits on. Detail is limited to what survives at 50px: a dark doorway with a small entry step at one gable end, one short dark stove pipe offset to one side of the ridge, and a narrow darker trim band along each eave. Corners are square and crisp and the outline is a clean hard-edged rectangle, never a soft or rounded blob. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set. No snow, no drift, no ground, no ice, no rock, no cast shadow, no antenna mast, no guy wires, no flag, no people, no vehicles
assets.note: ELEMENT for arctic-station. elementFill 0.64 rather than the profile's 0.88: compose.py rotates with expand=False, so an oblong only survives rotation if it fits inside its own inscribed circle. At 3:2 and 0.88 fill the half-diagonal is 0.53 of the frame and the corners are clipped past ~15deg — unmissable on a building. At 0.64 it is 0.385 and the hut rotates freely at any angle. The group's `scale` range is raised to compensate.

assets.subject: COMPOSED from arctic-hut — see that element for the art.
assets.note: COMPOSED by compose.py — three huts of one design, not three generations. Glacier Sound's first landmark, the arctic counterpart to bayou-shack. TUNED against a 3:2 stand-in rectangle, not guessed: the first numbers (spread 0.46 / minGap 0.80) failed to place all three huts on half of the seeds tried, because scatter() is rejection sampling biased INWARD (r = R*u^0.62) — an arrangement existing geometrically is not the same as the sampler finding it. spread 0.62 / minGap 0.72 fits 3/3 on 40/40 seeds. fillTo 0.86 because frame fill still swings 0.73-1.09 across seeds, which would make `world` mean a different on-screen size per seed; normalizing makes world 170 honest and leaves the seed controlling layout only. 0.86 rather than 0.88 clears the profile's 6% safeMargin tripwire instead of landing exactly on it. Seed 7 chosen by eye from six candidates: three separate buildings in an irregular triangle, where 4 and 31 clump a pair together and 19 and 23 leave a hollow centre. SIZING (measured after ingest, not predicted): fillTo rescales the composition by 0.86/0.65 = 1.32x, so huts land 49-69px on the long axis = 5.3-7.5m at 9.2px/m. That is Jamesway/Weatherhaven module size and deliberately LARGER than the 56px boat — a hut you can live in outsizes a 20ft sportboat. An earlier estimate here said 3.7-6.5m; it omitted the fillTo upscale. `rotate` is deliberately narrow (+/-40deg): station modules sit broadly aligned into the wind, fully random angles read as debris rather than a camp, and zero rotation reads as a copy-paste stamp.

assets.subject: Wind-packed snow lying over sea ice, seen from straight overhead in flat overcast light — a quiet near-white field worked over by wind. Across it run short broken sastrugi: shallow ridges of hard scoured snow, each only a fraction of the frame long, lying in loosely the same direction but at slightly varying angles, never lining up with the edges of the picture. Their crests take the palest white and the scoured troughs settle to a cool blue-grey. Between them sit low drift lobes with soft feathered lips, a scatter of shallow wind-scallops, and a few faint healed cracks reading as thin blue-grey hairlines that fade out rather than running across the frame. Everything is drawn in clean faceted planes with crisp edges — no airbrushed gradients, no fine speckle, no photographic snow grain. The whole image stays inside a tight range from near-white to pale blue-grey. No dark shadow, no exposed blue glacier ice, no rock, no meltwater, no crevasse, no footprints or animal tracks
assets.note: First texture-class asset. tileWorld 512 is measured against this venue, not guessed: the camera is 1:1 and the viewport runs ~1280x800 world units, so a 512 tile repeats ~2.5 x 1.6 per screen — small enough that Glacier Sound's 3000-5000 unit ice masses stop being one flat fill, large enough that the repeat is not countable at a glance. The 1024 master is a 2x supersample of that, so the 4px legibility floor lands at 8px in the master. WIRED: drawIslands() fills fixed `ice`-style land with it as a world-anchored canvas pattern (getSnowPattern in script.js), so it stays nailed to the ice as the camera moves. It ships at SNOW_TEXTURE_ALPHA 0.3 over the flat ISLAND_STYLES.ice body — at full strength it read as a chopped, busy surface that competed with the floes, and 0.5 was still louder than wanted. The blend is baked into the pattern source, so it still costs one fill; measured on screen, land contrast is 0.30x the master's (std 3.1 vs 10.2, range 228-243 vs 189-255). Floes and bergs deliberately keep their baked faceted sprite — they spin, and a world-anchored pattern would slide across a turning floe. Arctic is the only venue authoring `ice` shapes, so nothing else changed. Cost measured against the flat fill it replaced: 0.36 ms/frame in a real racing frame, 1.75 ms/frame with the camera buried in the biggest ice mass.

assets.subject: Bare wind-scoured granite seen from straight overhead in flat overcast light — cold blue-grey rock, hard and dry. It is broken into angular blocks by a network of joints and fractures: straight-edged cracks meeting at blunt angles, dividing the surface into irregular flat plates of slightly different tone, the way frost-shattered rock splits along its grain. A few of the plates are tilted enough to catch a shade lighter or darker than their neighbours, so the rock reads as broken relief rather than a painted slab. Scattered through it are patches of coarser rubble and a scatter of loose angular chips caught in the wider cracks, plus a faint mottling of paler feldspar and darker mineral grain in the stone itself — a suggestion of granite's speckle, drawn as shaped marks, never as fine noise or photographic grit. The whole image holds a narrow range of cold greys around a mid-dark value, with no black voids and no bright highlights. No snow, no frost, no ice, no meltwater, no lichen, no moss, no vegetation, no sand, no soil, no warm brown or orange rock
assets.note: Second texture-class asset, and the one that fixed the class's venue clause: textures used to COMMIT to the venue's dominant hue, which was right for arctic-snow only by coincidence and would have asked for blue rock here. NO SNOW ON IT, deliberately — arctic granite realistically drifts over, but the two textures then converge and rock stops being distinguishable from ice at a glance. `granite` is hard (grounds you) and `ice` is soft (costs speed), so they are different things to the player and must stay different to the eye. tileWorld 256 rather than snow's 512: the three granite shapes are r 90-382, so a 512 tile would show barely one repeat on the largest, and the smaller tile buys 4x supersample from the 1024 master for joint cracks that a 2x would smear. Repetition is a non-issue at these sizes. WIRED at alpha 0.3 through LAND_TEXTURES in script.js (the snow-specific getSnowPattern generalized to getLandPattern(ctx, style, base), keyed style -> {src, tile, alpha}). Until this landed the shapes were FLAT SLABS: bakeIslandSprite's granite facet fan is dead code for authored venues, because compileVenueDoc marks every fixed shape fromMask and that path only fills and strokes. ⚠️ THE BLEND LIGHTENS THE ROCK — the master's mean luma is 124 against the flat body's 84, so 0.3 lands the rock at 94.6 (measured), a 13% lift. Snow had no such shift because its master mean (239) already matched the ice body. If the rock should hold its value, the fix is to normalize the tile's mean to the base before compositing, not to drop the alpha. All three sit within ~400 units of the round-1 mark, so they are passed close aboard every lap.

assets.subject: Dry beach sand seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the pale warm tan of an open ocean-facing beach. AT THIS HEIGHT SAND IS ALMOST FEATURELESS, and that is the subject: a quiet, near-uniform field whose only structure is broad, soft, irregular patches of very slightly different tone, each blending into its neighbours with no hard edge, the way dampness and grain size drift across an open beach. NO RIPPLES OF ANY KIND. There are no crests, no troughs, no ridges, no parallel lines, no repeating waves in the sand and no direction the eye can follow — nothing in the frame lines up with anything else, and no spacing repeats. Scattered thinly through it, the only hard marks in the frame: a few small pale shell fragments and tiny stone chips, each drawn as a small shaped mark, never as fine speckle or photographic grain. The whole image holds a very narrow warm range from #cdb79f to #ecd6b7 around a mean of #e1c6a7 — a greyed, slightly brown tan, never a bright buttery yellow and never white. No water, no foam, no wave, no wet sand, no waterline, no shoreline, no vegetation, no beach grass, no seaweed, no driftwood, no dune, no dune shadow, no rocks larger than a chip, no cast shadows, no footprints, no tracks, no trails, no raked or combed pattern, no wind ripple, no sand ripple, no ridged or corrugated surface
assets.note: Third texture-class asset — Lighthouse Cove's shoreline, wired to the `tropical` LOOK rather than to the bay, so bay (10 isles), lake (4) and lagoon (2) all share it. Ships at tileWorld 128, alpha 0.7, over an ISLAND_STYLES.tropical body of #ddc39a. V2, AND THE V1 IT REPLACES IS THE WHOLE LESSON. v1 asked for wind ripples 'lying in loosely the same direction' — what a beach looks like from head height, not from the height this game is drawn at. Measured against aerial reference photography resampled to the game's own scale, the gap was never amplitude (v1 contrast 6.31 against a reference band of 2.95-11.92) but STRUCTURE: v1 carried one dominant crest direction (anisotropy 0.656) and a strong preferred wavelength (periodicity 5.77); real aerial sand has neither (0.15-0.48, 1.65-2.16). ⚠️ RETILING CANNOT FIX A PERIODICITY PROBLEM — the finding worth carrying to the next texture. Shrinking v1's tile 512 -> 90 moved periodicity 5.44 -> 6.70, i.e. not at all: a smaller tile makes a ripple smaller, never rarer. Only redrawing fixed it. Ask what structure the material has AT THE CAMERA'S ALTITUDE before writing the subject; when the honest answer is 'almost none', the texture's job is broad tonal drift, not a pattern. V2 MEASURED IN GAME: anisotropy 0.656 -> 0.177 (matches the most isotropic reference, 0.149) — the directional ripples are gone. Periodicity 5.77 -> 4.23, and the residual is NOT a defect: the peak sits at 21px on screen = 2.3m, which is the mottle's own blob size, not a tile harmonic (128/64/43px) and not a ripple. Real sand photographs score low here because their texture is scale-free down to the grain; v2 having a characteristic patch size is a fair description of sand, where v1's parallel crests every 4.35m were not. Closing it further would need mottle across several scales — a refinement, not a blocker. SIZING, unchanged by the reroll: tileWorld 128 is where the resolvable features land at true size. At 9.2 world units per metre (the 56.4-unit hull read as a 6.1m sportboat) it puts shell chips at 4.9cm median / 14cm p95. The 512 tile made them 20cm cobbles and 56cm boulders. v2 was authored FOR 128, so its minfeature was 32px in the master rather than the 8px a 512 intent implies. COLOUR, AND THE PROPERTY WORTH KEEPING: v2 came back at mean #ddc39a against the #e1c6a7 the subject asked for — 12 RGB units, almost all of it blue channel (154 vs 167), so slightly warmer and less grey than the Varkala plate. Inside the natural spread of the three references (#e1c6a7 / #eac8b1 / near-neutral #cdcac6) and accepted rather than rerolled. ISLAND_STYLES.tropical.body is set to the TILE'S OWN MEAN, not to the reference: with base equal to tile mean the blend cannot move the colour, only the spread around it, so alpha became a pure contrast knob and the rendered shore held #dac198 across alpha 0.5/0.7/0.85/1.0. That is the fix granite's note asked for (normalize the tile's mean to the base), reached from the other end, and it is why alpha could be tuned on looks alone. If the shore must sit exactly on a reference colour, normalize the TILE to it at pattern-bake time and set the body to match — do not split them, or alpha silently becomes a colour control again. ALPHA 0.7, up from v1's 0.5: v2's mottle is much softer than v1's ripples, and at 0.5 on-screen contrast fell to 1.94, BELOW the reference band. 0.7 gives 4.12, between the smooth-beach plate (2.95) and Varkala (8.33). The curve flattens past there (0.85 -> 4.39, 1.0 -> 4.78), so 0.7 buys nearly all the contrast available and keeps headroom. WRAP: delivered at 1254px, ingest resampled to the 1024 master through wrap_resize. Roll-by-half shows a faint tonal step at the horizontal midline and no hard seam; edge-to-edge difference is 2.4x (left-right) and 3.0x (top-bottom) the interior neighbour difference against the snow tile's 1.95x — slightly looser, invisible at the 8x downsample to 128. STILL MISSING, and it is the strongest sand cue in every reference: the WET BAND at the waterline. Reference runs #c89760 at the swash and #dcb78b damp against #e1c6a7 dry — a wide saturated dark band, not the 6px stroke drawIslands paints today. Engine work, not art. ONE AUTHORING CONFLICT, resolved in the subject: v2 first asked for the faint scuffed walking trails the reference shows, which argues with the texture class NEGATIVE's 'footprints, tracks'. The negative won — a trail is a distinctive feature and at 128 the tile repeats ~11 times per viewport, so it would stamp out countably. Trails belong in a decal or a much bigger tile.

assets.subject: A closed sward of coastal upland grass and low scrub seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the sun-faded green of a Cape Cod bluff top, salt-pruned and wind-dried rather than lush inland pasture. AT THIS HEIGHT INDIVIDUAL BLADES DO NOT RESOLVE, and that is the subject: the sward reads as a soft clumpy mottle, rounded tussock crowns a shade lighter where the grass mounds up and narrow sinks a shade darker between them, every clump blending into its neighbours with no hard edge and at roughly the same density everywhere. THROUGH THE SWARD, LOW SCRUB — broader, rounder, slightly darker and greyer patches where bearberry, beach plum and bayberry lie flat against the wind. Each is a soft-edged mound a little denser than the grass around it, scattered unevenly, covering perhaps a fifth of the frame. THEY ARE PATCHES OF A DIFFERENT PLANT, NOT BUSHES: no branch, no stem, no drawn outline, no cast shadow, and nothing tall enough to read as an object sitting on top of the ground. NOTHING LEANS ANY PARTICULAR WAY. No combed direction, no mowing stripes, no swirls, no rows, no terracing, nothing lining up with the frame or with itself, and no spacing that repeats anywhere in the image. A few broad drifts of paler, drier, straw-tinted grass move through at the largest scale, soft and wide, where salt and wind have burned the sward back — drifts of tone only, never a shape with an edge. THE WHOLE IMAGE HOLDS A NARROW SUN-FADED RANGE from #8CA03A to #BAC96C around a mean of #A3B845. IT IS SUN-BLEACHED, NOT SUN-GREYED, and that distinction is the whole colour brief. Bleached grass goes LIGHTER and YELLOWER; it does not go gritty or grey. So this is a bright, clean, confident yellow-green — paler and drier than a lush inland meadow, but every bit as alive. NOTHING HERE IS OLIVE, KHAKI, SAGE, GREYED-DOWN, DUSTY, MUTED OR ARMY-DRAB, and nothing is the cured tan-olive of a dead sward. If a green looks washed out or dirty it is wrong; take the fading upward into light, never sideways into grey. Hold the whole image inside a narrow value range. No visible soil, no sand, no rock, no flowers, no individual drawn blades, no fine hairline strokes, no paths, no tracks, no footprints, no fences, no stone walls, no water and no shoreline
assets.note: Lighthouse Cove's UPLAND GROUND — the material most of the venue's land is made of, and the one that has to bridge between the houses, the shore trees and the rock. Wired as LAND_TEXTURES.coastalscrub at tile 128 / alpha 0.5 over an ISLAND_STYLES.coastalscrub body of #A3B845. THE BODY IS THE SPEC MEAN AND MUST BE RESET TO THE DELIVERED TILE'S OWN MEAN ON INGEST, the coralsand precedent: with base equal to tile mean the blend cannot move the colour, only the spread around it, so alpha stays a pure contrast knob and the mean-luma-shift warning the arctic textures carry cannot happen. THE COLOUR IS DERIVED, NOT PICKED, and it is deliberately NOT the venue card's turf. Measured off assets/images/venues/bay.png, the card's sunlit headland turf runs hue 73-75 deg at saturation 0.92-0.99 across three separate headlands — a bright, almost fully saturated yellow-green. That is right for a 1254px illustration and wrong for a ground tile, on the texture class's own rule that this is the surface every boat, mark and prop is drawn ON TOP of and so must lose the contrast fight with them. #A3B845 holds the card's hue family (71 deg) and buys 'sun-faded' by lifting VALUE (L* 63 -> 71) while HOLDING saturation at 0.62. ⚠️ CORRECTED FROM #8CA24A, WHICH CUT SATURATION TO 0.54 INSTEAD, and the correction is the reusable part. Every shipped land body meant to read as alive holds its chroma — grass 0.83, redrock 0.75 — while 0.48 belongs to `swampgrass`, a CURED DEAD sward. Rendered beside the venue card, the desaturated version read army-olive: it had left the family. Sun-bleached grass is lighter and yellower, never greyer. This is the same error the cedar's note already warns about in this venue's own tree set ("when a subject wants muted, say which direction it is muted TOWARD, or you simply desaturate") — made again, one asset later, on a ground instead of a crown. It sits between the two existing swards by construction: dE 15.5 from `grass` (#7aaa1d, bright meadow) and 28.1 from `swampgrass`. Against what it actually touches in the cove it is far clear — dE 41.2 from the bay's sand and 52.0 from the coastal rock. ALTITUDE DISCIPLINE PER bay-sand v2, which is the transferable lesson of this class: ask what structure the material really has at ten metres before writing the subject. Blades do not resolve, so the honest structure is tussock mottle plus scrub patches, and any combed direction is banned outright — one dominant direction repeats as visible banding at tile scale, which is how bay-sand v1 died. ⚠️ THE SCRUB PATCHES ARE THIS TILE'S PERIODICITY RISK, the way ripples were sand's: they are the only discrete feature here, so if they arrive evenly sized and evenly spaced they will read as a countable stamp at 128 (the tile repeats ~11 times per viewport). Measure anisotropy and periodicity on delivery against bay-sand v2's accepted 0.177 / 4.23, and remember that retiling cannot fix a periodicity problem — only redrawing can. ALPHA 0.5 is the pre-registered sward value, not a measurement; the two existing swards use it because their mottle is busier than sand's. Retune on delivered contrast, and note the direction of travel is set by what the tile arrives at: if the sward reads dead at race scale the move is UP, as bayou-mud's note argues. DELIVERED AND INGESTED 2026-08-10. STRUCTURE PASSED OUTRIGHT: anisotropy 0.179, essentially bay-sand's 0.183 and grass's 0.174 and nowhere near the 0.656 that killed bay-sand v1, so no combing and no banding direction; wrap measured 1.62x left-right and 1.47x top-bottom against an ordinary neighbour difference, the TIGHTEST of the ten tiles in the library. The scrub patches that this note flagged as the periodicity risk did not become a countable stamp — dominant grain is 314px in the master, i.e. a 3.5m patch at tile 128, which is a patch of bearberry and not a tile harmonic. TWO THINGS MOVED ON DELIVERY. (1) ALPHA 0.5 -> 0.40, and it is the marsh's argument repeating: the pre-registered value assumed this tile would arrive at the two swards' contrast and it did not. Delivered luma sd is 14.30 at tile 128 against swampgrass's 10.20, half again as busy, so 0.5 would have landed on-screen sd 7.15 — the loudest ground in the game and past `grass` (6.75). Backwards for the material MOST of the venue's land is made of. 0.40 lands 5.72, between swampgrass and grass, structure intact. THE GENERAL RULE: a pre-registered alpha is a guess about a tile that does not exist yet, so it is a starting point and never a spec. (2) COLOUR DRIFTED 11.1 dE TOWARD YELLOW — hue 71 -> 62 deg, L* 71 -> 66 — almost all of it in the green channel. ACCEPTED RATHER THAN REROLLED, and the reasoning is worth keeping because the session's whole colour argument runs the other way. The drift is toward the cured-sward family this asset was rewritten to escape, and it did NOT arrive: dE to `swampgrass` is 17.5, down from the spec's 28.1 but still clear, and saturation held at 0.60 against the spec's 0.62 — the tile is yellower, not greyer, and greyer was the failure mode. Judged on the rendered fill with the three shore trees on it rather than on the swatch, which is the honest test: the sward reads as sun-faded coastal grass and the trees separate strongly on top of it. If it is ever regenerated, push the subject's mean hex greener to leave room for the same drift.

assets.subject: Bare weathered coastal rock seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the grey-tan stone of a New England headland, glacial rock rounded and smoothed by salt, ice and centuries of sea. AT THIS HEIGHT THE SHAPE OF THE ROCK IS THE SUBJECT AND ITS MINERAL GRAIN IS NOT: the surface reads as a mosaic of broad ROUNDED humps and whalebacks, each one a soft-edged swell of stone a shade lighter across its crown and a shade darker where it rolls away, packed against its neighbours with shallow seams and hollows between them. ROUNDED, NOT SHATTERED, and this is the whole difference between this rock and a mountain granite: there are no straight-edged fractures, no sharp angular plates, no jagged blocks, no knife-edged cracks meeting at blunt angles and no fresh broken faces. Every edge in this image has been worn soft. A few narrow JOINTS wander across the stone as thin darker lines, curving and irregular, dividing it loosely into large rounded panels — three or four in the whole frame, never a network, never a grid and never parallel. Scattered thinly, the only hard marks in the image: small pockets of coarse gravel and a few loose rounded pebbles caught in the hollows, each drawn as a small shaped mark and never as fine speckle or photographic grit. A LICHEN CAST RATHER THAN LICHEN PATCHES: a faint, soft, irregular paling across some of the crowns, a little cooler and a little lighter but still the stone's own colour, with no hard edge and no separate hue of its own — this is weathering, not a plant, so nothing orange, nothing yellow-green and nothing that reads as a drawn blotch. NOTHING LINES UP. No bedding direction, no parallel seams, no repeating spacing, no direction the eye can follow, and nothing in the frame agreeing with anything else. THE WHOLE IMAGE HOLDS A NARROW GREY-TAN RANGE from #83786B to #B9AFA0 around a mean of #9D9080 — a soft warm grey stone, never a cold blue-grey mountain granite, never an orange or rust sandstone, and never a brown earth or mud. Hold the whole image inside a narrow value range. No water, no foam, no spray, no wet rock, no waterline, no tide line, no seaweed, no barnacles, no shells, no sand, no soil, no moss, no grass and no vegetation of any kind
assets.note: Lighthouse Cove's HARD SHORELINE — points, islets, harbour edges, rocky coves, bridge abutments. Wired as LAND_TEXTURES.coastalrock at tile 256 / alpha 0.35 over an ISLAND_STYLES.coastalrock body of #9D9080; body is the SPEC mean and must be reset to the delivered tile's own mean on ingest, per coralsand and bay-sand. THE COLOUR IS THE INTERESTING DECISION AND IT WAS MEASURED TWICE. Sampled off the venue card's three rock areas (headland cliff, islet boulders, left shore) with water, foam and foliage masked out, the card's rock means #786C55-#8C7858 at hue 37-40 deg and saturation 0.24-0.38. Taking that mean directly gives #7D6F56 — and it FAILS, at dE 5.3 from the bayou's `mudflat` (#6e6449) and 11.0 from `marsh`, i.e. two materials a designer picks from the same twenty-three-row list. The card mean is dragged dark and warm by the shadow crevices BETWEEN boulders, which are not what the material looks like; the stone itself reads at the lit end. #9D9080 keeps the card's hue (33 deg) and moves to saturation 0.18 at L* 60, which is also what 'grey-tan' means in a number. If it reads too grey once the tile lands, move WARMER (toward #9a8c77) rather than more saturated: warmth is what the card's stone actually has. SEPARATION WAS SCORED IN TWO TIERS, and that distinction is the reusable part: IN-VENUE separation is what matters in play, because sand and rock share a shoreline and a player has to read them apart at race scale — this holds dE 23.9 from the bay's sand (#ddc39a) and 52.0 from the new coastal scrub. CROSS-VENUE separation is only a picker-swatch concern, since mudflat and coastal rock can never appear in the same race, so 19.2 there is acceptable where 5.3 was not. TILE 256, NOT 128, and it follows the material rather than the venue: rounded whalebacks are metre-scale features where a grass tussock and a shell chip are centimetre-scale, and 256 is the size both existing rock tiles use (arctic-granite, redrock-sandstone). At 9.2 units per metre a 256 tile spans 27.8m, which puts a hump at roughly 3-6m across — a boulder, which is what it should be. ALPHA 0.35 is the rock precedent (granite and sandstone both), pre-registered rather than measured; retune on delivered contrast. ⚠️ THE FAILURE TO WATCH FOR IS ANGULARITY. Every generator's prior for 'rock texture from above' is fractured plates, because that is what arctic-granite's own subject asks for and what most reference photography of bare rock shows. This material is the opposite and the subject spends its second-longest clause saying so. If the delivery comes back with straight-edged plates it has failed on MATERIAL, not on rendering — check that before checking colour. DELIVERED AND INGESTED 2026-08-10, PASSING EVERY GATE, and the numbers are all measured with ONE script across all nine shipped textures rather than quoted from their notes — which matters, because the figures recorded in this file were computed by different scripts at different times and are NOT comparable to each other. A first pass scored this tile's periodicity at 6633 against bay-sand's recorded 4.23 and looked like a catastrophic failure; re-running the same metric over every shipped tile put the set's range at 2098-38867 with bay-sand itself at 13642, i.e. this tile is mid-pack and better than half the library. ⚠️ WHENEVER A TEXTURE METRIC IS COMPARED TO A NUMBER IN A NOTE, RECOMPUTE THE BASELINE. THE MEASUREMENTS: anisotropy 0.155, inside the shipped range of 0.025-0.591 and below bay-sand's 0.183, so no directional bias — the failure that killed bay-sand v1 at 0.656. Dominant grain 179px in the master, which at tile 256 is a boulder 4.0m across, squarely inside the 3-6m the sizing argument asked for. Wrap measured 1.81x left-right and 1.65x top-bottom against an ordinary neighbour difference — tighter than the snow tile's 1.95x and bay-sand's 2.4x/3.0x — and confirmed by eye on a roll-by-half, which shows no seam cross. Colour landed at #a19481 against a spec of #9d9080, 5.8 RGB units warmer and lighter, accepted rather than rerolled and now carried into ISLAND_STYLES as the body. THE MATERIAL RISK THIS SLOT WAS WRITTEN AGAINST DID NOT MATERIALISE: the crown structure came back genuinely ROUNDED — packed whalebacks with soft seams and pebbles caught in the hollows — with no straight-edged plates and no fractured-granite prior anywhere in it. The second-longest clause in the subject is what bought that, and it should stay if this is ever regenerated.

assets.subject: A CRUSHED-SHELL AND SAND LANE seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the pale unpaved track that runs between the cottages of a Cape or Nantucket village. AT THIS HEIGHT A LANE IS ALMOST FEATURELESS, and that is the subject: a quiet, near-uniform pale surface whose only structure is broad, soft, irregular patches of very slightly different tone, each blending into its neighbours with no hard edge, the way a track packs harder in some places than others. SCATTERED THINLY THROUGH IT, the only hard marks in the frame: small pale SHELL FRAGMENTS — broken quahog and scallop, a shade whiter and cooler than the ground — together with a few tiny grey pebbles, each drawn as a small shaped mark and never as fine speckle or photographic grain. They are what makes this a shell lane rather than bare dirt, so they must read as chips with edges. ⚠️ NO WHEEL RUTS, NO TRACKS, NO PATH EDGES AND NO DIRECTION OF ANY KIND. There are no parallel lines, no twin ruts, no centre crown, no verge, no kerb and no boundary anywhere in the image — nothing in the frame lines up with anything else and no spacing repeats. This tile is the SURFACE only; the lane's shape and its edges are drawn by the engine, and any edge painted into the tile would repeat as a stripe every time it is laid. THE WHOLE IMAGE HOLDS A VERY NARROW PALE RANGE from #B0A68E to #D4CBB6 around a mean of #C2B8A0 — a soft warm grey-tan, cooler and greyer than beach sand and much paler than any soil, never yellow, never orange, never brown. Hold it inside a narrow value range. No water, no puddle, no wet patch, no grass, no weed, no moss growing through, no tyre mark, no footprint, no vegetation of any kind, no kerbstone and no drain.
assets.note: Lighthouse Cove's FOURTH GROUND, and the answer to the 'lanes' question that had been open since the town set was listed. A LANE IS A GROUND, NOT A PROP, and that is the whole design decision: a prop is a fixed-size sprite, so a village lane would be a dozen placements with a seam at every join — the exact problem cove-quay took two rounds to solve. A ground has no such limit. drawIslands walks the islands in DOCUMENT ORDER (compileVenueDoc's shapeOrder is the designer's stacking), so a thin lane polygon listed AFTER a scrub island simply paints over it, at any length, width or curve, with no seam anywhere by construction. Verified in the renderer before this slot was written. COLOUR CHOSEN AGAINST THE THREE SHIPPED GROUNDS IT WILL TOUCH: #C2B8A0 sits dE 39 from coastal scrub — which is the one that matters, since a lane is nearly always drawn across the scrub — and 12 from sand and 13 from coastal rock, which are close but rarely adjacent to it and are genuinely similar materials (a shell lane IS pale like a beach). tileWorld 128 with the sand family, because shell chips and pebbles are the same centimetre scale as the sand's. ALPHA 0.7 PRE-REGISTERED from bay-sand, whose quiet broad-mottle structure this shares; retune on delivery and reset ISLAND_STYLES.lane.body to the delivered tile's own mean, per coralsand. ⚠️ THE PERIODICITY RISK IS RUTS. bay-sand v1 died of directional ripples and the note there records the finding that RETILING CANNOT FIX A PERIODICITY PROBLEM — only redrawing can. A lane is the most rut-prone subject in the set, so the subject bans parallel lines, twin ruts, a centre crown and any verge outright, and measures against bay-sand v2's accepted anisotropy of 0.177 on delivery. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED AND WIRED. ⚠️ ANISOTROPY 0.039 — THE LOWEST OF ANY TEXTURE IN THE LIBRARY (sand 0.183, scrub 0.181, rock 0.155), so the rut risk this note called the asset's top danger did not materialise at all: there is no directional bias to become banding at tile scale. Colour landed #cac2ad against a #C2B8A0 spec, 8 units light. Wrap 1.69x left-right and 2.89x top-bottom — the vertical is the loosest of the bay's four grounds but sits inside bay-sand's accepted 2.4/3.0, and at the 8x downsample to tile 128 it is invisible. ALPHA 0.5, MEASURED RATHER THAN THE 0.7 PRE-REGISTERED FROM SAND: the delivered tile has sd 7.28 at tile 128 against sand's 4.00, so 0.7 would land on-screen 5.10 — near the top of the library's 1.38-6.75 band and wrong for a narrow strip whose job is to read as a path without pulling the eye off the water. 0.5 lands 3.64, between sand (2.80) and the scrub it is drawn across (5.72), with the shell chips intact. Same finding as the scrub's: A PRE-REGISTERED ALPHA IS A GUESS ABOUT A TILE THAT DOES NOT EXIST YET. body reset to the delivered mean so alpha stays a pure contrast knob.

assets.subject: coconut palm seen from directly above — a single crown of long feathered fronds radiating from a central hub, each frond one chunky tapering blade of clustered leaflet-mass in two flat greens (a sunlit top tone and a deep shade tone), with soft rounded tips. The fronds sit at UNEVEN lengths and angles, one or two drooping shorter or crossing a neighbour, so the crown reads as a living tree rather than a geometric star. At the hub, a tight cluster of three or four brown coconuts and the pale grey-brown top of the trunk just visible between the frond bases
assets.note: First lagoon asset — Pearl Lagoon's island palm, the lagoon counterpart to bayou-cypress. allowSymmetry because a top-down palm crown is genuinely radial, same reasoning as the mark; the subject asks for uneven frond lengths and angles so the rosette still reads organic rather than mandala. anchor trunk-base assumes a vertical palm — a leaning palm from overhead offsets crown from base, so the subject keeps it straight (the leaning variant is lagoon-palm-leaning). world 70 ≈ 7.6m crown at 9.2 units/m, a full-grown coconut palm.

assets.subject: coconut palm leaning far out sideways, seen from directly above — only the TOP of the tree is visible, never its side. The slim ringed grey-brown trunk runs as one gently curved line from its base in the lower third of the frame up to the crown in the upper third, so trunk and crown together read as a lollipop on a bent stick. The crown is a loose spray of long feathered fronds fanning out around the hub, fuller on the far side of the lean and sparser back toward the trunk, each frond one chunky tapering blade of clustered leaflet-mass in two flat greens with soft rounded tips. A couple of coconuts at the hub. The trunk's own top surface shows as a narrow lit band along the curve with a darker edge — a line with thickness, not a wire
assets.note: The postcard beach palm — the one shape that says 'tropical island' at race scale, and deliberately NOT radial, so it does NOT take allowSymmetry: the arrangement negatives (rosette, radial symmetry) are doing useful work here, pushing the generator away from collapsing it back into a centred star. Lean direction is toward the TOP of the frame per the class rule (sprite-up = zero heading), so code can aim the lean — over the water, downwind, wherever. ⚠️ anchor trunk-base is OFF-CENTRE by construction (base in the lower third, crown above): check what ingest measures for anchorPx and hand-correct it to the trunk-ground contact point if it defaults to bbox centre — a leaning palm anchored mid-trunk would stand in the water. world 84 is the base-to-crown-edge span, ≈9m at 9.2 units/m.

assets.subject: coconut palm seen from directly above — a full dense crown of feathered fronds radiating from the hub with no gaps, closed and lush, fronds at slightly uneven lengths and angles, two flat greens with soft rounded tips
assets.note: Fourth crown variant, owner-supplied art (2026-08-08): a dense closed crown that matched none of the three authored slots — not coconut-clustered (lagoon-palm), not leaning, not a trunkless tuft — so it got its own slot rather than being forced into the fan-palm slot, which stays open for a genuinely pleated-fan generation. The subject above is written to match the delivered art, not the other way round.

assets.subject: fan palm seen from directly above — a compact crown of large ROUND PLEATED FANS, completely different from a feather palm: each fan is one stiff chunky disc of folded pleats, drawn as alternating lighter and darker wedge facets radiating within the fan like a folded paper fan opened flat, with a bluntly toothed outer edge. Five to seven fans overlap at uneven heights and angles, the upper ones casting one hard flat shade tone onto the ones beneath, so the crown reads as layered plates rather than a single rosette. Fan colour a cooler slightly grey-green than a coconut palm. At the centre, the stout trunk top just visible in the gaps, wrapped in a rough criss-cross of old leaf bases in warm brown
assets.note: Second lagoon canopy shape — pleated fans against lagoon-palm's feathered blades, so mixed plantings read as two species at a glance even with colour removed. The pleat wedges are exactly the house style's faceted brush planes, which is why a fan palm suits this set better than most foliage. allowSymmetry as with lagoon-palm: each fan is genuinely radial and the crown is a rough rosette of them; the uneven overlap in the subject keeps it organic. world 60 ≈ 6.5m crown — fan palms carry a tighter head than coconuts.

assets.subject: young trunkless palm seen from directly above — a low dense tuft of short arching fronds erupting straight out of the sand from a single point, no trunk visible at all. The fronds are shorter, broader and more upswept than a grown palm's, so from overhead they foreshorten into a compact star-burst of stubby chunky blades, in a fresher yellow-shifted green than a mature crown, two flat tones with soft rounded tips. Frond count and spacing slightly uneven, one blade folded over another, so the tuft reads as a scruffy living plant rather than a geometric badge. A hint of the pale fibrous heart at the very centre
assets.note: The understory scale — scattered between the big palms it breaks up size monotony, and near beaches it reads as dune vegetation. Deliberately trunkless so it stays clearly a PLANT at 38px; a mini lollipop palm would just read as lagoon-palm placed wrong. allowSymmetry as with the other radial crowns. The yellow-shifted green is real (juvenile palms are paler) and doubles as the value separation from mature crowns when a young one sits under or beside a big one. world 38 ≈ 4m spread.

assets.subject: brain coral head seen from directly above — ONE massive rounded dome, its top covered in a dense meandering maze of ridges and valleys, drawn as bold wandering two-tone grooves that follow the curve of the dome, never as fine texture. Dusty rose-pink ridges over deeper mauve valleys — a soft chalky pastel pink, never hot and never saturated — with the crown of the dome washed to pale cream where it nears the surface: the pale heart is the warning. The outline is one heavy, slightly uneven circle: a boulder of coral, massive and immovable
assets.note: First of the five coral heads — the venue card's promised hazard, and the home of Pearl Lagoon's underwater accent. Destined for the props layer as a seabed-plane hard-contact prop (PROP_KINDS row: plane seabed, contact hard, contactR ~14) — ⚠️ add that row only AFTER ingest delivers the sprite, or its 404 trips test_editor's no-page-errors check, the LAND_TEXTURES lesson. allowSymmetry: a brain dome is genuinely round; the maze keeps it organic. THE FIVE ARE KEPT APART ON TWO AXES AT ONCE — silhouette AND hue, one family each, so no pair blurs at race scale in either colour or greyscale: dome+rose-pink (this) / spikes+lavender / plates+cream / mound-cluster+sage / columns+powder-blue / paddles+apricot — all of them SOFT CHALKY PASTELS, matched to the owner's reference plate, where the coral reads as dusty pink/lavender/cream/green/blue rubble, never jewel-saturated.

assets.subject: staghorn coral thicket seen from directly above — a bristling tangle of branching antler-like arms radiating outward, each branch a chunky tapering two-tone spike forking once or twice, the arms overlapping in an irregular spiky mass with deep dark water-shadow gaps between them. Dusty lavender branches, soft and chalky, with pale lilac growing tips — the pale tips are the highest points and the warning. The silhouette is ALL POINTS, unmistakably sharp, and clearly uneven: some arms long, some stubby, no two alike
assets.note: The spiky one — sharpest silhouette of the five, the hazard role's 'aggressive, spiky' read taken literally. No allowSymmetry: the arrangement negatives are load-bearing against a radial antler rosette. Same prop wiring plan and same 404 caution as lagoon-coral-brain.

assets.subject: table coral seen from directly above — three broad flat plates overlapping like shelves at slightly different heights, each plate an irregular rounded disc with a finely scalloped rim, drawn in two flat tones with a few bold concentric growth arcs, never fine texture. Warm CREAM plates edged in ivory with only the faintest blush undertone — the pale head of the five — the topmost plate palest and one lower plate carrying a clean bite-shaped notch in its rim. Deep shadow crescents where plate overhangs plate — the stacked-shelves read is the whole silhouette
assets.note: The flat one — plates against the brain's dome and the staghorn's spikes. The pink-tan family is the venue accent's warm half. Same prop wiring plan and 404 caution as lagoon-coral-brain.

assets.subject: coral bommie seen from directly above — one heavy central mound of lobed coral ringed by a clustered skirt of smaller knobs and stubby lobes, the cluster packed uneven with dark water-shadow seams between the members. Soft sage and sea-green lobes throughout — the GREEN head, a chalky pastel green, no red and no purple anywhere on it — with two or three small flecks of dusty pink at the crown and the highest central lobes washed pale. The biggest and most cluttered of the coral heads — a reef in miniature, its outline deeply lumpy but never spiky
assets.note: The big mound-cluster — the generic 'coral head' a course designer reaches for first. Olive is its whole hue family (the one green thing among the five; the pink flecks stay small enough not to blur it toward the table coral). Largest world of the five at 56 (~6m). No allowSymmetry: a skirt of knobs must not come back as a rosette. Same prop wiring plan and 404 caution as lagoon-coral-brain.

assets.subject: pillar coral seen from directly above — a close cluster of five to seven stout columns rising toward the surface, each column reading as a rounded knobby disc top in two flat tones, the cluster packed unevenly with deep dark shadow gaps dropping away between the columns. Powder-blue columns — a soft chalky slate-blue, clearly COOLER than every other head — each crown paler than its flanks, the tallest crown near-white: a fistful of towers reaching up at the viewer. Column tops clearly different sizes, the arrangement loose and lopsided, never a ring
assets.note: The columns — reads as depth where the others read as spread. Powder-blue is the risky family (it borders the water it sits in), so the near-white crowns and the near-black shadow gaps carry the contrast, which is also exactly what the hazard clause demands over both pale turquoise and night water. Smallest of the five. No allowSymmetry: 'never a ring' in the subject plus the arrangement negatives hold the cluster irregular. Same prop wiring plan and 404 caution as lagoon-coral-brain.

assets.subject: elkhorn coral seen from directly above — three to five broad FLATTENED branches like a moose's antlers radiating from a central base, each branch a wide flat paddle with rounded lobed ends, drawn in two flat tones with a bold midrib shadow where the paddle dips, never fine texture. Dusty apricot ORANGE — a soft chalky pastel orange, the one warm head in the lagoon, never neon and never brown — with the paddle rims and highest surfaces washed pale peach: the pale edges are the warning. The paddles are clearly unequal in length and reach, with deep dark water-shadow gaps between them — a lopsided open hand, never a symmetric star
assets.note: The sixth head, and the warm one — the paddle silhouette is the family the first five do not cover (broad flat radiating arms, against thin sharp spikes / solid discs / dome / mound / columns), and apricot-orange is elkhorn's true colour, kept chalky to sit in the set's pastel register. No allowSymmetry: 'never a symmetric star' plus the arrangement negatives keep the hand lopsided. Same prop wiring plan (plane seabed, contact hard) and same add-PROP_KINDS-only-after-ingest caution as lagoon-coral-brain.

assets.subject: Dry white Caribbean coral sand seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the pale near-white sand of a coral atoll beach, ground from coral and shell rather than rock. AT THIS HEIGHT SAND IS ALMOST FEATURELESS, and that is the subject: a quiet, near-uniform field whose only structure is broad, soft, irregular patches of very slightly different tone, each blending into its neighbours with no hard edge. A few of the patches carry the faintest warm blush of pink-cream, the ghost of ground coral, never a saturated pink. NO RIPPLES OF ANY KIND: no crests, no ridges, no parallel lines, no repeating waves, nothing lining up with anything else, no spacing that repeats. Scattered thinly through it, the only hard marks in the frame: a few tiny shell chips and coral fragments in off-white and the palest coral pink, each drawn as a small shaped mark, never as fine speckle or grain, plus the very occasional single dark fleck. The whole image holds a very narrow pale range from #e2d4b2 to #f5ecd8 around a mean of #ecdfc2 — a warm cream, clearly LIGHTER than ordinary tan beach sand, but never pure white and never grey. No water, no foam, no wet sand, no waterline, no vegetation, no seaweed, no driftwood, no dune, no rocks larger than a chip, no cast shadows, no footprints, no tracks, no raked pattern, no sand ripple
assets.note: Pearl Lagoon's own sand — a NEW look ('coralsand'), deliberately paler than the shared `tropical` bay-sand (#ddc39a mean) so lagoon beaches read as cream against every other venue's tan. RETARGETED 2026-08-08 to #ecdfc2 (warm cream, was near-white #efe6d5) when the venue's four-step colour ladder was matched to the owner's reference plate — the ISLAND_STYLES.coralsand body already sits at the new mean. Authored to the bay-sand v2 lessons wholesale: structure-at-altitude first (near-featureless, broad tonal drift, shaped marks only), tileWorld 128 so shell chips land at true size (~5cm median at 9.2 units/m), and WHEN WIRING set the new ISLAND_STYLES body to the DELIVERED TILE'S OWN MEAN, not to the #efe6d5 the subject asks for — with base equal to tile mean, alpha stays a pure contrast knob (the property that retired the arctic textures' luma-shift warning). The pink blush is held to the faintest cast on purpose: the venue clause excludes lagoon accents (coral pinks) from ground, and a pink beach would spend the accent that belongs to the underwater props. Value range is snow-tile territory — check contrast on the grid against ice, which is the nearest neighbour in value.

assets.subject: Wet bayou mud seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the dark olive-brown mud of a southern swamp bank, smooth and heavy. AT THIS HEIGHT MUD IS ALMOST FEATURELESS, and that is the subject: a quiet field whose only structure is broad, soft, irregular patches of slightly different tone — darker where the mud lies wetter, a shade lighter where it has begun to dry — each patch blending into its neighbours with no hard edge. EVERY SURFACE IS MATTE: wet mud here is dark, never shiny, with no sheen, no highlights and no reflections. NO CRACKS — this is soft wet swamp mud, not a dried lakebed, so no crack network, no polygonal plates, no curling edges. Scattered thinly through it, the only hard marks in the frame: a sparse fall of leaf litter — small dark dead leaves and a few short twig fragments in browns barely darker or lighter than the mud — each drawn as a small shaped mark, never as speckle. The whole image holds a narrow dark range from #4e4636 to #665c48 around a mean of #5a5140 — a heavy olive-brown, never orange, never grey, never black. No water, no puddles, no standing water, no reflections, no footprints, no animal tracks, no tire ruts, no vegetation growing, no grass, no roots, no rocks, no cast shadows
assets.note: Gatorgrass Bayou's bank and bar material — a new 'mud' look for the swamp's low ground, where the venue's islands stop being generic grass. Same altitude discipline as bay-sand v2: the honest answer for smooth mud at 10m is broad wet/dry tonal drift plus a thin scatter of shaped leaf litter, so that is all the subject asks for. NO CRACKS is stated twice over because generators equate mud with dried-earth crack networks, which are the wrong material (dry lakebed) AND a countable stamped feature at tile repeat. tileWorld 128 puts leaves at true size like the sand's shell chips. Wiring is the same recipe as the others: ISLAND_STYLES body = delivered tile's mean, LAND_TEXTURES entry keyed to the new style, alpha as pure contrast knob — start near sand's 0.7 and tune on looks; the mud's mottle is soft like sand v2, not busy like the arctic pair. DELIVERED 2026-08-09 at mean #524731 (spec asked #5a5140) with a p5-p95 of #4d432e..#584b34 — darker and warmer than spec, and MUCH flatter: luma sd 2.20 at tile scale against sand's 3.93, so it is the quietest tile in the set and its alpha has room only upward. Litter measured 18px median / 48px p95 in the 1024 master = 25cm/65cm at tileWorld 128, i.e. ~2x life size; kept anyway because the marks are 2.2px median ON SCREEN and halving the tile to fix the size would dissolve every one of them. Wrap checked: seam-to-interior gradient ratio 1.98/1.50, inside the shipped set's 1.67-2.54.

assets.subject: Bare wind-worn sandstone seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the orange-rust stone of a desert canyon rim, smooth and dry. AT THIS HEIGHT THE STONE IS NEARLY FEATURELESS, and that is the subject: broad, soft, irregular drifts of slightly different tone where wind has polished and stained the rock, each blending into its neighbours with no hard edge. Through them run a few SHORT STRATA FRAGMENTS — gently curved bands of slightly darker and slightly lighter stone, each fading out within a third of the frame, at scattered angles, never straight, never crossing the whole image, never lining up with the frame edges or with each other — and two or three short hairline fractures drawn as shaped dark lines that also fade out. A thin scatter of small rounded stone chips, each a shaped mark, never speckle or photographic grit. The whole image holds a narrow warm range from #a85a30 to #d98a52 around a mean of #c2703e — saturated orange-rust, never brown-grey, never pink, never yellow. No vegetation, no sand, no dunes, no cracked-earth polygon network, no cast shadows, no full-width strata banding, no water staining
assets.note: Redrock Reservoir's ground — the canyon rim rock the venue is named for, targeting ISLAND_STYLES.redrock.body (#c2703e) exactly so wiring is the standard recipe (LAND_TEXTURES.redrock, body = delivered tile's mean, alpha from ~0.3 like the arctic pair — rock reads at lower contrast than sand). tileWorld 256, the granite precedent: the redrock shapes are canyon-wall scale, and 256 buys 4x supersample for the strata fragments. THE STRATA ARE FRAGMENTS ON PURPOSE: real strata run for kilometres, but a band crossing the whole tile repeats as the most countable feature a texture can have — the same reason bay-sand v1's ripples died. Short fading arcs carry the sedimentary read without the tiling tell.

assets.subject: A closed sward of fresh meadow grass seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — bright healthy green turf growing so dense that no ground shows anywhere. AT THIS HEIGHT INDIVIDUAL BLADES DO NOT RESOLVE, and that is the subject: the sward reads as a soft, even, clumpy mottle — rounded tussock crowns a shade lighter where the grass mounds up, narrow sinks a shade darker between them — every clump blending into its neighbours with no hard edge, at roughly the same density everywhere. The clumps LEAN NO PARTICULAR WAY: no combed direction, no mowing stripes, no swirls, no rows, nothing lining up with the frame or with itself, no spacing that repeats. A few broader drifts of slightly deeper and slightly fresher green move through at the largest scale, soft and wide. The whole image holds a narrow mid range from #74a03e to #97c261 around a mean of #84b14e — fresh and clearly GREEN, never olive, never yellow, never emerald-dark. No visible soil, no flowers, no clover patches, no individual drawn blades, no fine hairline strokes, no paths, no tracks, no footprints
assets.note: The bright meadow look ('grass' style) — VENUE-LESS on purpose, like the mark: this ground is shared by every venue with a grass isle (the strait's islets, the lake's banks, one day Duckling Pond's lawn), so a single venue's palette clause would mislead the generator. Same altitude discipline and tussock-mottle structure as bayou-swampgrass; the two swards differ ONLY in colour, which is exactly the grass/swampgrass style split (2026-08-08: grass brightened to #84b14e, the old tan-olive moved to the swampgrass style). Wiring recipe as always: LAND_TEXTURES.grass entry when the art lands, ISLAND_STYLES.grass.body reset to the delivered tile's mean, alpha as pure contrast knob starting near 0.7.

assets.subject: A closed sward of swamp sawgrass seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the olive and yellow-green grass the bayou is named for, growing so dense that no ground shows anywhere. AT THIS HEIGHT INDIVIDUAL BLADES DO NOT RESOLVE, and that is the subject: the sward reads as a soft, even, clumpy mottle — rounded tussock crowns a shade lighter where the grass mounds up, narrow sinks a shade darker between them — every clump blending into its neighbours with no hard edge, at roughly the same density everywhere. The clumps LEAN NO PARTICULAR WAY: no combed direction, no swirls, no parallel streaks, no rows, nothing lining up with the frame or with itself, no spacing that repeats. A few slightly yellower dried patches and a few deeper olive hollows drift through at the largest scale, soft and broad. assets.note: The swamp's VEGETATED ground — hummock and island tops, closing the set the swamp's low ground opened: swampgrass (closed sward) / marsh (broken) / mud (bare). RETARGETED 2026-08-08 to mean #a89b6a: the 'swampgrass' STYLE now exists (ISLAND_STYLES) and carries the tan-olive the global grass used to be — this tile is its texture, so it targets that style's body exactly; the note that once warned against wiring onto the global grass look is resolved by the split (grass went bright meadow green and has its own venue-less `grass` tile). assets.subject: Broken marsh ground seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the ragged edge where a swamp's grass gives out into mud: scattered rounded clumps of olive and yellow-green sedge sitting on dark wet olive-brown mud, roughly half and half, so neither material dominates. THE CLUMPS ARE THE ONLY STRUCTURE: each is a soft rounded tussock a shade lighter at its crown, with the bare mud showing as irregular dark channels and openings between them. Clump sizes vary and their spacing is uneven and unaligned — no rows, no rings, no even scatter, no spacing that repeats, nothing lining up with the frame. The mud between them is smooth and matte with only broad soft tonal drift, no shine and no reflections. Grass tones hold #8a8246 to #b6a660 and mud tones hold #4d432e to #584b34, so the image runs one straw-olive-over-mud family and the value step between clump and mud stays gentle. No open water, no puddles, no reflections, no cracks in the mud, no reeds standing tall, no cattail heads, no flowers, no individual drawn blades, no paths, no tracks, no footprints, no rocks
assets.note: The TRANSITION material — half swampgrass, half mud, for the wide soft margins where bayou islands meet the channels, so the game's three swamp grounds grade into each other instead of butting: swampgrass sward -> marsh -> bare mud -> water.
