assets.subject: An inflatable racing mark floating on open water, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD — looking straight down onto it from a helicopter, with none of its side or bottom rim visible anywhere, not even at the near edge. THINK OF IT AS A LOW THREE-SIDED PYRAMID, not a flat cushion. It is a squat tetrahedron: a rounded triangular base with three big triangular faces that SLOPE UPWARD and inward to meet at a single blunt apex directly above the centre. Seen from above you are looking down at those three sloping faces, and the three ridges where they meet run from the central apex out to the three rounded corners, forming a clean three-spoke Y. A bold dark lifting ring sits on the apex at the centre — make it a solid, chunky ring, not a hairline, because it is the one focal dot. THREE FACES, THREE CLEARLY DIFFERENT VALUES — this is the hardest requirement and the whole point of the pyramid form. Because each face tilts in a different direction, each catches the single light source differently. Render them as roughly 100%, 75% and 50% brightness: one face bright, one clearly mid, one clearly dark, with a hard crisp edge along every ridge. The engine desaturates inactive marks to flat slate grey for most of the race, so hue differences are worthless — CONVERTED TO GREYSCALE the three faces, the Y-ridge and the centre ring must all still read instantly. A mark that is one even tone with faint seams is a failure. COLOUR: true safety orange, warm and mid-bright, not red and not scarlet. Flat poster-like colour within each face — absolutely no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient, no plastic sheen. A narrow band of deeper wetter orange runs around the very bottom edge where the fabric meets the water. ROTATION: placed at an arbitrary angle with no 'up' — the three faces, ridges and corners must be identical in size and shape so the three-fold symmetry looks deliberate however it is turned, and the apex must sit at the exact centre of the frame. Drawn at only about 30 pixels: bold simple silhouette, a thin clean contour no heavier than the rest of the set, no detail that would not survive that size. No numbers, no letters, no flag, no water, no ripple, no shadow
assets.note: Venue-agnostic: the only prop on all ten venues, so no venue palette clause. Replaces the 160x140 oblique mark.png with a 2048 square master. ENGINE FACTS: drawMarkBodies() draws it at W=30 and applies an arbitrary per-mark rotation, so the art has no 'up' and three-fold symmetry is correct here — the opposite of the group-prop rule against symmetry (hence allowSymmetry). THE INACTIVE-STATE TEST WAS UNWINNABLE AND TWO CANDIDATES WERE REJECTED FOR FAILING IT. getMarkImgGray() tints inactive marks with source-atop rgba(148,163,184,0.8), i.e. 0.2*art + 0.8*slate, so exactly 20% of any value difference survives BY CONSTRUCTION. Measured three-face value spread, active -> inactive: incumbent 54.4 -> 10.9, candidate A 39.7 -> 7.9, this one 28.8 -> 5.8. At 30px all three are the same grey triangle when inactive. Inactive legibility is a CODE parameter, not an art problem: dropping the tint from 0.8 to ~0.55 recovers 45% instead of 20% and visibly helps whatever art is used. SHIPPED: the higher-contrast candidate, chosen by eye. It also measured best of the two new ones on three-face value spread (39.7 active / 7.9 inactive, against the alternative's 28.8 / 5.8), so the preference matched the metric. Its known deviation is colour: body RGB (202,57,9) reads scarlet rather than the safety orange the subject asked for — the incumbent sat at (225,108,44). Left as-is because the extra saturation is part of why it reads at 30px, but if the mark ever looks too red against the warm venues (redrock, swamp), that is the number to change. Sized at world 30 with fillTo 0.96, giving ~29px visible. It went 30 -> 60 while ingest was mis-measuring the master (invisible alpha-1 residue inflated the bbox, so world 60 was only drawing 41px). Once that was fixed the same 60 drew 58px, which was too big, so it came back to 30. The collider markRadius = 12 (24 units across) is unchanged throughout. MARK TAXONOMY (design decision, 2026-07-28): the orange tetrahedron is a TEMPORARY mark — an inflatable laid by the race committee for this race. The yellow can is a PERMANENT mark — a fixed installation the course is built around. Which one a course uses is a per-course choice, not a global one. Currently every course uses the orange temporary mark.

assets.subject: A RED LIGHTED STEEL CHANNEL BUOY floating on open water, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD. COLOUR: the buoy's red is canonical buoyage and carries navigational information, so it must be matched and must NOT be shifted toward the surrounding water's hue — a deep warm signal red around #BB3220, never scarlet, never orange, never pink, never maroon. The green buoy is this same object in green and the two must be drawn the same way — same proportions, same light direction, same facet treatment — because they stand either side of one channel and a player reads them as a PAIR. THE SHAPE OF THIS WHOLE PICTURE IS A CIRCLE, AND THAT IS THE FIRST THING TO GET RIGHT. The buoy's round steel FLOAT is the widest part of it and the entire silhouette: a full solid disc in the buoy's colour, filling the frame. Everything else in the picture sits ON that disc and INSIDE its outline. If the finished image is square, or is an open framework with gaps at its outer edge, or has no disc under it at all, it is wrong however good it looks — that is a bare tower with its float missing, not a buoy. ON TOP OF THE DISC, AN OPEN SQUARE LATTICE TOWER, and it is the buoy's identity: thick welded steel members forming a bold square frame with one rail crossing the middle each way, so the pattern is FOUR OPENINGS IN A TWO-BY-TWO GRID and nothing finer. THE TOWER NEVER REACHES THE EDGE OF THE DISC. It spans about three-fifths of the disc's width and sits square to the frame, which leaves a clear unbroken RING OF BARE DECK about one-fifth of the disc wide on every side of it — that ring of plain colour between the tower and the rim is as important as the tower itself, and it is what makes the object read as a structure standing on a float rather than as a grille filling a circle. Judge it on the OPENINGS: the four dark squares taken together should span a little under HALF the disc's width. If they reach two-thirds of the way across, the tower is too big and the ring has been squeezed out. THROUGH THE FOUR OPENINGS YOU SEE STRAIGHT DOWN to the deck below, in deep shadow — four dark square windows, the darkest thing in the picture apart from the lamp, each a flat hard-edged shape with nothing drawn inside it. Those dark squares against the bright deck are what make this buoy findable at a distance, so keep them clean and keep them dark. AT THE EXACT CENTRE, THE LANTERN: a small pale cylindrical housing ringed around a DARK lens cap, with a tiny bright finial dot at the very top. The dark cap is the one focal point of the whole sprite. SEEN FROM DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, NONE OF THE BUOY'S SIDE IS VISIBLE, and on a lattice this is the easiest thing in the world to get wrong. You are looking down the tower, not at it. A vertical corner post shows ONLY its small flat top face — never its length, never a side face, never a box drawn in three dimensions. No diagonal cross-bracing is visible anywhere, because bracing runs down the tower's sides and the sides do not exist in this picture. No part of the float's rim shows its thickness. Every part of the buoy is the same distance from the camera. IT MUST STILL READ IN GREYSCALE. A buoy seen from above has almost no silhouette to read by — it is a disc — so the STRUCTURE has to live in flat steps of lightness: bright deck, darker tower members, near-black openings, pale lamp housing, dark cap. Each is a flat hard-edged shape of clearly different value, and the whole thing must still make complete sense with the colour removed. THE DECK IS FLAT PAINTED STEEL AND IT IS LIT EVENLY. There is no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight, no wet or plastic sheen, no smooth gradient, no glow or halo, and no mottled or speckled surface texture. In particular there is NO BRIGHT CURVED SWEEP OF LIGHT ACROSS ONE SIDE OF THE DISC — a broad soft highlight arcing over the float is the single most likely way to spoil this, and it turns a working steel buoy into a shiny plastic button. Keep the deck one even tone, with any shading done as flat hard-edged facets rather than as a sheen. Fill the frame — reach close to the edges with only a hair of margin. Engine rotation transforms the coordinate system rather than sampling a fixed frame, so nothing clips at any angle and padding only makes the buoy smaller than it should be. A thin clean dark contour. No numbers, no letters, no text, no rust streaks, no birds, no flag, no water, no ripple, no wake, no shadow on the water
assets.note: Form and colour taken from the Lighthouse Cove venue card (assets/images/venues/bay.png), where these buoys already appear: a drum float with a white band, a tapered tower and a lantern with a dark cap. Reds sampled at #BB3220/#B8341E, green at #268B34. NOTE the pair is coded by COLOUR ALONE, which normally conflicts with the never-colour-alone rule — but the card draws them identically and matching the established art wins. An earlier draft distinguished them by a triangular vs square topmark; dropped as off-reference. ACCEPTED WITH THREE RECORDED DEVIATIONS, all invisible at the 28px display size and none affecting the nav function. (1) The pair is not identical as specified: the red carries a flat spoked X-frame at its centre, the green a raised domed lantern with a specular highlight — they should share one lantern. (2) Both carry mottled surface texture against the base prompt's 'minimal microtexture', and the green's dome highlight is gloss, which the subject refused. (3) Colour drifted brighter than the venue card: red #D11F15 against the card's #BB3220, green #51AD26 against #268B34 — more saturated and, for a nav aid, arguably more findable, but no longer a match for the buoys in bay.png. Worth one more pass only if these ever appear above ~3x race scale. ⚠️ RETYPED 2026-08-10 FROM A CONE PILLAR BUOY TO A STEEL LATTICE BUOY, on Wes's call, and the type change is the whole edit — the colour hexes, the world size, allowSymmetry and fillTo are all unchanged. WHAT THE OLD SUBJECT WAS AND WHY IT IS GONE: it described a tapered cone buoy as a set of CONCENTRIC RINGS (drum, white band, tapered tower, lantern) and told the generator to MATCH THE BUOYS IN THE LIGHTHOUSE COVE VENUE CARD. That was faithful — the shipped card really does carry cone pillar buoys with a white band — but the reference Wes is working to is a US steel lateral buoy: flat drum, open square lattice cage, number board, small light. The two are different objects, and the card is being rerolled to match rather than the props being bent back (see the `bay` illustration slot). ⚠️ UNTIL THAT CARD LANDS THE VENUE HOLDS TWO BUOY TYPES — props lattice, card cone — which is a known, accepted, temporary inconsistency and not a bug to be 'fixed' by reverting these subjects. THE EXAGGERATION IS DECLARED, per the manifest's scale block, and it is the reason this subject can ask for a lattice at all. At world 28 against a 1024 master, one screen px is ~36.6 master px and prompt.py's 4-screen-px floor is ~14% of the sprite's whole width. A real buoy of this class has a drum about 2.7m across, which is 25u — so world 28 is honest and stays. But its cage is about 1.2m square, i.e. 39% of the drum, and its lattice members are about 10cm, which is 0.9px on screen and INVISIBLE. Drawn at true scale the identity would simply not exist. So two numbers are moved and both are stated in the subject as shape rather than as measurements: the cage goes to THREE-FIFTHS of the drum (60% against a true 39%), and its members are drawn at about 3 screen px (a 3.3x exaggeration). That leaves the four openings at ~3.9px each, which lands exactly on the floor — which is why the subject insists on a TWO-BY-TWO grid and calls any finer mesh a mistake. A 3x3 grid would put the openings at 2.3px and the structure would dissolve into grey. THE LIFTING EYE ON THE DRUM RIM IS DELIBERATELY OMITTED for the same reason: ~25cm is 2px, under the floor, and it is the only asymmetric feature on the object, so drawing it would cost orientation noise and buy nothing. ⚠️ THE ONE THING THIS RETYPE GIVES UP, AND THE FIRST THING TO CHECK ON DELIVERY: the old subject had a crisp WHITE BAND ringing the drum and called it, correctly, 'the thing that makes it findable'. The reference buoy has no such band — its only white is the number board — so the band is gone and the findability job now falls to the FOUR DARK OPENINGS against the bright deck, which is a value cue rather than a hue cue and is why the greyscale clause was strengthened. If the delivery does not read as a nav aid at 28px on the contact sheet, the fix is to restore a white band at the drum's outer edge — and note that doing so would put the band back on the card's reroll too, so decide it once, on the contact sheet, before the card is generated. STATUS IS BACK TO `slot` DELIBERATELY even though a PNG still ships, and the distinction is worth drawing: the delivered art is not a poor version of the right object, it is the WRONG object, so it belongs in prompt.py --all-slots' queue rather than being annotated as stale. The shipped files stay on disk so the game keeps drawing a buoy until the reroll lands, and there is no master in inbox/ for either key, so an `ingest.py --all` cannot silently flip this back to art. planRound ADDED, which the old entry never carried and should have: the drum is the silhouette and it is round in plan, so ingest can measure the camera angle directly. The two candidates reviewed on 2026-08-10 came in at 1.023 and 1.011, so this gate costs nothing and catches the one failure this library cannot talk a generator out of. allowSymmetry STAYS TRUE: a buoy is deliberately four-fold symmetric and the new square cage is more so, so ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE's mandala/radial-symmetry terms would make the prompt argue with itself. ⚠️ THE PAIR MUST MATCH, AND THE LAST PAIR DID NOT — measured, so the next one can be checked the same way. Sampling the outer drum annulus of the two 2026-08-10 candidates, the red swung 19.5 in luminance with 79% of that in a single directional lobe (faceted, with a clear light direction) while the green swung 5.4 with only 9% (nearly flat, its modelling moved inward to the dome). Same words, two different objects. Both subjects now state the pair requirement explicitly and name light direction and facet treatment as part of it; generate them together and compare that number before accepting either. ACCEPTED 2026-08-10 AS THE FIRST LATTICE DELIVERY, with one recorded defect. Aspect 1.026; CIRCULARITY 0.974, i.e. the float really is the whole silhouette; lit deck #B93825 at dE 3.4 from the #BB3220 spec, the closest colour any buoy delivery has managed; four dark openings in a clean two-by-two; lantern present with pale housing, dark cap and finial. Ingested from a 2816x1536 frame padded to 1479px square, drawing 26x27px at world 28. ⚠️ THE DEFECT IS GLOSS, and it is the reason the subject's finish clause was rewritten after acceptance rather than before: the float carries a broad specular sweep, measured as a 37.8 luminance swing around the outer deck with 80% of it in a single directional lobe. The old wording listed `no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight` among a dozen other refusals at the end of the subject and it did not bite. The clause is now its own paragraph, names the exact artefact (a bright curved sweep of light across one side of the disc), says what it costs (a shiny plastic button instead of working steel) and gives the correct alternative (flat hard-edged facets). Shipped as-is because at 28px the sheen is invisible; fix it if this is ever regenerated. THE WHITE NUMBER BOARD IS GONE FROM THE SUBJECT, and this is a scale decision rather than a fidelity one. Both delivered candidates omitted it, the sprite reads correctly without it, and at world 28 the board is about 2px — under the 4-screen-px floor. Every element removed from a 28px sprite is a legibility gain, so it stays out. ⚠️ IT STAYS IN THE `bay` CARD SUBJECT, where the buoys are drawn at illustration scale and the board is plainly visible — the same object gets a different parts list at different sizes, which is the whole reason props and cards get separate subjects. AND THE WHITE DRUM BAND QUESTION IS SETTLED: it stays OFF. The retype note left this open pending the contact sheet, because dropping the old cone buoy's white band moved findability onto the four dark openings — a value cue instead of a hue cue. The sheet answers it: at 28px over both Glacier Sound and Pearl Lagoon this reads clearly as a nav aid, a coloured disc with a dark cross and a bright centre. So no band on the props and no band on the card reroll.

The reference buoy has no such band — its only white is the number board — so the band is gone and the findability job now falls to the FOUR DARK OPENINGS against the bright deck, which is a value cue rather than a hue cue and is why the greyscale clause was strengthened. If the delivery does not read as a nav aid at 28px on the contact sheet, the fix is to restore a white band at the drum's outer edge — and note that doing so would put the band back on the card's reroll too, so decide it once, on the contact sheet, before the card is generated. STATUS IS BACK TO `slot` DELIBERATELY even though a PNG still ships, and the distinction is worth drawing: the delivered art is not a poor version of the right object, it is the WRONG object, so it belongs in prompt.py --all-slots' queue rather than being annotated as stale. The shipped files stay on disk so the game keeps drawing a buoy until the reroll lands, and there is no master in inbox/ for either key, so an `ingest.py --all` cannot silently flip this back to art. planRound ADDED, which the old entry never carried and should have: the drum is the silhouette and it is round in plan, so ingest can measure the camera angle directly. The two candidates reviewed on 2026-08-10 came in at 1.023 and 1.011, so this gate costs nothing and catches the one failure this library cannot talk a generator out of. allowSymmetry STAYS TRUE: a buoy is deliberately four-fold symmetric and the new square cage is more so, so ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE's mandala/radial-symmetry terms would make the prompt argue with itself. ⚠️ THE PAIR MUST MATCH, AND THE LAST PAIR DID NOT — measured, so the next one can be checked the same way. Sampling the outer drum annulus of the two 2026-08-10 candidates, the red swung 19.5 in luminance with 79% of that in a single directional lobe (faceted, with a clear light direction) while the green swung 5.4 with only 9% (nearly flat, its modelling moved inward to the dome). Same words, two different objects. Both subjects now state the pair requirement explicitly and name light direction and facet treatment as part of it; generate them together and compare that number before accepting either. ⛔ FIRST LATTICE DELIVERY REJECTED 2026-08-10: IT CAME BACK WITH NO FLOAT AT ALL. The picture was a bare square cage — measured CIRCULARITY 0.634, which is the exact value of a square (a disc scores ~0.97, and the accepted red scored 0.974). The round steel float was not undersized or off-centre, it was simply never drawn. It also showed the tower's SIDES: corner posts rendered as three-dimensional boxes with their side faces visible, and diagonal cross-bracing along the bottom edge, which is a side elevation of a structure this camera cannot see the sides of. Colour was fine, at dE 7.2. ⚠️ THE GATE THAT MATTERED IS NOT THE ONE THAT WAS THERE, and this is the transferable finding. planRound measures the content bbox RATIO, and both candidates passed it comfortably — 1.026 for the red and 1.047 for this one — because A SQUARE IS ALSO AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE. The aspect test catches a tilted camera and is blind to a subject that came back the wrong SHAPE. What separates them is CIRCULARITY: filled area divided by the area of the smallest enclosing circle, where a disc lands near 0.97 and a square at 0.64. ADD THAT TO THE DELIVERY CHECKLIST FOR ANY ASSET WHOSE SILHOUETTE IS SUPPOSED TO BE A DISC — it is one line of arithmetic and it is the only check that would have caught this. THE PROMPT CAUSED IT, and the diagnosis is the beach plum's all over again: a CONSTRUCTION beats a CONSTRAINT. The old subject did say the drum was `the widest thing and the whole silhouette`, but it said it once, in clause (1), and then spent four consecutive clauses describing the cage. The cage dominated the reading and the float fell off the end of it. The rewrite binds the two together instead of stating them apart: the circle is now declared as the shape of the whole picture BEFORE the tower is introduced, the tower is defined by what it does not reach (`a clear unbroken RING OF BARE DECK shows all the way round it`), and a bare framework with no disc under it is named as the failure in the subject's own words. The no-visible-sides clause was also rewritten from a general statement into the specific artefacts that arrived — a post drawn as a 3D box, and diagonal bracing. WHAT TO CHECK ON THE REROLL, in order: circularity (under 0.90 is a reject), then that no post shows a side face and no diagonal bracing appears anywhere, then the ring of bare deck between tower and rim, then colour, then the gloss artefact the red shipped with. AND COMPARE IT AGAINST THE ACCEPTED RED BEFORE ACCEPTING IT: three consecutive pairs have failed to match each other, so the pair check is the one that keeps being skipped and keeps being wrong. ACCEPTED ROUND 2, 2026-08-10, clearing every gate the first lattice green failed. CIRCULARITY 0.997 and aspect 1.001 — both the best numbers any buoy has returned, and the float is unambiguously the whole silhouette. FOUR clean openings in a two-by-two, each ~2.8% of the sprite against the accepted red's 2.7-2.8%, so the openings themselves match the pair almost exactly. Lit deck #379A4F at dE 8.8 from the #268B34 spec — inside the <=10 gate, though plainly looser than the red's 3.4. NO SPECULAR SWEEP: 3% of the deck's luminance variation sits in a directional lobe, against 76% on the shipped red, so on the one axis the red actually failed, this green is the better sprite. The rewritten subject did its job: the clause that declares the circle before introducing the tower, and names a bare framework as the failure, took circularity from 0.634 to 0.997 in one roll. ⚠️ THE REMAINING DEFECT IS PROPORTION, AND IT IS THE FOURTH CONSECUTIVE PAIR MISMATCH — a new one each time: round 1 cone-vs-cone differed in finish, round 2 lattice differed in SHAPE (disc vs square), and this one differs in SCALE. The green's four openings span 66% x 66% of its disc against the red's 45% x 44%, so its tower is about 1.5x larger relative to its float and its ring of bare deck is correspondingly squeezed. Opening-pattern IoU between the two sprites is 35%. ACCEPTED ANYWAY, on the evidence rather than on tolerance: rendered side by side over bay water at the 28px they are actually played at, both read as a coloured disc with a dark cross and a bright centre, and the colour — which is the functional information — separates them instantly. The proportion gap is obvious at 112px and marginal at 28px, and nothing in this game draws them at 112px. THE PROMPT CAUSED IT AND THE FIX IS IN, which is the part worth carrying: the subject said `a clear unbroken RING OF BARE DECK shows all the way round it`, which is a description, not a specification — it is satisfied by any ring wider than zero, and two generations read it as 45% and 66%. It now names a fraction (ring about one-fifth of the disc on every side) and gives the measurable acceptance test in the terms the delivery check uses (the four openings together span a little under half the disc; two-thirds means the tower is too big). ⚠️ NOTE THE SHIPPED GREEN RUNS OVER THAT NEW LINE — it is the art that taught the lesson, so its own subject now describes something slightly tighter than what is on disk. Fix it whenever the pair is next regenerated, and generate the two TOGETHER when that happens. ONE MINOR STYLE DEVIATION, recorded and not acted on: the green carries a soft CAST SHADOW under the lantern and along the tower's lower-right, dark enough that at a 0.30 luminance threshold it bridges the four openings into one blob. The base NEGATIVE carries `drop shadow`. Invisible at 28px, and it is also the reason a first pass at counting the openings reported two instead of four — a measurement trap worth knowing about on any asset with interior shadow: threshold tight (0.22) before counting dark blobs, or a shadow will merge them.

assets.subject: A yellow cylindrical racing mark — the classic inflatable 'yellow can' — floating on open water, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, with none of its side visible anywhere. From this angle it is a FLAT CIRCULAR DISC with a taut inflated top: a narrow band of deeper, wetter yellow around the waterline, then a broad flat top face, and a bold dark lifting ring sitting at the exact centre as the one focal dot. Three or four faint radial seams run from the ring out to the rim, spaced evenly, reading as slightly darker lines that show the fabric panels. COLOUR: vivid safety yellow, warm and high-visibility, never mustard, never lime, never cream. It must be findable at a glance against pale turquoise shallows, olive swamp water and near-black polar water alike. Fill the frame: the buoy should reach close to the edges, with only a hair of margin. Engine rotation transforms the coordinate system rather than sampling a fixed frame, so nothing clips at any angle and padding only makes the buoy smaller than it should be. Build the form from FLAT HARD-EDGED BANDS OF CLEARLY DIFFERENT LIGHTNESS, not from smooth shading — a concentric object seen from above has no silhouette to read, so its value steps ARE its structure, and it must still make sense converted to greyscale. Absolutely no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient, no plastic sheen, no reflection. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set. No numbers, no letters, no text of any kind, no flag, no water, no ripple, no shadow
assets.note: Alternative race mark to the orange tetrahedron. Circular and radially symmetric, so it reads identically at any of the arbitrary rotations drawMarkBodies applies. MARK TAXONOMY (design decision, 2026-07-28): the orange tetrahedron is a TEMPORARY mark — an inflatable laid by the race committee for this race. The yellow can is a PERMANENT mark — a fixed installation the course is built around. Which one a course uses is a per-course choice, not a global one. Currently every course uses the orange temporary mark. SHIPPED AND READY BUT UNUSED: drawMarkBodies() resolves a single global markImg, so nothing renders this yet — using it needs marks to carry a sprite reference rather than share one. Measured contrast against water is ~2.4x the orange mark's at every venue (Glacier Sound 10.4:1 vs 4.4, Pearl Lagoon 2.7:1 vs 1.1, Gatorgrass 5.5:1 vs 2.3), and being a circle it is rotation-invariant where the tetrahedron is not.

assets.subject: A race committee boat anchored at the end of a start line, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating level, bow pointing to the TOP of the frame. It is a beamy 30-foot club launch — a working motorboat, never a yacht and never a racing hull: a long hull with a full wide midsection, near-parallel sides through the middle, a bluntly rounded bow, and a SQUARE cut-off transom across the stern. ABSOLUTELY NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING, no sail number, and nothing triangular anywhere on the deck — seen from directly above a racing sailboat is a pair of white triangles, and the single worst failure this sprite can have is being mistaken for one of the boats racing around it. THE READ IS A DARK CORE INSIDE A WHITE OUTLINE, which is the exact inverse of a sailboat's white sails inside a dark hull line — this is the whole point of the design. Working from the bow aft: a short pale foredeck with a small dark windlass block at its tip; then a hard-edged RECTANGULAR DECKHOUSE filling the forward half of the boat, its flat roof CHARCOAL and the darkest thing in the sprite, carrying one small pale dome at its centre; then a clear step of pale open deck; then a MID-NAVY canvas awning stretched over the open aft cockpit as a second rectangle, clearly LIGHTER than the charcoal roof so the two never merge into one smear. The white of the hull survives only as a clean margin running all the way around that dark core, widening at the bow and across the transom. THE SIGNATURE IS AN ORANGE FLAG, and it must be unmistakable. A short staff stands on the after deck and a bold rectangular safety-orange flag streams STRAIGHT AFT from it, out past the transom and clear of the hull, breaking the silhouette at the stern — the boat lies head to wind, so the flag blows down the frame. Render it as one flat solid orange rectangle with a slight ripple in its trailing edge, big enough to be the second thing the eye finds after the hull. This flag is what tells the player where the starting line ends, so it is functional information: keep it true safety orange and never shift it toward the colour of the water. COLOUR AND VALUE: clean off-white hull and deck with a single crisp deep-navy stripe following the sheerline the whole way around, charcoal deckhouse roof, mid-navy awning, safety-orange flag. Those extremes are deliberate — this sprite has to be findable on near-black polar water, where the white hull and the flag carry it, AND on pale turquoise shallows, where the charcoal roof and the navy stripe carry it. CONVERTED TO GREYSCALE the hull margin, the two roof rectangles and the flag must still read as separate steps. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps of lightness, absolutely no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient, no plastic sheen, no reflection. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set. Drawn at only about 85 pixels: bold simple shapes and no detail that would not survive that size. No crew, no figures, no water, no wake, no spray, no ripple, no anchor line, no cast shadow, no numbers, no letters, no lettering on the hull
assets.note: SHIPPED. A third mark KIND for the line ends, alongside the orange inflatable (temporary) and the yellow can (permanent): the vessel the line is sighted from. venuedoc's MARK_KINDS is now the one list — validator, editor dropdown and script.js's sprite registry all read it — and the eval fixtures already named the ends `sf-pin` and `sf-boat`, so the concept predated the art. VENUE-NEUTRAL like mark/zodiac/buoy-channel-*: race furniture at all ten venues, no palette clause. ROLE IS `traffic`, NOT `nav`, even though it is functionally a mark — the nav add-on emits 'use canonical buoyage shape and colour coding', which is buoy language and would push a boat toward red/green. The contract that binds is traffic's: never confusable with a competitor. The mark-function requirements (the orange flag, the line end) live in the subject text instead. SIZING: world 92 with fillTo 0.92 gives 37x85px = 9.2m at 9.2px/m, a 30ft club launch and 1.5x the 56px racing boat. That gap is the OPPOSITE call from the zodiac, which is deliberately SHORTER than a racer: a support RIB stays off the competitor read by being small, a committee boat by being big, boxy and white. 85px on an 1100-unit start line is 7.7% of it. Content filled 0.757 of the master, so fillTo upscales 1.22x — visible softening at 1024, invisible at 85. MEASURED CONTRAST (WCAG vs median water, at true race scale): Glacier Sound median 1.28:1 but brightest 10% 9.74:1; Pearl Lagoon median 2.84:1 with darkest 10% 5.32:1. That split IS the design — the white hull carries it on near-black water, the charcoal roof on pale turquoise — and both ends beat the zodiac (2.53 / 2.27 median). Judge it on the plates, as the zodiac's note argues: the player's own hull is 2.01:1 on lagoon. THREE RECORDED DEVIATIONS, none blocking. (1) The orange flag does NOT break the silhouette as the subject demanded: it is 107px of a 337px beam, entirely inside the hull footprint, and streams to starboard rather than aft. At 85px it is a ~12px orange dash on the white transom and still reads on both plates, but it is less findable than the macaroni-crest trick intended. If the line end is ever hard to spot, that is what to redraw. (2) A ~14px transparent slot separates a detached 13px navy contour ring from the hull, a background-remover artifact; 1.5px at race scale and invisible on the plates. (3) Teak deck striping is microtexture beyond spec and blurs to tan. Ingest passed with no warnings. ENGINE, ALL THREE BLOCKERS NOW FIXED. (1) drawMarkBodies resolved a single global markImg; it now resolves MARK_SPRITES[kind], which also lights up mark-can-yellow after a week shipped-but-unused. (2) It rotated every mark by an arbitrary per-position scramble, right for a tetrahedron and wrong for a vessel. orientCourseMarks() now freezes a heading from the LINE'S OWN NORMAL, signed by the direction of travel on the line's FIRST route use — not from the live wind (which oscillates every frame, so the hull would swing with every puff and the baked flag would fight the real breeze) and not per leg (a line sailed twice would spin the boat 180 degrees when the fleet came back to finish). The wobble stays: on a hull it reads as lying to an anchor. (3) markRadius 12 is now a per-mark body — a 3-circle r=19 capsule for the hull, and the sprite is nudged 19 units outboard along the line so the line's sailable span stays clear with the flagstaff on the mark point. Every consumer is written as (constant + bodyR) so a buoy's bodyR of 12 reproduces the old 50 and 115 exactly. Covered by eval/test_marks.js. The committee boat belongs on the STARBOARD end of its line; venuedoc warns when it is not, rather than enforcing it, because it is a convention. NOT YET PLACED ON ANY VENUE — that is an authoring decision, and it must not land on Sea Trial Bay, which is the eval anchor.

assets.subject: A rigid-hull inflatable boat — a Zodiac-type work RIB — seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating level, bow pointing to the TOP of the frame. THE SILHOUETTE IS THE WHOLE POINT: two fat parallel buoyancy tubes run the length of the boat and sweep together into a blunt rounded point at the bow, leaving a long open U-shaped well between them, and the stern is cut square and OPEN across the back — a horseshoe, never a pointed racing hull. The tubes read as thick cylinders, tapering to sealed conical ends at the transom, banded by three or four dark seams. Inside the well: a flat pale deck, one small dark centre console set just forward of amidships, and a plain bench seat behind it. A dark blocky outboard motor sits on the transom and overhangs the stern beyond the tubes. ABSOLUTELY NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING and no sail number — this is a powered working boat and must never be mistaken for a racing sailboat at a glance. COLOUR: bright safety orange tubes, warm and saturated, the canonical colour of a rescue and support RIB, with a mid-grey deck and near-black console and outboard for internal contrast. It has to stay findable against near-black polar water, deep blue and pale turquoise shallows alike. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps of lightness, no gloss, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set. No water, no wake, no spray, no ripple, no cast shadow, no crew, no figures, no flag
assets.note: VENUE-NEUTRAL like mark/buoy-channel-*: a support RIB is race furniture at every venue — committee boat, safety boat, and Glacier Sound's station tender for arctic-station. Kept venue-neutral deliberately so no palette clause tints it; safety orange is canonical everywhere. SIZING: world 54 with fillTo 0.92 gives a 50px hull = 5.4m at 9.2px/m, a real Zodiac Pro size and deliberately SHORTER than the 56px racing boat. That size gap is part of the `traffic` contract, but the silhouette does the real work: a horseshoe of tubes with an open transom shares no family with a pointed sailing hull, and it survives colour removal. Do NOT exaggerate it up to boat size for readability — that trades away the one thing keeping it off the competitor read. MEASURED CONTRAST (WCAG ratio vs flat water, at 54px): Glacier Sound — orange tubes 4.22:1, median pixel 2.53:1. Pearl Lagoon — median 2.27:1, tubes only 1.36:1, because orange and turquoise are opposed in HUE but nearly equal in LUMINANCE, so on lagoon water this prop is carried by hue and by its dark contour, not by value. That reads as a fail against the 3:1 floor until you measure the thing the floor is calibrated on: the player's own hull is 2.01:1 on Pearl Lagoon, WORSE than this. The 3:1 figure in the acceptance rubric is not met by the game's hero asset on lagoon water, so treat it as a target for dark venues and judge lagoon on the plate. Accepted on that basis.

GESTURE: holding station on a slight diagonal, both pectoral fins flat blades hinged low on the flanks and kept BELOW the jacket's shoulder line — fins, never arms, and never overlapping the chest panels.  LIMBS — Rainbow Trout has PECTORAL FINS: one pectoral fin lifted a little from the flank — a flat flexible blade, never a hand. BODY COVERING: this creature is covered in smooth wet skin with fine scales and nothing else — no feathers and no plumage, no fur, no wings. assets.subject: FLAT 2D VECTOR ART ON A FLAT UNIFORM BACKGROUND, and this is the first thing to get right: every shape is a solid fill of one colour with hard edges, and the background is ONE flat colour edge to edge, the same at the corners as it is against the hull — no vignette, no gradient, no glow, no halo, no drop shadow, and no coloured light spilling off the hull. A small coastal container ship underway. Seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating level, bow to the TOP of the frame — true plan view at both ends, top surfaces only, no hull side visible anywhere. THE SILHOUETTE IS A TALL RECTANGLE WITH ITS TWO TOP CORNERS ROUNDED INTO A BLUNT NOSE, about five times as long as it is wide. The bottom edge is a single straight horizontal line spanning the full beam: that line is the transom, it is the stern, and it is the LAST thing in the frame — below it there is only background. The sides run parallel for most of the length; only the top fifth narrows into the nose, which is blunt, never a point. A working cargo vessel — never a yacht, warship, ferry or racing hull. NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING and no white triangle anywhere: from above a racing sailboat is a pair of white triangles, and this ship shares the water with ten of them. THE READ, FROM BOW AFT. (1) A short triangular FORECASTLE deck at the stem in the hull colour, carrying one small dark anchor-windlass block. (2) The CARGO FIELD filling the middle three-fifths: containers in crisp transverse BAYS, each bay separated from the next by a thin seam of bare dark deck, so the field reads as a rhythm of coloured bands — the top-down signature of a container ship. (3) Hard aft, a crisp WHITE SUPERSTRUCTURE BLOCK spanning the full beam: the bridge, the brightest thing in the sprite. (4) Behind it, the funnel — from directly above a chimney is only its rim, so draw ONE SMALL DARK FLAT CIRCLE and nothing else: never a cone, never a cylinder with sides, never anything with height. (5) Behind that, a SHORT STRIP of plain navy deck, no more than a tenth of the ship's length, and then the transom line. That strip is the entire stern, and nothing is drawn aft of it: no second deck, no raised block, no darker band, no bevel, no step, no rounded stern face. Every generation so far has ended the ship with a rounded or stepped stern and every one was wrong. CONTAINER SIZE IS THE SCALE CUE and it is the clause to get right: each bay is a band of SIX NARROW containers spanning nearly the full beam, each an UPRIGHT rectangle about three times taller than it is wide, long side fore-and-aft. Many small slabs are what make this read as an enormous vessel; a bay of two or three oversized boxes makes it read as a toy tug, the single worst failure this sprite can have. EACH CONTAINER IS ONE FLAT RECTANGLE OF ONE FLAT COLOUR, drawn the way a colour-blocked flag is drawn — one solid fill with nothing inside it: no corrugation, no ribbing, no stripes across a slab, no lettering, no logos, no black outline around a box. The thin dark deck seams are the only thing separating one container from the next. COLOUR. The hull, forecastle and bare deck are DEEP NAVY, hex #2A3350 — a dark blue-grey surviving as a clean margin all the way around the cargo field, widening at the bow and across the transom. Every container is one of exactly five vivid colours: crimson, sunflower yellow, emerald green, cobalt blue, crisp white. NO CONTAINER IS BLACK, CHARCOAL, NAVY, TEAL OR ANY DARK TONE — a dark slab reads as a hole in the deck rather than as cargo, and cannot be told from a genuinely empty slot. No two touching containers share a colour, and exactly two slots in the field are empty, showing bare navy deck. THE VENUE'S SIGNAL COLOURS STAY OFF THE SHIP: no buoy red, no buoy green and no safety orange on the hull, deck or superstructure, and NO CONTAINER IS ORANGE — the orange race marks belong to the player's course reading. VALUE STEPS: in greyscale the navy hull margin, the mid-tone container field and the white bridge must read as three separate steps — the white bridge at the stern tells the player at a glance which way the ship is moving. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps, no gloss, no specular highlight, no gradient, no reflection. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set — never a fat sticker outline. No crew, no water, no wake, no spray, no cast shadow, no crane, no cables, no flags, no text and no numbers anywhere.
assets.note: Lighthouse Cove's signature traffic (venues.md 1): slow, utterly predictable, dragging an enormous moving WIND SHADOW — the hazard is its air, not its hull, and the shadow is engine-drawn, so the sprite carries no baked wake or disturbance. ROLE IS traffic, NOT hazard, by the committee-boat's reasoning: the hazard add-on asks for a spiky danger silhouette, and this ship's binding contract is never-confusable-with-a-competitor; the danger lives in the engine. SIZING: world 256 is the RESOLUTION CEILING, and the flagship takes all of it — ingest bakes world-props at world x 4 from a 1024 master (ingest.py), so 256 x 4 = 1024 is the largest bake that is a straight 1:1 copy with no resample; anything bigger upscales the master, and the committee boat's note records visible softening at just 1.22x. With fillTo 0.92 the visible hull is ~236px = ~25.6m at 9.2px/m — deliberately UNDER real feeder size (a true 90m coaster would be ~830px, past the master's budget and unmanageable on an 8750-unit world with an 1100-unit start line) but 4.2x the 56px racing hull and 1.5x the largest existing prop (arctic-station, 170), the biggest object in the game, which is the venue's whole brief. CONSTRUCTION taken from top-down reference photography: transverse container bays separated by bare-deck seams, triangular forecastle at the stem, full-beam bridge block aft. CONTAINERS ARE BRIGHT per the base style's 'vivid saturated jewel-toned color'; the buoy guardrail covers only the ship's own large surfaces plus a total ban on orange containers, because the inflatable race marks own orange. FAMILY: -b and -c are the same species at world 216 and 176 with oxide-red and bottle-green hulls, per the arctic-orca-b distinguishable-at-a-glance precedent; venues.md specifies THE cargo ship, singular, on a schedule — three liveries exist so different races draw different ships, not so three steam at once. ROUND-1 REVIEW (all ships): two-across toy-tug scale, corrugation, grey gradient bg with baked glow, fat sticker outlines — each now banned by name, generate with --bg white. ROUND-2 REVIEW (this ship, closest to acceptance): white bg finally clean and the six-across scale read landed; remaining were the stern step AGAIN (transom clause now says NOTHING beyond the transom line, naming the repeat), a still-daggerish bow, teal drifting to emerald (ACCEPTED — emerald is now the specified green: it matches reference photography, and a lone 8px slab among many cannot read as an isolated buoy can; the signal ban only ever protected large surfaces), and one black container ambiguous with an empty slot (black/charcoal containers now banned as hole-readers). WARNING, twice now: this manifest entry has been silently reverted to the committed file between working sessions — commit after editing. ROUND-3 (still the leader): cargo field fully correct — eight bays, six across, flat slabs, emerald in the mix. Two failures left, and both look procedural: the stern rounded off with a step AGAIN — negation was not beating the model's rounded-stern prior, so the clause now describes the silhouette positively as a rounded-top rectangle with a flat bottom edge — and the grey glow background returned after round 2 came back clean white, which suggests the round-3 generation was not pasted from the --bg white prompt output; verify the pasted text before rerolling. ROUND-4: ACCEPTED AND INGESTED as the venue's working flagship, with two known defects left standing because the bay level needed a ship to build against. The cargo field is right at last — six across, upright flat slabs, correct bay rhythm, blunt bow, white bridge reading as the stern. Defects carried: the stern step AGAIN (a large empty navy panel below the bridge, then a rounded bottom), and three or four black slabs in the field, ambiguous with the intentional empty slots. HULL COLOUR CHANGED BY ACCEPTANCE, graphite charcoal -> DEEP NAVY #2A3350: the round-4 roll came back navy (measured #323B52, H=223 S=0.44), it looks better than graphite and it separates the ship from the tug's charcoal fender rim, so the subject now specifies navy rather than spending rolls fighting back to grey. Anyone rerolling this ship should know the shipped bake is ~3.8:1 length to beam and the level is built against that footprint. ROUND-4 REWRITE (all three subjects rebuilt, not patched): rounds 1-3 grew each subject to ~700 words that were mostly negations, and the same four failures came back anyway — stern step, corrugation, glow background, 3D funnel. The rewrite applies four rules the entry's own history had already proved. ONE, ORDER BY WHAT BLOCKS THE PIPELINE: the medium and background clauses now open the prompt instead of closing it, because the background ban spent three rounds in the weakest position in the text — the last sentence — and was ignored every time. TWO, POSITIVE CONSTRUCTION OVER NEGATION: the one clause that ever landed first try was the funnel, stated as what a chimney IS from above rather than as a list of what not to draw. assets.subject: FLAT 2D VECTOR ART ON A FLAT UNIFORM BACKGROUND, and this is the first thing to get right: every shape is a solid fill of one colour with hard edges, and the background is ONE flat colour edge to edge, the same at the corners as it is against the hull — no vignette, no gradient, no glow, no halo, no drop shadow, and no coloured light spilling off the hull. A SECOND small coastal container ship, a different vessel from the first: the same overhead construction, told apart at a glance by its colour and its lading. Seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating level, bow to the TOP of the frame — true plan view at both ends, top surfaces only, no hull side visible anywhere. THE HULL COLOUR IS THE HARDEST PART OF THIS SPRITE AND IT IS NOT A RED. It is TERRACOTTA — oxide brown, the colour of an unglazed clay flowerpot, of rusted iron, of a weathered brick wall — hex #A64B32 exactly: a dusty, muted, brownish orange, dark and clearly desaturated. This ship shares the water with a RED CHANNEL BUOY painted hex #E61E14, and the two can never be mistakable for one another: the hull must read visibly duller, browner and darker than that buoy. Every previous attempt came back a bright saturated signal red and every one was rejected — if the hull looks like a fire engine, a pillar box, a stop sign or a ripe tomato, it is wrong. Mix brown and grey into it until it looks dusty and old. THE SILHOUETTE IS A TALL RECTANGLE WITH ITS TWO TOP CORNERS ROUNDED INTO A BLUNT NOSE, about five times as long as it is wide. The bottom edge is a single straight horizontal line spanning the full beam: that line is the transom, it is the stern, and it is the LAST thing in the frame — below it there is only background. The sides run parallel for most of the length; only the top fifth narrows into the nose, which is blunt, never a point. A working cargo vessel — never a yacht, warship, ferry or racing hull. NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING and no white triangle anywhere: from above a racing sailboat is a pair of white triangles, and this ship shares the water with ten of them. THE READ, FROM BOW AFT. (1) A short triangular FORECASTLE deck at the stem in terracotta, carrying one small dark anchor-windlass block. (2) The CARGO FIELD of SIX transverse bays, PART-LOADED IN AN EXACT PATTERN: counting from the bow, bays 1, 2, 4 and 5 CARRY CONTAINERS and bays 3 and 6 are EMPTY, showing a broad flat hatch cover in the deck's own terracotta. Four loaded, two empty, and the two empty bays are never next to each other — a working freighter with two gaps in its load. A deck that is mostly bare, or bare all the way through the middle, reads as a BARGE rather than a freighter, and that is this sprite's characteristic failure. (3) Hard aft, a WARM CREAM superstructure block spanning the full beam: the bridge, the brightest thing in the sprite. (4) Behind it, the funnel — from directly above a chimney is only its rim, so draw ONE SMALL DARK FLAT CIRCLE and nothing else: never a cone, never a cylinder with sides, never anything with height. (5) Behind that, a SHORT STRIP of plain terracotta deck, no more than a tenth of the ship's length, and then the transom line. That strip is the entire stern, and nothing is drawn aft of it: no second deck, no raised block, no darker band, no bevel, no step, no rounded stern face. Every generation so far has ended the ship with a rounded or stepped stern and every one was wrong. The deck, the hatch covers and the hull are ONE plain flat terracotta with nothing drawn on them: no plank lines, no wood grain, no striping, no hatching, no ribbing along the hull sides. CONTAINER SIZE IS THE SCALE CUE and it is the clause to get right: each loaded bay is a band of FIVE NARROW containers spanning nearly the full beam, each an UPRIGHT rectangle about three times taller than it is wide, long side fore-and-aft. Many small slabs are what make this read as a big vessel; a bay of two or three oversized boxes makes it read as a toy tug, the single worst failure this sprite can have. EACH CONTAINER IS ONE FLAT RECTANGLE OF ONE FLAT COLOUR, drawn the way a colour-blocked flag is drawn — one solid fill with nothing inside it: no corrugation, no ribbing, no stripes across a slab, no lettering, no logos, no black outline around a box. The thin dark deck seams are the only thing separating one container from the next. COLOUR. Every container is one of exactly four vivid colours: crimson, sunflower yellow, emerald green, cobalt blue. No crisp-white containers here — the cream bridge must stay the single brightest mass — and none black, charcoal or any dark tone, because a dark slab reads as a hole. No two touching containers share a colour. THE VENUE'S SIGNAL COLOURS STAY OFF THE SHIP: no buoy red, no buoy green and no safety orange on the hull, deck or superstructure, and NO CONTAINER IS ORANGE — the orange race marks belong to the player's course reading. VALUE STEPS: in greyscale the terracotta hull margin, the container bands and the cream bridge must read as three separate steps — the bright bridge at the stern tells the player at a glance which way the ship is moving. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps, no gloss, no specular highlight, no gradient, no reflection. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set — never a fat sticker outline. No crew, no water, no wake, no spray, no cast shadow, no crane, no cables, no flags, no text and no numbers anywhere.
