BEAM FOLLOWS: the shipped roll is 3.8:1, which at world 720 draws 3.2 boat lengths WIDE; a real feeder is 6:1, so the subjects now ask for 5:1 (-c 4:1). That also settles the tug conflict below — -c at 4:1 clears the tug's 3:1 outright, so neither entry has to move. BACKGROUND KEY, CORRECTED: generate this family --bg magenta, NOT --bg white as rounds 2-3 instructed. dekey.py's own docstring gives the reason and the ships are its worst case — limit 2 is a pale mass touching the silhouette edge, and the full-beam white/cream bridge is exactly that (on -b it visibly overhangs the hull sides). Magenta sits 255 RGB units from white so no threshold that clears the key can reach the bridge. If a generation still arrives on a vignette or a glow, dekey.py --gradient keys it: the flat fill measures tolerance against the seed pixel and therefore has NO correct threshold on a graded backdrop (the round-4 flagship ran 140 at the corners to 68 at the hull, so clearing it needs >216 while the hull sits at 303 — the --inspect sweep walks the bbox inward and never plateaus). --gradient measures neighbour to neighbour instead, where backdrop noise is ~6 and the hull contour is ~400. That is a fallback for a bad roll, not a licence to stop asking for a flat background: the glow still costs contrast at race scale. MASTER RAISED 2026-08-09 from 1536 to the delivered size. These are the biggest props in the game — world 720 against a 40-unit buoy — so they are exactly the subject master_for's own note has in mind when it says master size is a per-subject question and the cove cargo ship is not finished at 1024. At 1536 the ship held 1325px of hull against a 1440px bake, i.e. the bake was inventing the top 8%; at the delivered size the bake is a real downsample throughout.

assets.subject: A harbour TUGBOAT, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating level, bow pointing to the TOP of the frame. COMPLETELY FLAT 2D VECTOR-STYLE RENDERING, and this is where this sprite goes wrong: every shape is a flat fill seen square from its top — no bevelled edges, no isometric walls on the wheelhouse, no 3D depth anywhere, and the deck is ONE unbroken flat ochre colour with no mottling, no camouflage patches, no pixel texture of any kind. TRUE PLAN VIEW AT BOTH ENDS: only top surfaces show — no hull side, no curved stern face, no perspective step anywhere. THE PROPORTION IS THE IDENTITY: short and very beamy, barely three times as long as it is wide, with a broad bluntly rounded bow and a squared transom — the stubby silhouette belongs to this boat alone, the exact opposite of every sleek hull in the harbour, and it must read as a tug even in silhouette with colour removed. It is a working powerboat — never a yacht, never a cabin cruiser and never a racing hull: ABSOLUTELY NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING, no sail number and no white triangle anywhere — seen from directly above a racing sailboat is a pair of white triangles, and this boat shares the water with ten of them. THE SIGNATURE IS THE FENDER RIM: a thick charcoal-black rubber fender band runs unbroken around the entire hull edge, swelling noticeably thicker across the bow's push face — the one feature that says TUG from any angle. Draw it as ONE SMOOTH CONTINUOUS band of a single flat dark colour — no segment lines, no tyre bumps, no links, no texture inside the band. THE READ, FROM BOW AFT: inside the fendered bow a short OCHRE-YELLOW foredeck with one small dark anchor-windlass block; just forward of amidships a compact WHITE WHEELHOUSE BLOCK — from directly above a flat white rounded square with NO visible walls and no drawn sides — the brightest thing in the sprite, and immediately behind it the funnel, which from directly above is nothing but a SMALL DARK FLAT CIRCLE, because a chimney seen from its top is only its rim: never a cone, never a cylinder with visible sides, never anything with height; then the whole aft half is open working deck in the same ochre-yellow, carrying a single dark H-shaped towing bitt at its centre and nothing else — the big empty aft deck is what separates a tug from a pleasure boat. COLOURS: warm ochre-yellow deck — a rich mustard, clearly duller and browner than a sunflower-yellow shipping container and nowhere near safety orange — charcoal-black fender rim and funnel, crisp white wheelhouse. THE VENUE'S SIGNAL COLOURS STAY OFF THIS BOAT: never buoy red, never buoy green, never safety orange anywhere — those belong to the navigation marks and race furniture the player is reading. VALUE STEPS: converted to greyscale, the dark fender rim, the mid-tone ochre deck and the white wheelhouse must read as three separate steps. THIS IS A SMALL BOAT AND MUST READ SMALL: one wheelhouse, one funnel, one bitt, and no other deck furniture — bold simple shapes with no fine detail, designed to stay legible at roughly 70 pixels. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps of lightness, no gloss, no shine, no specular highlight, no smooth gradient, no reflection. A thin clean dark contour, no heavier than the rest of the set — never a fat sticker outline. Absolutely no rim light, no outer glow, no halo, no backlight, no vignette and no drawn drop shadow; the background is one flat uniform colour edge to edge. No crew, no figures, no water, no wake, no bow wave, no spray, no cast shadow, no towline, no barge, no crane, no flags, no text or numbers anywhere
assets.note: Fourth vessel of Lighthouse Cove's working-harbour traffic. ROLE traffic, same contract as the cargo family: never confusable with a competitor, danger (if any) lives in the engine. THE STUBBY SILHOUETTE IS RESERVED: the cargo ships' round-1 review named 'reads as a toy tug' as their single worst failure, so the real tug owns the short-and-beamy proportion exclusively — ships are long, banded and sleek; the tug is short, plain-decked and rimmed in black fender. That division of silhouette space is the design, and it is what makes both reads survive with colour removed. SIZING: world 76 with fillTo 0.92 is ~70px visible = ~7.6m at 9.2px/m — deliberately far under a real 25-30m harbour tug, because the visual hierarchy (zodiac 54 < player 56 < tug 76 < committee 92 << ships 176-256) matters more than true scale, per the scale registry's exaggeration rule. IDENTITY COLOUR is the ochre-yellow deck: chosen against the fleet — committee boat is white-hulled with a dark core, zodiac is grey tubes, the ships are dark-hulled with jewel cargo — and specified as mustard so it cannot drift into sunflower-container yellow or safety orange; drift toward orange is the reroll trigger at review, since the orange inflatable marks and committee flag are race furniture. The fender rim doubles as the greyscale dark step, so the sprite still reads on pale turquoise water where a dark hull margin would carry it, and the white wheelhouse carries it on near-black water — the committee boat's two-ended contrast strategy. Schedule and behaviour (harbour crossings, ship escort) are engine/authoring work recorded with the venue; if a towed barge is ever wanted it is a SEPARATE sprite composed behind the tug at runtime, never baked into this one — a baked towline fixes the tow angle and the class rule already bans baked water and cables. WARNING: the cargo-family manifest entries have twice been silently reverted to the committed file between working sessions — commit after editing. ROUND-1 (closest first roll of the project — proportion, fender rim, windlass, H-bitt and layout all landed): every failure was the same disease, a 3D render — bevelled isometric wheelhouse walls, a leaning 3D cone funnel, a drop shadow, and mottled pixel-camo patches on the deck. The subject now opens with the cargo-b flat-2D clause, the wheelhouse is a flat rounded square with no visible walls, the funnel a flat dark circle (a chimney from its top is only its rim), the deck one unbroken flat ochre, and the fender band explicitly seamless — the round-1 rim came back segmented like tyre links.

assets.subject: A WORKING FISHING TRAWLER, bow to the TOP of the frame, about three and a half times as long as it is wide. Everything about it should say WORKING BOAT — battered, purposeful, cluttered with gear — and never pleasure craft, never warship, never cargo carrier. THE OPEN AFTER DECK IS THE SUBJECT AND THE PROOF OF THE CAMERA: the back two thirds of the boat is a bare open working deck and you are looking straight DOWN into it, so its planked floor and everything lying on it are flat shapes seen from above. No bulwark wall, no freeboard, no side of the hull anywhere — the gunwale is a clean outline around the deck and nothing more. Forward, a compact WHITE WHEELHOUSE block set across the boat, with a short dark mast beside it carrying a small radar scanner that reads from above as a flat dark bar on a disc. Behind the wheelhouse, on the open deck: a NET DRUM lying ACROSS the boat near the stern, which from directly overhead is a broad rectangle with the wound net drawn as tight parallel bands along it — you see the wound roll, never the round end of the drum. Just aft of it the GANTRY, reading as two short feet planted at the deck edges with a single beam lying flat across between them — a frame seen in plan, not standing up. Two long OUTRIGGER BOOMS lie stowed fore-and-aft, one along each side, overhanging the stern slightly. Scattered over the deck, a few pale crates, two coils of rope drawn as flat spirals, and three or four orange floats. The hull is a deep TEAL-GREEN with a black boot-top line around the outside and rust streaks bleeding down from the deck fittings; the transom is squared off. No net in the water, no wake, no water, no fish, no people
assets.note: Fifth working vessel of Lighthouse Cove's harbour, and it fills the ladder's biggest hole: the cove ran 32 dinghy / 48 motorboat / 76 tug and then jumped to 496 for the smallest cargo ship. 140u is 4.4 boat lengths — a ship-sized working boat that is unmistakably not a freighter. DISTINGUISHABLE AT A GLANCE from the two vessels nearest it in size, on the axis that survives reduction: the tug is stubby (2.4:1) with a fendered bow and a bare deck, this is longer (3.5:1) with an open after deck full of gear and two booms down its sides. Teal is the last hull colour the harbour has not spent — navy, rust-red, bottle-green, ochre and white are all taken — which is the arctic-orca-b rule the whole family follows. MASTER 1536, not the profile's 1024 and not the ships' 2752: bake is world*4 = 560px, so 1536 leaves 1413px of content feeding it at 2.5x oversampled, which is real headroom without archiving a 3072 square for a 140u prop. world 140 is well under master/4, so bake 4 is free here and no pixel is invented. ROLE traffic, same contract as the rest: never confusable with a competitor, danger lives in the engine. When the art lands: plane surface, contact none like the family — though at 3.5:1 and 140u a circle fits it better than it fits the ships, so if the harbour ever gets colliders this and the motorboat are the two to do first.

assets.subject: A LEISURE MOTORBOAT — a white fibreglass sport cruiser of the kind moored all over a sailing bay, about three times as long as it is wide. Bow to the TOP of the frame. WHAT YOU SEE LOOKING STRAIGHT DOWN INTO AN OPEN BOAT, and this is the whole test of the camera: the cockpit is OPEN and you are looking down into it, so its floor and seats are visible as flat shapes lying inside the hull, seen from above and never from in front. No freeboard, no topside, no side of the hull, no wall of any kind — the gunwale reads as a clean outline around the opening and nothing more. Forward, a small pointed white foredeck with a low rail and a cleat. Across the middle, the WINDSCREEN as a single narrow dark band spanning the boat, with the helm console just behind it to one side — a compact dark block with a small wheel. Two pale seats side by side at the helm and a bench across the stern, all drawn as simple rounded pads seen from above. At the transom, a single dark outboard engine reading as a squat block overhanging the stern. Hull white with ONE bold colour stripe running the length of each side — deep marine blue — and a pale non-slip deck. No wake, no spray, no water, no people
assets.note: Lighthouse Cove's small craft, and the only vessel in the venue anywhere near a competitor's size — 48u against a 32u racing dinghy. That makes its ONE job the traffic contract's hardest case: never confusable with a boat in the race. It wins that on silhouette rather than size — no rig, no sail, an OPEN cockpit full of seats and an outboard on the transom, none of which a dinghy has from above. Fills the gap between the dinghy and the 76u tug, which was the only stretch of the cove's size ladder with nothing in it. bake 4 (the profile default) is right here: world 48 is far under master/4, so nothing is upscaled.

assets.subject: A CRUISE SHIP, the largest vessel in the harbour — a long white liner about seven times as long as it is wide, bow to the TOP of the frame. From straight above a cruise ship is a WHITE DECK, and the ship's identity is the row of small shapes down each side of it. THE LIFEBOATS ARE THE SIGNATURE and the proof of the camera: a regular row of eight to ten little enclosed boats hangs along EACH side of the ship, evenly spaced, and from directly overhead you see the TOP of each one — a small rounded orange capsule lying lengthways, never its side and never a davit standing up beside it. The superstructure is TIERED, and tiers seen from above are nested outlines, not stacked walls: a broad white deck the length of the ship, a narrower white deck inset within it, and a smaller one again on top, each step reading as a clean line with a thin shadow and no visible height. On the open upper deck, two rectangular swimming pools in bright pool-blue with pale surrounds, and a scatter of tiny deck furniture. Aft of midships one broad funnel in a deep navy blue, seen end-on as a rounded oval cap. The bow is a fine point with a small foredeck; the stern is squared off with a rounded open deck. The hull shows as a thin navy band just outside the white all the way round. No wake, no water, no people
assets.note: The biggest hull in the game — 820u, over the 720u lead cargo ship and under the 870/920u bridges it is meant to pass beneath, which is the size relationship worth protecting if any of these move. Role traffic, same contract as the cargo family: never confusable with a competitor, danger lives in the engine. DISTINGUISHABLE FROM THE CARGO SHIPS AT A GLANCE, and on the axis that survives reduction: they are a field of multicoloured container blocks, this is a plain white deck with two orange lifeboat rows and two blue pools. allowSymmetry because those lifeboat rows are DELIBERATELY evenly spaced, which ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE otherwise forbids — the bridges' lattice made the same argument. bake 2 like the cargo family: world 820 is past master/4, so bake 4 would invent pixels.

assets.subject: A DOUBLE-ENDED CAR FERRY, the kind that shuttles cars across a cold northwestern sound between evergreen shores, about four and a half times as long as it is wide. BOTH ENDS ARE THE SAME END and that is the whole design: this vessel has no bow and no stern. Fold the picture in half across its waist and the two halves match — the same broad blunt chisel-shaped end at the top of the frame and at the bottom, the same open car deck inside each, the same pilot house standing over each. It drives forward in both directions and never turns round, so the bottom edge of the frame is a SECOND BOW and never the flat transom line every other ship in this harbour ends with. THE OPEN CAR DECKS ARE THE PROOF OF THE CAMERA. A quarter of the length at each end is open vehicle deck in dark asphalt grey and you are looking straight DOWN into it: three lanes of cars running FORE AND AFT, two rows deep, each car a small rounded rectangle seen from its roof with a darker glass band across each end of it — never a side, a wheel or a headlight. Two spaces left empty, showing bare deck. The lanes run the LONG way and never as bands across the beam: a colour field banded across the deck is how the container ships here read, and this must not read as one. Between them, filling about half the length, the PASSENGER CABIN — one long clean WHITE roof, its edges parallel to the sides, carrying a few pale vents and skylights and, down its centre, a narrow open sun deck with two rows of tiny benches. At each end of that cabin a PILOT HOUSE: a small white box set across the vessel with a dark window band wrapping right round it and a DEEP GREEN roof, a short dark radar bar on a disc beside it. Two of them, identical, facing opposite ways. Amidships, one small dark flat oval on each side of the cabin roof — a stack seen from directly above is only its rim, so draw the rim and nothing else: never a cone, never a cylinder with sides, never anything with height. COLOUR IS WHITE AND EVERGREEN. Hull, bulwarks, cabin and pilot houses are CRISP WHITE. One broad DEEP EVERGREEN band, hex #14523A, runs the full length of each side just inside the silhouette edge and wraps around both ends — a single unbroken stripe framing the whole vessel, about a twelfth of the beam wide, and the only large colour in the picture. It is a dark forest green with a blue lean, never the bright green of a channel buoy. Vehicle decks asphalt grey, hex #454C55. The cars carry the only vivid colour — crimson, sunflower yellow, cobalt blue, silver-grey, crisp white, no two touching cars alike. In greyscale it reads as a PALE VESSEL WITH A DARK PATCH AT EACH END. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps: no gloss, no specular highlight, no gradient, and no glow or halo bleeding off the white hull into the background. A thin clean dark contour, never a fat sticker outline. NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING and no white triangle anywhere — from above a racing sailboat is a pair of white triangles and this ferry shares the water with ten of them. No rows of orange lifeboats down the sides; those belong to the liner it shares the harbour with. No buoy red, no buoy green, no safety orange. No crew, no water, no wake, no spray, no cast shadow, and no lettering, name, text or numbers anywhere
assets.note: Eighth vessel of Lighthouse Cove's harbour and the first drawn FOR the traffic engine rather than adapted to it. THE DOUBLE END IS AN ENGINE ARGUMENT, not a styling choice: js/traffic.js implements end: 'pingpong' and script.js draws the return leg with `v.heading = reverse ? p.heading + Math.PI : p.heading`, so every other hull in this harbour would run its return leg STERN-FIRST. A double-ender is the one shape for which that is correct — a vessel with no stern to run first. cove-traffic-plan.md 11 records pingpong as implemented and unexercised because no venue authors it; this is the asset that gives it something to be for, and a ferry shuttling a crossing on a fixed period is the cyclic class venues.md asks the cove for (dangerous on a learnable rhythm). THE LOOK IS THE PUGET SOUND DOUBLE-ENDER: white hull, one evergreen band wrapping the whole vessel, a white passenger cabin filling the middle half, twin pilot houses standing at its ends facing opposite ways, twin stacks amidships, and an open car deck at each end. IT IS DESCRIBED AND NEVER NAMED — no operator, no vessel name and no lettering anywhere in the subject or on the sprite. Naming a real fleet asks the generator for that fleet's branding, and what should ship is the TYPE, not a particular boat off someone else's water. The 4.5:1 proportion comes from the reference too: real hulls of this class run 4.2:1 to 5.2:1. SCALE IS A LADDER DECISION, NOT A FIDELITY ONE, and the reference makes that visible: a real vessel of this class is 100-140 m, which at the bay's 9.2 px/m would be 920-1290u — bigger than anything in the game. The whole harbour is compressed the same way (the 720u flagship stands in for a 150 m feeder at 78 m), so the ferry sits where the LADDER needs it. The cove ran 32 dinghy / 48 motorboat / 76 tug / 140 trawler and then jumped 3.5x to 496 for the smallest freighter; 300u lands 2.1x over the trawler and 1.65x under the coaster, at 5.5 racing hulls of 55u. DISTINGUISHABLE AT A GLANCE, and this one needed thought because the obvious ferry read is dangerous: a deck full of small coloured rectangles is precisely how the three container ships read at race scale. Three things separate them and all three are load-bearing. (1) WHERE THE COLOUR SITS — cars in two bounded clusters at the ENDS with a white cabin between them, against a container field running the whole middle. (2) LANE DIRECTION — cars in lanes fore and aft, containers in transverse bays, so one is dotted lines along the hull and the other a striped ladder across it. (3) VALUE — the freighters are a dark hull margin around a bright field with one white block at the stern, this is a pale vessel with a dark patch at each end; in greyscale they are each other's negative, and the freighters' read is DIRECTIONAL where this one deliberately is not. If the delivered roll still smears against the cargo family on the contact sheet, the fix is FEWER AND BIGGER cars or a shorter car deck, not a new hull colour — see next. IT DOES NOT TAKE A FREE HULL COLOUR, and that breaks the family's own arctic-orca-b rule knowingly, twice over. White is already worn by the 48u motorboat and the 820u liner, and the evergreen band at #14523A lands within a few units of the coaster's bottle green #1F4D2E. Both are accepted deliberately: white and evergreen ARE the look; a stripe a twelfth of a 67u beam wide is not in a squint contest with a 496u green hull; and inventing a different green to dodge a collision that does not exist at race scale would cost the only thing this asset is for. Separation is bought on size (6.3x over the motorboat, 2.7x under the liner), on the double end, and on the value pattern above. THE PAIR TO CHECK ON THE CONTACT SHEET IS THIS AGAINST cove-cruise-ship: two white vessels, and the answer has to hold at race scale — 4.5:1 against 7:1, green edge against navy edge, two dark car decks against orange lifeboat rows and blue pools. PROPORTION ARITHMETIC, since the cars are the clause most likely to be fudged: at 300u and 4.5:1 the beam is 67u, a 1.8 m car is 17u wide and a 4.5 m car is 41u long. Three lanes is 51u of the beam plus walkways, and two rows deep needs about 85u — a quarter of the length — at each end. That is why the cabin covers about half the length here where a real one covers nearer two thirds: the cars are what say FERRY from above, so they were given the room. A roll that comes back with two enormous cars per row is the container family's toy-tug failure in another costume; reroll it. SILHOUETTE NEIGHBOURS: 4.5:1 sits between the coaster's 4:1 and the flagship's 5:1, and neither is a collision — they are 1.65x and 2.4x bigger and read as dark-margined container fields. The tug's reserved stubby band (barely three times as long as it is wide) is nowhere near this asset. allowSymmetry, and it earns it twice: ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE forbids symmetrical arrangement and evenly spaced, and this vessel is mirror-symmetric FORE AND AFT by construction and near enough port and starboard as well — only the car colours break it. It is also the only hull in the harbour that passes ORTHO_LONG's acceptance test literally: the far end is exactly as wide as the near end is a tilt check everywhere else and a construction rule here. SIZING: world 300 with bake 4 is a 1200px bake; master 2048 at fillTo 0.92 holds 1884px of content, so the bake is a real 1.57x downsample and no pixel is invented. 1536 would also clear it (1413px, 1.18x) and leaves nothing if world ever moves, which is why this asks for 2048. gen 1024x3072 for a long subject — a square frame spends three quarters of itself on empty water and caps the length, per the profile's own note. THE SUBJECT IS DELIBERATELY SHORTER THAN THE CARGO FAMILY'S — 617 words, against 822/1007/1021 for the three ships and 314/250/231 for the trawler, the liner and the motorboat. It sits between the two groups rather than with the short ones, and the words it does spend are all on claims nobody in this library has generated before: the double end, the three-band layout, and the anti-container clauses. That split is the experiment those cargo entries asked for in writing: four rounds of GROWING them did not stop the stern step, the corrugation, the glow or the 3D funnel coming back, and their round-4 rewrite records that cutting hard is the untried lever. The three shortest subjects in this family are also the three whose notes record no reroll history at all. So this one drops the cargo family's long medium-and-background preamble and keeps a single compact anti-glow line, which is the one clause a white hull on a chroma key cannot afford to lose. If the first roll lands, that is a data point for short; if it fails, write down WHICH clause failed before adding words to the others. BACKGROUND: if dekey.py is the path, generate --bg magenta. The cargo family's argument applies here at full strength — its worst case is a pale mass touching the silhouette edge, and on this vessel the pale mass IS the hull, all the way round. Never key a white ferry on white. REGISTERED 2026-08-10 as bay-cove-ferry: plane surface, contact none like the family, hull [0.920, 0.279] measured off the bake. The measured hull IS the registration — the editor gates its vessel list on one, so the kind is authorable as traffic the moment it exists. STILL OPEN: no venue authors it yet. It wants end: 'pingpong' across the cove mouth, which would be the first venue use of that lifecycle. DELIVERED 2026-08-10, FIRST ROLL, KEPT. Everything the three-band layout asked for landed: no transom at either end, cars in fore-and-aft lanes on both open decks, the white cabin between them with two green-roofed pilot houses facing opposite ways, twin stack ovals, and the evergreen band wrapping the whole hull. MEASURED off the bake: hull [0.920, 0.279], 276u x 84u, aspect 3.30:1 against the 4.5:1 asked — a quarter beamier than specified, which moves it from between the coaster and the flagship to between the tug's 2.45:1 and the coaster's 4:1. Kept: the identity is the double end and the deck content, not the ratio, and nothing at 300u is in a squint contest with a 76u tug. THE VALUE INVERSION IS CONFIRMED AND MEASURABLE — greyscale thirds run 112 / 192 / 109, dark at both ends and bright in the middle, which is the freighters' pattern turned inside out exactly as the subject asked. The green came back #004830 against #14523A asked: deeper and purer, so it moved AWAY from the coaster's #1F4D2E and the collision this entry worried about got smaller rather than larger. White is a cyan-leaning #D8F0F0 rather than neutral, which costs nothing on azure water. SIGNAL-COLOUR AUDIT: five warm saturated masses on the car decks, worst #D04030 at dE 49 from buoy red #E61E14 and 0.19% of the hull — two orders below the -b hull failure that set the family's standing trigger (a whole hull at dE ~20), and a 0.2% speck on dark asphalt is not a buoy. Nothing near safety orange. NOT FIXED, NOT WORTH A REROLL: the pilot houses and stacks carry soft drop shadows the style bans; they are visible at 4x and gone at race scale.

assets.subject: A HIGH-SPEED PASSENGER CATAMARAN — a lean white fast ferry, bow to the TOP of the frame, about five times as long as it is wide. It is a bright civilian day boat carrying holidaymakers to an island: never grey, never naval, never a warship. TWO HULLS ARE THE SILHOUETTE AND THE FIRST THING TO GET RIGHT. This vessel rides on a PAIR of slender parallel hulls with a tunnel of open water between them, and one broad deck bridges across the top of both. The deck covers the tunnel amidships, so the water between the hulls shows in exactly two places: a narrow V-SHAPED NOTCH of background cut into the TOP of the frame between TWO SEPARATE FINE POINTED BOWS, and a matching square notch at the BOTTOM between two squared transoms. Those two notches are the proof that there are two hulls and they must survive at a glance — everything else about this boat could be a monohull. The outer sides run parallel the whole length. THE OPEN SUN DECK IS THE SIGNATURE AND THE PROOF OF THE CAMERA. The aft half of the bridging deck is an open passenger deck and you are looking straight DOWN into it: it is filled with NEAT ROWS OF SEATS — small BRIGHT BLUE pads in regular rows across the deck, six or seven to a row, a clear aisle down the middle, and a plain white rail line closing the stern. You see the tops of the seats and nothing else — never a seat back, never a seat seen from in front, never a person in one. A dense field of small blue rectangles aft is what says FAST FERRY from directly above. FORWARD, the enclosed CABIN fills the front half as one clean WHITE ROOF with its edges parallel to the sides, a dark wraparound window band across its leading face where the wheelhouse looks out over the two bows, and one short dark radar bar on a disc set on the roof behind it. A low white foredeck runs from the cabin front out to the two stems. COLOUR IS WHITE AND AZURE. Hull, cabin and rails are CRISP WHITE, the decks a pale cool grey. The livery is a bold AZURE band, hex #1E7ACD, of even width running the full length of each outer deck edge and wrapping around both bows — one clean stripe down each side, never tapering, never a flame, never a graphic. The seat field is the same azure a shade deeper. Nothing else is coloured. In greyscale it must read as a PALE VESSEL WITH A DARK SPECKLED BLOCK AFT and a clean bright roof forward. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps: no gloss, no specular highlight, no gradient, and no glow or halo bleeding off the white hull into the background. A thin clean dark contour, never a fat sticker outline. THIS BOAT IS FAST AND IS DRAWN AT REST: no wake, no bow wave, no spray, no foam, no water anywhere in the frame — the engine draws all of that. NO SAIL, NO MAST, NO BOOM, NO RIGGING and no white triangle anywhere — from above a racing sailboat is a pair of white triangles and this ferry shares the water with ten of them. No rows of orange lifeboats down the sides; those belong to the liner it shares the harbour with. No buoy red, no buoy green, no safety orange. No crew, no cast shadow, and no lettering, name, text or numbers anywhere
assets.note: Ninth vessel of Lighthouse Cove's harbour and its second ferry — the island fast-ferry catamaran, the counterpart to cove-ferry's Puget Sound double-ender. Described and never named, for that entry's reason: no operator, no vessel name, no lettering. NOT cove-ferry-b, AND THE KEY IS THE ARGUMENT. In this library the -b/-c suffix means the SAME vessel in another livery — cove-cargo-ship-b is the rust one, -c the green one, all three the same construction. This shares nothing with the double-ender but the word ferry: different hull count, different directionality, different speed class, different deck. A descriptive key keeps the call site honest. THE TWIN HULL IS THE ONLY SILHOUETTE IN THE GAME THAT IS NOT ONE OBLONG, and it is worth saying what that does NOT cost. cove-traffic-plan 5 and 6 model a vessel as a single capsule for both collision and wind shadow, and that stays correct here: at 200u and 4.8:1 the beam is 42u and the tunnel between the hulls is ~10u, far narrower than the 32u racing dinghy, so nothing can sail between them and a capsule over the whole footprint is honest rather than approximate. No engine change. The notch is a drawing, not a hole in the collider. SPEED IS THE POINT AND IT IS NOT IN THIS FILE. cove-traffic-plan 4 puts speed on the traffic ENTRY in knots, not on the kind, so the venue doc decides it — but the art has to be able to cash the cheque. The cargo ship's whole design virtue is 4 knots and utterly predictable; this is the other end of the same mechanic at 25-30 knots, which at the plan's 1 kt = 15 u/s is 375-450 u/s against a fleet doing 60-120. You cannot outrun it, you time it, and that is a genuinely different question from the one the freighter asks. Fine bows, lean proportion and a low clean deck are the art's whole job here. It will also be the first entry to push the wake's speed scaling (plan 7) anywhere near the top of its range; look at that on the water before authoring a second one. SIZE 200u, and the ladder wins over fidelity again. The cove runs 32 dinghy / 48 motorboat / 76 tug / 140 trawler / 200 fast ferry / 300 double-ender / 496 coaster, which spaces 1.43x and 1.5x either side of this — even. A real boat of this type is ~47 m against the double-ender's 100-140 m, a 2.5x ratio that would put it at 120u, on top of the trawler; the same call the double-ender's entry made, for the same reason. 200u is 3.6 racing hulls of 55u. THE PAIR TO SOLVE IS THE TWO FERRIES, and it is closer than any other pair in the harbour: white with a coloured edge at 4.5:1 and 300u against white with a coloured edge at 4.8:1 and 200u. Four axes carry it. (1) THE SPLIT BOW — two fine points with a notch between them, against one broad blunt chisel end. (2) DIRECTIONALITY — the double-ender is deliberately identical at both ends, this one has an unmistakable bow and stern. (3) DECK CONTENT — dark asphalt car patches at BOTH ends with white between, against a blue seat field aft of a white cabin. (4) HUE — evergreen against azure. On the contact sheet put them side by side at race scale, and if the bow notch does not survive, widen the tunnel before touching anything else: it is the one axis the other three cannot replace. AZURE JOINS AN OCCUPIED HUE, knowingly, as the double-ender's white did. The 48u motorboat carries a deep marine-blue stripe and the 820u liner a navy band; this is a brighter azure on a 200u hull, and the blue that actually reads at race scale is the SEAT FIELD, which nothing else in the game has. White and blue is what this boat is, and the family rule about unspent hues is worth less than the livery being right. NEVER GREY, NEVER NAVAL: a lean wave-piercing catamaran is the one subject in this library with a strong military prior, and NEGATIVE's bare `military` is unlikely to hold it alone. The subject states the civilian read positively in its first two lines, which is the technique the cargo family's funnel clause proved. allowSymmetry, twice over on the cruise ship's precedent: the seat rows are DELIBERATELY regular and evenly spaced, and the two hulls are mirror images of one another. ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE forbids both. SIZING: world 200 with bake 4 is an 800px bake; master 1536 at fillTo 0.92 holds 1413px of content, so the bake is a real 1.77x downsample and no pixel is invented. gen 1024x3072 for a long subject, per the profile's note on square frames capping length. REGISTERED 2026-08-10 as bay-cove-fast-ferry: plane surface, contact none like the family, hull [0.921, 0.310] measured over the WHOLE footprint including the tunnel, per the corrected capsule argument below. That gives a 184u x 62u capsule and a 620u lee off the beam. STILL OPEN: no venue authors it yet. It wants a SCHEDULE rather than a shuttle — end: 'despawn' with respawn, on a straight lane at 25+ knots. The double-ender is the one that wants 'pingpong'; between them the two ferries exercise both halves of the lifecycle. DELIVERED 2026-08-10, FIRST ROLL, KEPT. The split bow landed hard — two fine points with a deep notch between them, which this entry named as the one axis the other three separators could not replace — along with the blue seat field aft, the white cabin forward with its dark window band and radar disc, the azure band, and the stern notch between two transoms. Blue came back #1878C0 against #1E7ACD asked, within a few units. No warm saturated masses anywhere on the sprite, so zero signal-colour risk. MEASURED off the bake: hull [0.921, 0.310], 184u x 62u, aspect 2.97:1 against the ~5:1 asked — the largest deviation across both ferries, and it lands the boat in the stubby end of the harbour beside the tug (2.45:1) and the trawler (2.26:1). Kept because the twin-spike bow is unmistakable at 1x and no other hull in the game has one. ⚠️ THE TUNNEL ARGUMENT IN THIS ENTRY WAS WRONG, AND THE MEASUREMENT CORRECTS IT. The slot argued a capsule was honest because the tunnel would be ~10u, narrower than the 32u racing dinghy. Delivered it is 39u at its widest — WIDER than a dinghy. The conclusion survives on a different fact: the tunnel is open on only 18% of the length, at the bow notch and the stern gap, because the bridging deck closes it amidships. There is no through-passage, so one capsule over the whole footprint is still honest — but for the geometry, not for the width, and anyone re-deriving this from the original sentence would get it wrong. THE VALUE READ IS WEAKER THAN ASKED: greyscale thirds 181 / 180 / 148, so the dark speckled block aft is a 33-point step rather than the strong mass the subject specified — the seat field reads as texture, not as a dark patch. It survives because the split bow carries the identity on its own. THE PAIR-TO-SOLVE TEST PASSES: composited beside cove-ferry at true race scale on the bay plate, the two are not confusable — green-edged with a car speckle at both ends against white with twin spike bows and one blue block aft. The bow notch survives at 1x, so no tunnel widening is needed.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A BRIDGE, shot straight down from a drone or a survey aircraft — the picture a satellite tile makes of a crossing. THE BRIDGE RUNS UP AND DOWN THE FRAME, deck along the tall axis, one end toward the top and one toward the bottom, both ends stopping short of the edges. It is a long thin object in a tall thin frame and it should nearly fill that frame end to end. WHAT A BRIDGE LOOKS LIKE FROM STRAIGHT ABOVE, and this is the test that proves the camera: you see the ROAD SURFACE and nothing else of its height. No pier is visible below the deck, no underside, no side of any tower — a tower reads as a shape lying ACROSS the deck, not standing up beside it. There is no horizon, no bank, no water, no shadow. Nothing tapers or converges toward either end: the far end of the deck is exactly as wide as the near end, because in this projection they are the same distance from the camera. A SUSPENSION BRIDGE in the manner of the Golden Gate, painted that bridge's INTERNATIONAL ORANGE — a deep red-orange, near #C0362C, warm and slightly earthy, never fire-engine red and never safety orange. Down the middle runs the deck: a flat roadway band in dark asphalt grey, its surface plain and UNMARKED — no centre line, no lane line, no edge line, no arrow, no lettering, no paint of any kind anywhere on it. It is bare asphalt, weathered a little unevenly along its length, with a slim orange guard rail down both outer edges. TWO TOWERS, one about a fifth of the way down from each end, each reading as a bold orange crossbar lying square across the deck and reaching a little way out past both rails — an H of steel seen from directly overhead, with the two vertical legs showing as thicker blocks where they straddle the road. TWO MAIN CABLES run the whole length of the bridge, one just outside each rail, drawn as two clean unbroken orange lines PERFECTLY STRAIGHT AND PARALLEL TO THE DECK — and that is the point to get right, because from straight above the famous sag is invisible: a catenary seen in plan is a straight line, and any curve or droop in these cables means the camera has tilted. Between each cable and the deck edge, a regular close-spaced comb of short thin orange hangers, evenly repeated along the whole span. The roadway is EMPTY: no cars, no traffic, no people
assets.note: Lighthouse Cove's landmark crossing, and the venue's tallest object. SIZED FOR SCALE, NOT FITTED TO A GAP. Wes will move the land to suit, so the deck length is chosen to read right against the fleet — a boat is ~32u long, so a ~900u deck is about 28 boat lengths, which is a substantial crossing without being the whole 5200u world. For reference the bay's real water gaps today are 703u across the main strait and 668-669u island-to-mainland. THE REAL BRIDGE WOULD NOT FIT: Golden Gate is 2737m, which at ~9.2 units per metre is 25,000u — five times the world — so the reference gives the PROPORTIONS and the venue gives the size. ⚠️ ROAD MARKINGS REMOVED 2026-08-11, BEFORE EITHER BRIDGE WAS EVER GENERATED. Both subjects originally asked for a pale broken centre line, and the suspension bridge for solid edge lines too. The deck is now specified as bare unmarked asphalt with painted markings banned by name. TWO REASONS, and the second is the one that generalises. Lane paint is the closest thing to LETTERING this library allows, and the base NEGATIVE already carries 'text' — a broken white line is a regular repeating mark that invites a generator to keep going into arrows and numbers. And at race scale it does not survive to pay for itself: these decks draw about 25 units wide at world 870-920, so a centre line is under a pixel and a broken one is sub-pixel dashes that alias into a shimmering dotted seam as the camera pans. A bare deck is both cleaner and cheaper. NOTE cove-pier-ferry SHIPPED WITH ITS LANE PAINT and is left alone: its apron is far wider in proportion, the paint reads there, and it is already on disk and placement-ready.

A STEEL TRUSS CANTILEVER BRIDGE, the working companion to the cove's red suspension span and deliberately its opposite in every way that reads from a distance: painted SILVER-GREY STEEL, a cool mid grey with lighter grey highlights and charcoal shadow lines, with nothing red or orange anywhere on it. Down the middle the deck: a flat roadway band in dark asphalt grey, narrower than the suspension bridge's, its surface plain and UNMARKED — no centre line, no lane line, no edge line, no arrow, no lettering, no paint of any kind anywhere on it. Bare asphalt, weathered a little unevenly along its length. THE TRUSS IS THE WHOLE IDENTITY — running the full length down BOTH sides of the deck is a continuous steel lattice drawn as a repeating row of clean triangles, a regular zig-zag of straight members meeting at bold joints, the pattern unbroken from one end of the bridge to the other. That endless rhythm is what tells it from the suspension bridge at a glance: no towers, no cables, no hangers, just the same triangle repeating. Four or five heavier CROSS BEAMS lie square across the deck at even intervals along the span, each a plain grey bar a little wider than the roadway. The roadway is EMPTY: no cars, no traffic, no people

NOTE cove-pier-ferry SHIPPED WITH ITS LANE PAINT and is left alone: its apron is far wider in proportion, the paint reads there, and it is already on disk and placement-ready. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED. The unmarked deck arrived — measured across the roadway band, p50 104 and p95 108 luma, so there is no pale stripe anywhere on it and the markings edit did what it was for. Ratio 6.52:1, i.e. a 94m span on a 14m deck at world 870, which is right for a two-lane through truss; the continuous zig-zag runs unbroken down both sides with five cross beams; steel is silver-grey with nothing red or orange on it; no cars. Resolution comfortable at 0.57x — the 3663px delivery covers the 1740px bake with room to spare. ONE DEPARTURE ACCEPTED: the span narrows to 68% of beam over its last 2%, because the generator drew RAKED END PORTALS. That is a real feature of a truss bridge rather than a tilt, it is confined to one end, and the subject's 'nothing tapers' clause was aimed at perspective convergence, not at portal geometry. DELIVERED OPAQUE ON WHITE and cut with the border-flood key on near-white AND unsaturated. ⚠️ THAT CHOICE SAVED THE ASSET: the cut kept 296,632 enclosed pale pixels, which are the truss's own bright steel members. A plain luminance threshold would have punched every one of them out and returned a bridge with no bridge in it. This is the single clearest vindication of bayou-oak's saturation-key finding in the whole venue. ⚠️ REGISTERED AS `bay-bay-cove-bridge-truss`, AND THE DOUBLED PREFIX IS CORRECT. propSprite splits a kind at its FIRST hyphen, and paths.py leaves the bay's keys unstripped, so this manifest key ships to props/bay/bay-cove-bridge-truss.png and only a doubled id finds it. It is exactly the case the harbour block's note predicted, and the reason every other cove asset in this venue is keyed `cove-*`. Verified by resolving the path from the id before shipping. PLANE `canopy`, the only asset in the venue on it: ships pass beneath a bridge, and on `surface` an 820-unit cruise ship would draw over the top of a span it is meant to go under.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE SMALL HOUSE, shot straight down from a drone hovering directly over its roof — the picture a survey flight makes of a building. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE. No wall appears anywhere: no clapboard, no shingled siding, no window, no door, no porch, no step, no foundation, and no gable end seen face-on. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. A HALF-CAPE COTTAGE — the plainest house on the Cape: one simple rectangular block under one straight ridge. WHAT A ROOF IS FROM STRAIGHT ABOVE, and it is the whole picture: two flat slopes meeting along a RIDGE. The ridge is a crisp straight line, and the slopes either side are FLAT PLANES AT CLEARLY DIFFERENT TONES — one lit, one in shade, with a hard edge between them along the ridge. That tonal step is the only thing that says ROOF rather than RECTANGLE, so it must be unmistakable. The roof OVERHANGS the walls it sits on, so the building's outline is the roof's own edge, finished with a thin darker line of eaves shadow all the way round. THE ROOF IS A RECTANGLE ABOUT 5:4 IN PLAN — only a little longer than it is wide. Do NOT stretch it into a long thin building to suit; its two long edges run parallel, its two short edges run parallel, nothing tapers or converges, and no end wall is visible. The single RIDGE runs straight down the middle of the long axis, splitting the roof into two equal slopes. WEATHERED CEDAR SHINGLE SEEN FROM TEN METRES: individual shingles do not resolve, so the surface reads as faint COURSES — soft banding running parallel to the ridge — with a gentle mottling where some shingles have weathered lighter or darker than their neighbours. Never draw shingles one by one, never a crisp grid, never photographic grain. COLOUR, TAKEN FROM THE VENUE'S OWN CARD: a warm weathered grey around #9C968B, ranging from #747068 in the shaded slope to #B9B1A4 on the lit one. The eaves and the ridge cap are picked out in a clean white trim around #F5F5F3, a crisp thin line and no wider. ONE BRICK CHIMNEY STANDS ON THE RIDGE, AND IT POINTS AT THE CAMERA. It foreshortens to a small squat RECTANGLE seen from above — a soft weathered brick red-brown around #8A5B48, with its flue as a smaller dark rectangle inside it. It is never a tower with visible sides, never a column, never lying across the roof. It casts one short hard-edged shadow onto the slope beside it, and that is the only shadow in the picture. THE CHIMNEY SITS OFF-CENTRE, close to one gable end rather than in the middle — that is what makes this a HALF-Cape and it is the only cue in plan that says so. NO DORMERS on this one: the roof slopes are clean and unbroken. NO GROUND IS DRAWN: no lawn, no path, no drive, no garden, no fence, no wall, no hedge, no tree, no cast shadow on the ground, no water. The house stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the ground it is built on. NOTHING MODERN AND NOTHING ALIVE: no car, no person, no washing line, no solar panel, no aerial, no satellite dish, no roof vent. THE BUILDING DOES NOT FILL THE PICTURE. Draw it at the plan proportion stated above and leave empty background around it on all four sides. Do NOT stretch, widen or lengthen it to reach the edges of the frame — the frame's shape says nothing about the building's shape, and a house pulled out to span a wide picture is the wrong building.
assets.note: The workhorse and the smallest: a HALF-CAPE, the plainest house on the Cape and the one to place most often. SIZE IS HONEST: a half-Cape runs about 8.7m on its long side, and 8.7 x 9.2 units/m = 80. Its job in the set is to be unremarkable — one rectangle, one ridge, one chimney — so the ell and the saltbox read as variants of something. THE OFF-CENTRE CHIMNEY IS THE ONLY THING THAT MAKES IT A HALF-CAPE rather than a generic shed, and it is visible in plan, which is why it is specified. Part of Lighthouse Cove's TOWN SET — three cottages plus cove-shrub, sized and coloured together. SEEN FROM DIRECTLY ABOVE A BUILDING IS A ROOF, so the five things that can differentiate one house from another are: roof OUTLINE, RIDGE arrangement, roof TONE, roof FURNITURE (chimney, dormers) and SIZE. Walls, windows, doors and porches — everything that makes the venue card's buildings charming — are invisible in plan, so none of them can carry variety. The three cottages are separated on all five axes deliberately: plain rectangle / L-plan with a valley / off-centre saltbox ridge with dormers, at 80 / 118 / 100 world units, in warm weathered grey / dark cool slate / pale silvered grey. COLOURS MEASURED OFF assets/images/venues/bay.png with the buildings masked by saturation and luma: the dock building's cedar-shingle roof means #9C968B over a #747068-#B9B1A4 range, the bluff house's slate roof means #646C73, white trim #F5F5F3. The brick chimney could NOT be measured — only 145 px of it exist on the card — so #8A5B48 is a style pick, not a measurement, and is flagged as such. allowSymmetry TRUE ON ALL THREE, AND IT IS REQUIRED RATHER THAN PERMITTED. ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE bans 'symmetrical arrangement', 'evenly spaced' and 'tiled pattern' — and a gable roof IS symmetric about its ridge, dormers ARE evenly spaced, and shingle courses ARE a tiled pattern. Left off, the prompt would forbid three things the subject asks for and the generator would drop one at random. Same call as the lighthouse, for the same reason. ⚠️ planRound FALSE, WITH A KNOWN WORDING GAP THE SUBJECT WORKS AROUND. planRound false is correct — it gets ORTHO_LONG, whose parallel-sides test is exactly how a tilt shows on a rectangular roof — but ORTHO_LONG opens by asserting the subject is 'much longer than it is wide', which is false for a 5:4 cottage and could be read as an instruction to stretch it. Each subject therefore states its own true plan proportion and says not to stretch it. THE REAL FIX IS A THIRD ORTHO STATE (a `planRect`: parallel sides AND a stated aspect), which would serve every building in the town set; it is not done here because it changes shared prompt.py infrastructure. ROLE ambient and plane surface, contact none — they stand on land the fleet cannot reach, exactly as the shore trees do. ⚠️ PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF. The editor's spin checkbox randomises heading, which is right for trees and catastrophic for buildings; the prop inspector's `heading °` field is how a town gets aligned to its lanes and its waterfront. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ THE 2026-08-10 BUILDING BATCH CAME BACK STRETCHED TO THE CANVAS, and it is one systemic cause rather than three separate failures. Measured across the three deliveries: subject plan ratios of 1.90, 2.04 and 1.88 against requested 1.33, 1.25 and 1.20 — i.e. all three landed on the generation canvas's own 1.83 aspect, each filling 81-94% of BOTH canvas dimensions. The generator fills the frame it is given, and a requested proportion loses to the frame's shape every time. TWO FIXES, both applied: a `gen` field on every building slot so the operator asks for a SQUARE frame (or a 3:2 one for the church and boat shed, which really are long), and a clause in each subject saying the building must not be stretched to reach the edges. This is why the bridges carry `gen: 1024x3072` — the field already existed for exactly this and the town slots simply did not use it. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED. Ridge centred at 46%, shingle courses parallel to it, clean white eaves, plan ratio 1.38 against the 5:4 asked. ONE DEFECT ACCEPTED: the chimney came back at 51% across the ridge rather than near a gable end, which makes this a full Cape rather than a half-Cape. That is an architectural distinction and not a legibility one — the sprite's job is 'the plain small cottage you place most often' and it does that — so it is recorded rather than rerolled.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE SMALL HOUSE, shot straight down from a drone hovering directly over its roof — the picture a survey flight makes of a building. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. A CAPE COTTAGE WITH A KITCHEN ELL — an L-SHAPED house: a main rectangular block, and a narrower, LOWER wing running off the back of it at a right angle. WHAT A ROOF IS FROM STRAIGHT ABOVE, and it is the whole picture: two flat slopes meeting along a RIDGE. The ridge is a crisp straight line, and the slopes either side are FLAT PLANES AT CLEARLY DIFFERENT TONES — one lit, one in shade, with a hard edge between them along the ridge. The roof OVERHANGS the walls it sits on, so the building's outline is the roof's own edge, finished with a thin darker line of eaves shadow all the way round. THE FOOTPRINT IS THE LETTER L AND THE TWO RIDGES CROSS AT A RIGHT ANGLE. Describe it by the frame, because that is unambiguous: THE MAIN BLOCK lies across the picture with its ridge running LEFT-TO-RIGHT, a rectangle about 5:4. THE ELL runs away from one end of it toward the BOTTOM of the picture, narrower and shorter, and ITS ridge runs UP-AND-DOWN — at ninety degrees to the main ridge, so the two ridges together form a T-junction or an L-junction and NEVER a single straight line. ⚠️ IF BOTH RIDGES RUN THE SAME WAY THE BUILDING IS WRONG: that is two sheds butted end to end, not a house with an ell, and it is the single most likely way to fail this picture. The ell's roof also sits LOWER than the main one, so the main block's slope overlaps and overhangs it slightly where they meet. WHERE THE TWO ROOFS MEET THERE IS A VALLEY, and it is the detail that proves the L: a crisp straight line running DIAGONALLY — at about forty-five degrees to both ridges — from the point where the ell's ridge dies into the main roof's slope, outward to the eaves. There is one such diagonal on each side of the ell, so the junction reads as a shallow V opening away from the main block, with the roof surface falling into it from both sides and a soft dark line along its length. Draw both cleanly. Every edge of the L runs parallel to the edge opposite it, nothing tapers or converges, and no end wall is visible. WEATHERED CEDAR SHINGLE SEEN FROM TEN METRES: individual shingles do not resolve, so the surface reads as faint COURSES — soft banding running parallel to the ridge — with a gentle mottling where some shingles have weathered lighter or darker than their neighbours. Never draw shingles one by one, never a crisp grid, never photographic grain. COLOUR, TAKEN FROM THE VENUE'S OWN CARD, and this house is SLATE rather than cedar: a cool blue-grey around #646C73, from #555D64 in the shade to #7C8D90 on the lit slope — flatter and cooler than a shingle roof, with the courses finer and less obvious. The eaves and ridge caps carry the same clean white trim around #F5F5F3. ONE BRICK CHIMNEY STANDS ON THE RIDGE, AND IT POINTS AT THE CAMERA. It foreshortens to a small squat RECTANGLE seen from above — a soft weathered brick red-brown around #8A5B48, with its flue as a smaller dark rectangle inside it. It is never a tower with visible sides, never a column, never lying across the roof. It casts one short hard-edged shadow onto the slope beside it, and that is the only shadow in the picture. THE MAIN CHIMNEY IS CENTRAL, standing on the main block's ridge at its middle, and a SECOND smaller stove chimney stands on the ell's ridge. Both foreshorten to rectangles as described. NO GROUND IS DRAWN: no lawn, no path, no drive, no garden, no fence, no wall, no hedge, no tree, no cast shadow on the ground, no water. The house stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the ground it is built on. NOTHING MODERN AND NOTHING ALIVE: no car, no person, no washing line, no solar panel, no aerial, no satellite dish, no roof vent. THE BUILDING DOES NOT FILL THE PICTURE. assets.note: The biggest and most complex of the three: a Cape with a KITCHEN ELL, the L-plan that turns a row of cottages into a village. SIZE: 12.8m on the longest side = 118. THE VALLEY IS THE WHOLE ASSET. An L-plan roof from above is defined by the diagonal VALLEY line where the ell's slope runs into the main roof, and it is the one shape in the town set that no other building has — it is worth more variety than the size or the colour. If a delivery comes back with the two wings simply butted together and no valley, it has failed on FORM, not on detail. Dark slate rather than cedar shingle, so the set carries two roof materials and not just two greys. Part of Lighthouse Cove's TOWN SET — three cottages plus cove-shrub, sized and coloured together. SEEN FROM DIRECTLY ABOVE A BUILDING IS A ROOF, so the five things that can differentiate one house from another are: roof OUTLINE, RIDGE arrangement, roof TONE, roof FURNITURE (chimney, dormers) and SIZE. assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE SMALL HOUSE, shot straight down from a drone hovering directly over its roof — the picture a survey flight makes of a building. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE. No wall appears anywhere: no clapboard, no shingled siding, no window, no door, no porch, no step, no foundation, and no gable end seen face-on. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. A DORMERED CAPE COTTAGE — a rectangular house under one straight centred ridge, with two small dormers breaking the front slope. That tonal step is the only thing that says ROOF rather than RECTANGLE. The roof OVERHANGS the walls, so the outline is the roof's own edge with a thin darker line of eaves shadow all round. THE ROOF IS A RECTANGLE ABOUT 4:3 IN PLAN — do not stretch it. Every edge runs parallel to the edge opposite it and nothing tapers or converges. TWO SMALL GABLED BUMPS stand on the upper slope, evenly spaced along it. Each is nothing more than A TINY ROOF: a short ridge running up-and-down at right angles to the main ridge, with two little slopes falling away either side, poking out of the main surface and notching its outer edge. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE TOP OF EACH ONE. Its window faces sideways and is completely hidden beneath its own eaves from this camera, so there is NO glass, NO pane, NO glazing bar, NO frame and NO transparent or reflective face anywhere on them. It must read clearly LIGHTER than a plain cedar cottage roof standing next to it; if the two look like the same grey, this one has come back too dark. Eaves, ridge cap and the dormer cheeks carry clean white trim around #F5F5F3. ONE BRICK CHIMNEY STANDS ON THE RIDGE, AND IT POINTS AT THE CAMERA. It foreshortens to a small squat RECTANGLE seen from above — a soft weathered brick red-brown around #8A5B48, with its flue as a smaller dark rectangle inside it. It is never a tower with visible sides, never a column, never lying across the roof. It casts one short hard-edged shadow onto the slope beside it, and that is the only shadow in the picture. assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SMALL NEW ENGLAND YACHT CLUB, shot straight down from directly overhead. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE of the building: no wall, no window, no door, no porch post and no gable end seen face-on. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. THE BUILDING FACES THE WATER AT THE TOP OF THE FRAME. THREE THINGS MAKE THIS A CLUB AND NOT A LARGE HOUSE, and all three must be present. (1) THE DECK, AND EVERY GOOD YACHT CLUB HAS ONE. On the WATER side of the building — the top of the frame — a broad open TIMBER DECK runs the full width of the clubhouse and reaches out toward the water about two thirds as deep as the building. IT IS OPEN TO THE SKY AND HAS NO ROOF, so unlike every other building in this town you are looking at its FLOOR: pale weathered planks laid straight across, board by board, several visibly paler than their neighbours. That expanse of open planking beside a shingled roof is the clearest possible cue that this is a club and not a house — nothing else on this shore shows a floor. Around its three outer edges runs a RAILING: a thin dark line for the top rail with a row of short evenly spaced dark TICKS just inside it, one per baluster, seen END-ON and foreshortened to almost nothing. Ticks, never uprights. At one end a short flight of STEPS runs down and out as three or four narrow parallel bars. THE DECK IS BUSY AND HAPPY — this is where the club sits and watches the racing, and it should look like it. Along the seaward rail, FOUR ADIRONDACK CHAIRS in a row, evenly spaced and all facing out to the water: seen from above each is an unmistakable little shape, a WEDGE of narrow parallel slats wider at the front than the back, with two broad flat ARM boards standing out either side, in pale weathered timber. Further in on the deck, TWO ROUND TABLES, each a disc of pale timber with three small dark chair-backs set round it like commas. OVER EACH TABLE A PARASOL, seen from directly above as a CIRCLE: a shallow cone of canvas with eight straight seams running from the rim to a small dark cap at the centre, its panels alternating warm cream and deep harbour green, hiding most of the table beneath it — which is what proves it stands above. The two parasols are at slightly different angles. Everything on the deck is furniture and nothing is a person: no figures anywhere. (2) THE RACE COMMITTEE DECK, standing on the main ridge: a small rectangular railed platform, flat-topped, its floor a pale deck, with the same handrail-and-ticks treatment and no wider than a third of the ridge. (3) THE CLUB BURGEE, PAINTED FLAT ON THE ROOF, and it is the identity of the whole asset. THERE IS NO FLAGPOLE AND NO FLYING FLAG ANYWHERE IN THIS PICTURE. The club's burgee is painted directly onto the roof shingles as an aerial marking — the way a boathouse or a hangar carries its mark for the benefit of anyone passing — so it is PAINT ON A FLAT SURFACE and lies perfectly in the plane of the roof. It has no thickness, no pole, no halyard, no shadow, no ripple, no curl and no lift: it is a flat coloured shape on the shingles, exactly as a painted line on a road is. Where the roof's slope changes tone at the ridge, THE PAINT CHANGES TONE WITH IT, because paint takes the light of the surface it sits on. IT IS DRAWN LARGE, spanning about half the length of the main roof and centred on the seaward slope so it faces the water. ⚠️ ITS GEOMETRY IS EXACT AND IS MEASURED FROM THE CLUB'S OWN BURGEE; copy these numbers rather than drawing a flag from memory. IT IS A CLEAN ISOSCELES TRIANGLE lying on its side, about ONE AND A HALF TIMES AS LONG AS ITS UPRIGHT EDGE IS TALL (1.45 to 1) — a stubby broad pennant, NOT a long thin streamer. Its tall edge is at the left and its two long edges are PERFECTLY STRAIGHT, tapering evenly to ONE SHARP POINT at the right: at the halfway station it is exactly HALF as tall as its left edge, at three quarters along exactly a QUARTER. No swallowtail, no forked or notched tail, no wave, no fold. THE DESIGN IS FIXED: a NAVY field around #1C2E6E, crossed by a single BROAD vertical RED band around #D83839. ⚠️ THE BAND'S PLACE AND WIDTH ARE MEASURED: it begins about a QUARTER of the way along from the tall edge and ends about TWO THIRDS along, covering a good TWO FIFTHS of the whole length — a broad band dominating the middle, never a thin stripe near the edge. Navy shows either side of it, and the navy behind the point is the wider of the two. Centred on that red band, a WHITE PAW PRINT — one larger rounded pad below and four small oval toes arched above it. No other mark, no letter, no word, no number, no star. The paint is slightly weathered, its edges a touch soft where the shingle texture shows faintly through. ON THE MAIN ROOF, otherwise plain: one squat brick CHIMNEY at one end of the ridge, pointing at the camera and therefore a small rectangle with a darker flue inside it, never a tower with sides. WEATHERED CEDAR SHINGLE SEEN FROM TEN METRES: shingles do not resolve individually, so the surface reads as faint COURSES running parallel to each ridge with a gentle mottling where some have weathered lighter. Never shingle by shingle, never a crisp grid. COLOUR: the roofs are a warm weathered grey around #9C968B, from #7B766C in the shaded slope to #B4AEA3 on the lit one, with the veranda band a shade darker than the main roof so the step reads. Eaves, ridge and the committee deck are picked out in clean white trim around #F5F5F3. THE BURGEE'S NAVY AND RED ARE THE ONLY SATURATED COLOURS IN THE PICTURE. NO GROUND IS DRAWN: no lawn, no terrace, no path, no dock, no cast shadow on the ground, no water. The club stands alone on a transparent background. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no boat, no car, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing.
assets.note: THE FLEET'S HOME, and the only asset in the game that carries the SaltyCritter Yacht Club's own mark. The base prompt every asset in this library is built from opens 'Stylized polished 2D game art for SaltyCritter Yacht Club'; this is the first time the club appears as an object in the world rather than as a house style. Role LANDMARK — venue identity, on land, never an obstacle in the water. SIZE 168 units = 18.3m, deliberately between the boat shed (150) and the church (184): the church stays the largest building in the town, which is right for a New England harbour, and the club is the largest thing on the WATERFRONT after the marina. THE BURGEE IS THE ASSET AND THE PHYSICS ARE WHY IT WORKS. A flag flies HORIZONTALLY, so unlike the lighthouse's vertical lightning rod it does not collapse to a dot — you see the whole pennant from directly above. This is the same reasoning that made cove-church's weathervane succeed where the lighthouse's rod failed, and it is now the third asset in this venue to turn on the same question: STATE WHICH AXIS THE PART LIES ON AND THE ANSWER FOLLOWS. Vertical parts foreshorten to a dot (rod, chimney, flagpole, baluster); horizontal parts are seen whole (weathervane arrow, burgee). COLOURS COPIED FROM assets/images/misc/salty-crew-yacht-club-burgee.png, measured rather than eyeballed: navy #1C2E6E over 72k px, red #D83839 over 47k, white paw. Those two saturated hues appear nowhere else on this shore, which is deliberate — the club's flag should be the thing your eye finds. THE PENNANT IS DRAWN OVERSIZE at about a fifth of the building's length (~34 units), and that is a declared exaggeration in the scale block's sense: a real burgee on a real clubhouse pole would be a few pixels and would read as dirt. THE RAILING CLAUSE IS REUSED VERBATIM from cove-lighthouse and cove-house-captains, where it has now delivered twice — sixty correct balusters on the light's gallery and a clean widow's walk on the captain's house. Handrail as a line, balusters as end-on ticks. It is the most reliable sentence in this venue's whole prompt set and should be copied rather than rewritten. THE VERANDA IS THE SECOND CUE and it is the ell's valley applied to a wrap: a lower roof band stepped down from the main block, with a diagonal valley at each corner where it turns. cove-cottage-ell round 2 proved the generator can draw a valley when the geometry is stated in frame directions, so this asks for the same thing round a corner. If the veranda comes back as three separate awnings rather than one continuous band, that is the failure to watch for. PAIRS WELL WITH cove-parasol on the lawn and cove-marina in front of it — the club, its float and its boats are the one part of this waterfront that is about the regatta rather than about the working port. planRound false, allowSymmetry true (a gable roof is symmetric, the balusters are evenly spaced, the shingle courses are a 'tiled pattern' — the three reasons every building in this town needs it). PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF and set `heading °` so the veranda faces the water. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ REVISED AFTER ROUND 1 ON THREE COUNTS. (1) A CLUB NEEDS A DECK, and the first subject not only lacked one, it BANNED it ('no deck on the water') while asking for a wraparound veranda instead. The veranda was an invention; the deck is what a yacht club is. It is also the better top-down subject: a deck is OPEN TO THE SKY, so you see its FLOOR — pale planking beside a shingled roof, and every other building in this town is roof-only, so visible planking is the strongest 'this is a club' cue available. AND IT IS FURNISHED rather than left bare: four Adirondack chairs facing the water, two tables with chairs, two parasols. The bayou-dock 'leave it empty' rule does NOT apply here, and the reason is worth stating — that rule exists because a baked-in boat can only be placed once before it reads as a copy of itself, and there is exactly ONE yacht club in a venue. A single placement cannot repeat, so baking the furniture in costs nothing and buys the thing the building is FOR. (2) THE FLAGPOLE WAS DRAWN IN ELEVATION — a diagonal stick with a ball finial, a side view sitting in an otherwise-nadir image, and the same failure as the lighthouse's lightning rod. It now gets its own warning clause: a vertical pole IS A SMALL CIRCLE from above, and the burgee is visible only because a flag lies FLAT. That contrast — pole invisible, flag whole — is the clearest statement of the axis rule this venue has produced. (3) THE BURGEE CAME BACK WRONG IN THREE MEASURABLE WAYS. Measured against the club's own burgee file: the real flag is 1.45:1, the delivery 2.15:1; the real red band covers 43% of the length running 24%-67% along, the delivery's 26% at 23%-49%, so it read as a thin stripe near the hoist rather than a broad central band; and the real outline tapers linearly to one point (100/75/50/25% of hoist height at each quarter) where the delivery had a wavy swallowtail. THE SWALLOWTAIL WAS THE SUBJECT'S OWN FAULT — it asked for 'a soft ripple along its trailing edges', which on a shape whose identity IS a clean straight taper is an instruction to destroy it. THE GENERAL LESSON, recurring across this venue: WHEN A SUBJECT HAS AN EXACT REFERENCE ON DISK, MEASURE IT AND QUOTE THE NUMBERS — 'about a third of the way along' loses to '24% to 67%, covering two fifths' every time. ⚠️ ROUND 2: THE FLAGPOLE IS GONE AND THE BURGEE IS NOW PAINTED ON THE ROOF. Round 2 came back with the deck exactly right — four Adirondack chairs in a row, two tables, two parasols, committee deck, chimney — and the flag apparatus wrong AGAIN: the pole drawn as a vertical stick with a ball at each end, and the pennant blown up to half the sprite. THE DIAGNOSIS IS THAT A FLAGPOLE IS THE WORST POSSIBLE SUBJECT FOR THIS CAMERA, and it is not a wording problem. Its entire identity is height; the plan view deletes all of it and leaves a dot; and every reference image in existence is side-on. That is the red cedar's problem, the lighthouse rod's problem and the church steeple's problem stacked on one object, and two escalating rewrites did not move it. THE FIX IS TO CHANGE WHAT THE OBJECT IS. A burgee PAINTED on the roof cannot fail the orthographic test, because paint on a flat surface is two-dimensional by construction — there is no height for the camera to lose and no side for it to show. It is also REAL (boathouses and hangars carry aerial markings), it makes the club's mark LARGE and legible where a flown burgee at true scale would be a few pixels, and it puts the game's own brand where every boat racing past can see it. THE GENERAL LESSON IS THE MOST USEFUL ONE THIS VENUE HAS PRODUCED: when a subject's identity IS its verticality, do not keep rewording the camera clause — REPLACE THE OBJECT WITH A FLAT ONE THAT CARRIES THE SAME MEANING. The alternative considered and rejected was a burgee weathervane on the ridge (too small to read, and the church already owns that device) and signal bunting along the deck rail (hangs vertically, so it foreshortens to dots — the same trap in miniature). ROUND 3 ACCEPTED, AND THE PAINTED BURGEE WORKED FIRST TIME. Measured against the club's own burgee file: the taper is now EXACT — 78 / 52 / 25 / 5 percent of hoist height at the quarter stations against a linear ideal of 75 / 50 / 25 / 5 — so the swallowtail and the ripple are gone and it is a clean isosceles triangle. ⚠️ THE ASPECT 'ERROR' IS NOT AN ERROR AND MUST NOT BE 'FIXED'. The painted flag measures 2.03:1 against a reference of 1.45:1, and that is CORRECT PHYSICS: a marking painted on a PITCHED roof is foreshortened across the slope when seen from directly above, and 1.45 / cos(44deg) = 2.02. The delivery is exactly a 1.45:1 burgee lying on a 44-degree roof, which is a normal Cape pitch. Anyone re-measuring this later and 'correcting' the flag to 1.45:1 in plan would be drawing a burgee lying on a FLAT roof, which this building does not have. ONE GENUINE MISS, ACCEPTED: the red band came back 24% of the flag's length running 23-47% along, against a measured reference of 43% running 24-67% — so it reads as a narrower stripe than the real burgee. Band width is measured ALONG the length and is therefore NOT foreshortened, so unlike the aspect this one is real. It is invisible at race scale, where the paw is what carries the mark, so it ships. TONES 119 TO COVER 90%, well over the venue band of 16-46 and the highest of any bay building (church 37, marina 75, shop-row 76) — the cost of a deck full of furniture with its own soft shadows. Judged on the race-scale render rather than the number: at 168 units it reads clean and is the most identifiable building on the shore. Watch it if the deck ever gains more clutter.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE BUILDING, shot straight down from a drone hovering directly over its roof — the picture a survey flight makes of a building. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE. No wall appears anywhere: no clapboard, no shingled siding, no window, no door, no porch, no step, no foundation, and no gable end seen face-on. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. A NEW ENGLAND MEETING HOUSE — a white clapboard church, and after the light the tallest thing in the town. From above it is TWO PARTS JOINED. (1) THE NAVE: a long rectangle about 2:1 in plan under one straight ridge running its whole length, two equal slopes falling either side. (2) THE TOWER: a SQUARE block projecting from one gable end of the nave, narrower than the nave is wide, reading clearly as its own separate mass rather than as part of the roof. WHAT A ROOF IS FROM STRAIGHT ABOVE: flat slopes meeting along a RIDGE, the ridge a crisp straight line and the slopes either side FLAT PLANES AT CLEARLY DIFFERENT TONES — one lit, one in shade, with a hard edge between them. That tonal step is the only thing that says ROOF rather than RECTANGLE. The roof OVERHANGS the walls below it, so the building's outline is the roof's own edge, finished with a thin darker line of eaves shadow all the way round. THE STEEPLE IS THE IDENTITY AND IT IS THE HARDEST PART OF THIS PICTURE. On top of the tower stands a tall slender SPIRE, and its whole height runs straight into the camera and disappears. FROM DIRECTLY OVERHEAD A SPIRE IS A SQUARE PYRAMID SEEN FROM ABOVE: a square with four crisp seams running from its corners in to a single point at the exact centre, its four faces at four slightly different tones. It is never a cone lying across the frame, never a tower with visible sides, never a triangle, and never a spike. AT THE APEX, A WEATHERVANE — and unlike a lightning rod this one IS visible from above, because a weathervane's arrow lies HORIZONTALLY. Draw it as a small flat dark silhouette crossing the spire's point: a slim pointer one way, a tail the other, lying flat on the picture. The mast it turns on is vertical and foreshortens to a single dot at the centre beneath it. COLOUR, AND THE CONTRAST IS THE WHOLE SIGNATURE. The nave's roof is a dark cool SLATE around #58606A, from #474E57 in shade to #6E7681 on the lit slope, its eaves and ridge lined in crisp white trim around #F5F5F3. THE TOWER AND THE SPIRE ARE WHITE — painted clapboard around #F5F5F3, shading no darker than #DCDCD8 on their shaded faces. A dark nave with a bright white tower standing at one end of it is what says CHURCH at a distance, and it is the only place in this town where two parts of one building are opposite in value. Keep both clean: no third hue anywhere on it. NO GROUND IS DRAWN: no lawn, no path, no drive, no yard, no fence, no wall, no hedge, no tree, no cast shadow on the ground, no water. The building stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the ground it is built on. NOTHING MODERN AND NOTHING ALIVE: no car, no person, no washing line, no solar panel, no aerial, no satellite dish, no roof vent beyond what is described here. THE BUILDING DOES NOT FILL THE PICTURE. Draw it at the plan proportion stated above and leave empty background around it on all four sides. Do NOT stretch, widen or lengthen it to reach the edges of the frame — the frame's shape says nothing about the building's shape, and a house pulled out to span a wide picture is the wrong building.
