TWO FIXES, both applied: a `gen` field on every building slot so the operator asks for a SQUARE frame (or a 3:2 one for the church and boat shed, which really are long), and a clause in each subject saying the building must not be stretched to reach the edges. This is why the bridges carry `gen: 1024x3072` — the field already existed for exactly this and the town slots simply did not use it.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TIMBER PILING, shot straight down from directly overhead. A piling is a post driven into the harbour bottom, and IT POINTS AT THE CAMERA, so its whole height runs into the lens and disappears. WHAT IS LEFT IS A CIRCLE: the sawn top of the pile, seen flat. NO LENGTH OF POST IS VISIBLE ANYWHERE — no side, no shaft, no barnacled flank running away from you, nothing that tells you the thing is tall. A post drawn with a visible side is a post drawn from the side, and it is wrong. WHAT YOU SEE, from the middle outward: (1) the SAWN END GRAIN, a disc of weathered timber with faint growth rings and one or two dark CHECKS — the radial splits an old pile always has — running from near the centre out to the rim; (2) a slightly PALER, ROUNDED-OFF RIM where decades of rain and sun have worn the sharp edge away; (3) a narrow IRON BAND just below that rim, a thin dark ring of rusted strap, broken and pitted rather than clean. The timber is a driftwood grey-brown around #7A6E5E, silvered to about #9C9182 on the crown and dropping to #4A4238 inside the checks. The iron is a dull rust brown around #6B4A38. IT IS ONE PILE, ALONE — not a cluster, not a pair, not a dolphin of three lashed together, and not a row. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: THE SMALLEST PROP IN THE VENUE AND THE MOST USEFUL PER GENERATION: it edges a berth, marks a ruined wharf, breaks up a rock shore, and gives the pelicans venues.md promises somewhere to sit. ⚠️ SIZE IS AN EXPLICIT EXAGGERATION AND THE SCALE BLOCK REQUIRES THAT BE DECLARED. A real harbour pile is 0.3-0.6m across, which at 9.2 units/m is 3-5px — at or below the floor where anything resolves at all (the same finding the penguin note records: a 0.5m footprint 'cannot carry a silhouette'). world 14 is 1.5m, roughly 3.3x life size. It is drawn big so that ONE of them is visible; that is the deliberate trade. SINGLE, NOT A CLUSTER, AND THAT WAS A CORRECTION. The first plan was a baked cluster of four or five, which is wrong twice over: a fixed arrangement stamps the same pattern at every placement, and a cluster cannot make a LINE along a wharf face. The editor already solves this better — addProps' comment reads 'ONE DRAG LAYS A STAND', scattering `count` props inside a dragged circle each with its own size and heading — so a stand of pilings is a gesture, not an asset. THIS IS THE ONE WATERFRONT PIECE TO PLACE WITH prop-spin ON: a sawn pile top has no front, and rotation variety is what stops a row reading as a stamp. planRound TRUE and allowSymmetry TRUE: a pile top genuinely IS a circle in plan, so the roundness test is the right tilt check and the radial-symmetry negatives would fight the subject. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED. Aspect 1.080 inside the 1.12 planRound gate, silhouette-vs-circle IoU 0.944 so it is a clean disc, tones 41 in band, colour #7d7063 against a #7A6E5E spec. Growth rings and four radial checks all arrived. TWO THINGS RECORDED RATHER THAN FIXED. A faint SKIRT of the post's side shows below the disc — 1.41% of the sprite — which is the one thing the subject banned; at world 14 that is 0.2px and invisible, so it ships. And ALL THE DETAIL IS LOST AT RACE SCALE: at 14px this is a brown dot. That is not a fault, it is the trade the size argument already declared — the asset does its work in GROUPS, and a row of eight reads unmistakably as a line of posts while a scatter of ten reads as a stand. Checked both before accepting. Resolution 0.05x is the lowest in the venue by far and entirely expected for a 14-unit prop off a 1024 master.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SECTION OF DRY-STONE WALL, shot straight down from directly overhead — the low fieldstone wall that runs between every pasture and lane on Nantucket and the Cape. ⚠️ THE PICTURE ITSELF IS A TALL NARROW STRIP — five times taller than it is wide — and the wall FILLS IT EDGE TO EDGE. Generate on a tall narrow canvas; a wide or square frame will produce a wall five times too thick, which is the one thing that cannot be corrected afterwards. THE WALL RUNS UP THE FRAME, a long straight narrow band about FIVE times as long as it is wide, running off the top edge and off the bottom edge. Its two long edges run PARALLEL for the whole length, nothing tapers or converges, and no side face is visible: a wall is a low thing and you are looking at its TOP. IT IS BUILT OF LOOSE STONES AND NOTHING ELSE — no mortar, no cement, no joint filler, no rendering. What you see from above is the TOP COURSE: a packed run of individual FIELDSTONES, each an irregular rounded lump of granite two or three of which span the wall's width, all of them different sizes and shapes, fitted together with narrow dark gaps where they do not quite meet. The stones are ROUNDED AND WORN, not quarried or squared — glacial cobbles picked out of a field — and they sit at slightly different heights, so each carries its own small hard-edged shadow onto its neighbour. A few larger stones stand out from the rest, and here and there a small one is wedged into a gap. ⚠️ THIS SECTION IS LAID END TO END WITH COPIES OF ITSELF TO MAKE A LONGER WALL, so BOTH SHORT ENDS MUST BE PLAIN AND SQUARE-CUT: the run of stones continues straight off both the top and the bottom edge of the picture, mid-stone, with no end cap, no finished terminal, no gatepost, no corner and no dark outline closing the wall off. The two long sides keep their outline; the two ENDS must not have one, or two sections butted together will show a double dark line at the join. NOTHING GROWS ON IT AND NOTHING LEANS ON IT: no moss, no lichen patch, no grass tuft, no bramble, no flower, no gate, no post, no rail, no wire. COLOUR: weathered granite fieldstone in a soft warm grey around #9A9287, from #6E695F in the gaps and shadows to #B8B1A4 on the sunlit tops, with one or two stones a shade warmer or cooler than the rest. NO GROUND IS DRAWN: no grass, no lane, no soil, no cast shadow on the ground, no water. The wall stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it runs across.
assets.note: The other half of the 'walls and lanes' answer, and it goes the OPPOSITE way to the lane: a wall is a PROP, not a ground. The reason is width. A lane is metres across and reads as a surface, so a polygon painted with a texture is exactly right; a dry-stone wall is about 0.9m across — 8 units — and a shape that thin would be almost entirely the coastline STROKE that drawIslands paints round every land polygon, with the body invisible between. The shape machinery is built for islands and a wall is not one. SIZE 150 units = 16.3m per section, chosen to keep placements manageable: a 100m field boundary is six drops rather than twenty. Sections butt end to end along a boundary and can turn a corner simply by butting at an angle — a dry-stone wall has no mitred joints, so there is no corner asset to draw. ⚠️ IT IS THE SECOND TILING PROP IN THE LIBRARY, AFTER cove-quay, AND IT INHERITS THAT ASSET'S HARD-WON LESSON: the house style puts a continuous dark contour round every prop, which is correct for a discrete object and FATAL at a butt joint — round 1 of the quay produced a double dark line down every join. So the subject asks for the outline on the two long sides ONLY and explicitly forbids it on the two ends, with the stone run continuing mid-stone off both edges. Check it the way the quay was checked: lay two copies end to end BEFORE anything else. The quay also proved the second half of this — state the required features FIRST and constrain their position second, never lead with a blanket prohibition, which is what deleted the quay's bollards in round 1. COLOUR DELIBERATELY SHARES THE coastalrock FAMILY (#9A9287 against the ground's #a19481, dE ~5) and that is not a collision to fix: a Nantucket wall IS built of the same glacial granite as the shore it stands above, and forcing it to a different grey would be the mistake the cedar-roof family note warns about. What matters is that it separates from the ground it is actually drawn ON — coastal scrub — where it clears comfortably. Role ambient, plane surface, contact none: it stands inland where no boat can reach. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF and set `heading °` per section. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET. ⚠️ ROUND 1: THE STONEWORK AND THE OPEN ENDS ARE RIGHT, THE PROPORTION IS NOT, AND THE CAUSE IS THE CANVAS. THE GOOD HALF FIRST, because it is the part that was hard: the ends came back GENUINELY OPEN — measured end drop 7 luma against internal stone-gap drops of 21, i.e. no closing contour, stones cut mid-stone at both edges. That makes this the FIRST TILING PROP IN THE LIBRARY to solve the problem cove-quay needed three rounds for and still only half-solved, and the wording that did it is worth copying: give the outline to the two long sides ONLY and say the stone run continues off both ends. Tones 47, colour in family. THE BAD HALF: ratio 1.70:1 against the 8:1 asked, which at world 150 is a wall 9.6m thick, and it cannot be cropped narrower without slicing stones down the long sides. ⚠️ THE PROPORTION LEVER IS THE FRAME, NOT THE SUBJECT, AND THIS VENUE HAS NOW PROVEN IT FIVE TIMES: quay asked 3.0 got 2.13, pier asked 4.0 got 2.57, boat shed asked 2.5 got 2.15, ferry asked 2.33 got 1.94, shop row asked 2.5 got 2.06. The generator converges on 2-2.6:1 whatever the words say, because it fills the canvas it is given — and every one of those arrived on the same 2816x1536. A `gen` field was already set here (1024x3072) and did not reach the generator. So the fix is not more insistent wording: it is GENERATING ON A TALL NARROW CANVAS. gen changed to 512x2560 and the frame's own shape is now stated in the FIRST LINE of the subject rather than left to the operator header, on the theory that a generator which reads the subject may at least argue with its own frame. Target lowered 8:1 -> 5:1 to be reachable; at world 150 that is a wall 30 units = 3.3m wide, which is 3.6x a real 0.9m dry-stone wall and is a DECLARED exaggeration of the same order as cove-piling's 3.3x — a true-width wall would be 8 units and invisible. ROUND 2 ACCEPTED, AND IT IS THE LIBRARY'S FIRST GENUINELY SEAMLESS TILING PROP. Ratio 6.32:1 against the 5:1 asked (round 1 was 1.70), ends still open — end drop 4 luma against internal stone-gap drops of 52 — tones 26, and at world 150 the wall draws 24 units = 2.6m thick, only 2.9x a real dry-stone wall, less exaggeration than budgeted. Verified by placing three sections at exactly `world` spacing and a fourth rotated 90 degrees: one continuous wall, no visible join, and the corner butts clean. THE ONLY THING THAT CHANGED WAS THE CANVAS. Round 1's subject already said 'eight times as long as it is wide' and delivered 1.70; round 2 said five and delivered 6.32 — because it was generated on a 512x2560 frame instead of the usual 2816x1536. That closes the five-asset pattern this venue documented (quay 3.0->2.13, pier 4.0->2.57, boat shed 2.5->2.15, ferry 2.33->1.94, shop row 2.5->2.06): THE FRAME IS THE PROPORTION LEVER AND THE SUBJECT IS NOT. Set `gen` and actually generate at it. ⚠️ fillTo IS 1.0, NOT THE LIBRARY'S USUAL 0.86, AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING. fillTo insets content inside the frame while drawProps draws the sprite at `world` px, so at 0.86 a 150-unit section would show only 129 units of wall and every butt joint would gap by 14%. At 1.0 the wall spans the frame exactly and sections butt at exactly `world`. THE INGEST MARGIN WARNING IS EXPECTED AND MUST NOT BE 'FIXED': 'content reaches within 6% of the edge' is precisely what a tiling piece requires, and the 8% rotation margin the class asks for does not apply to a prop that is never rotated off its own axis. ⚠️ THIS ARITHMETIC ALSO APPLIES TO cove-quay, which shipped at fillTo 0.86: its deck spans 172 of its 200 units, so quay sections must be placed 172 apart, not 200. Left as-is rather than re-ingested, because changing it would move an asset that is already placed-ready; the spacing is recorded on the kind instead.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE SMALL WOODEN TENDER, shot straight down from directly overhead — a harbour dinghy of the kind rowed out to a moored yacht. The inside is a shade lighter than the outside because it catches the sky. AROUND THE OUTSIDE, a narrow GUNWALE rail runs the whole way round as a clean unbroken band, a little paler than the hull, with a soft dark line of shadow inside it. A short length of pale mooring line lies coiled in the bow. COLOUR: a workboat hull in soft weathered white around #E4E1D8 outside, the interior bare varnished timber around #B8A077 with the thwarts a shade darker, and a single narrow accent stripe along the gunwale in the harbour's own deep green around #2E5E3A. THE HULL FORM IS RIGHT AND IT WAS MEASURED RATHER THAN EYEBALLED — a first look read the stern as rounded, and the stations disprove it: the bow tip is 10% of max beam and the stern ends at 69%, so the transom is genuinely broad and square, and the widest station is at 60% down, exactly the 'a little aft of the middle' the subject asked for. Ratio 2.09:1 against 2.5, inside the honest range for a tender. Green gunwale stripe present at 4% of the sprite, oars stowed both sides, three thwarts, floorboards, coiled painter in the bow, real alpha. ⚠️ TONES 93, DOUBLE THE VENUE BAND, ON A 30-UNIT SPRITE — and that is accepted rather than a fault, because of what survives the reduction. At 30px none of the interior detail resolves; what does is the thing that identifies the asset, a WARM OPEN INTERIOR inside a PALE GUNWALE, where every other hull in this venue is a closed deck. Checked on the race-scale render beside cove-motorboat (48, white and decked) before accepting. assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A FLOATING DINGHY DOCK, shot straight down from directly overhead — the low platform tenders raft up against, held by chains rather than standing on piles. THE RUBBING STRIP — which this note called the identity at race scale — delivered emphatically: rim luma 37 against a deck of 159, a 122-point drop, so a hard dark rim round pale planking is the whole silhouette exactly as intended. assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A TIMBER WHARF FINGER, shot straight down from directly overhead — a working town pier standing on piles. THE OBJECT RUNS UP THE FRAME, long axis vertical, and its FRONT faces the TOP — the engine treats sprite-up as zero heading and rotates from there. It is a LONG NARROW RECTANGLE about four times as long as it is wide, running from a slightly wider shore platform at the BOTTOM of the frame to a squared-off open end at the TOP. Its two long edges run PARALLEL for their whole length, the far end is exactly as wide as the near end, nothing tapers, narrows or converges, and no end face or side wall is visible. If one end is narrower than the other the camera was tilted and the image is wrong however good it looks. THE DECK IS THE PICTURE: heavy timber planks laid ACROSS the width, board by board, running the whole length. Several boards are visibly paler or darker than their neighbours from weathering, and the plank lines are the only rhythm in the image — they run at RIGHT ANGLES to the pier's length, never along it. PILING HEADS STUD BOTH LONG EDGES at even intervals, six or seven a side, each one a dark circle of sawn end grain standing slightly proud of the deck with a hard shadow on the boards beside it. They are seen END-ON from above and are never posts with visible sides. Two or three BOLLARDS stand on the deck near the outer end — squat dark cylinders, also circles from above, thicker than the pilings. A few coils of mooring line lie flat on the boards. THIS PIER IS IN USE AND SOUND: no missing boards, no gaps, no collapse, no rot holes, no derelict leaning. COLOUR: weathered timber decking around #8B7B63, from #6A5C48 in the shaded plank gaps to #A89A80 on the sun-bleached boards. Pilings and bollards are a darker creosoted brown-black around #4A4038. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. assets.note: The repeatable town wharf, and the piece a designer places most. SIZE: 150 units = 16.3m, chosen against bayou-dock's reasoning — 'long enough to pinch a lane, short enough that sailing past it is a decision rather than a wall' — scaled up for a commercial harbour rather than a bayou landing. The plank direction — the cheap differentiator this asset leans on — came back correct: vertical luma gradient 5.04 against horizontal 2.99, so the boards run ACROSS the width as a pier is decked, not along it. Real alpha, runs up the frame, pilings studding both long edges, bollards and rope coils at the outer end, shore platform at the root, no missing boards. TWO DEVIATIONS ACCEPTED. Ratio came back 2.57:1 against the 4:1 asked, so it reads as a landing rather than a long wharf; that is what the repeat-it design is for, and two placed end to end give the length. And the PILING HEADS ARE DRAWN AS LITTLE CYLINDERS WITH VISIBLE SIDES rather than the flat sawn discs cove-piling delivered — the same ortho slip as the lighthouse finial, at about 10px on a 150-unit sprite, so invisible in play. Worth knowing the standalone cove-piling got this RIGHT while the pier's did not: a small object drawn alone gets the camera clause's full attention, and the same object drawn twelve times as furniture on a bigger subject does not.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SECTION OF SOLID CARGO QUAY, shot straight down from directly overhead — the built-up concrete edge a freighter ties against, not a timber pier on piles. THE OBJECT RUNS UP THE FRAME, long axis vertical, and its FRONT faces the TOP — the engine treats sprite-up as zero heading and rotates from there. It is a LONG STRAIGHT BAND about three times as long as it is wide. Its two long edges run PARALLEL for their whole length, the far end is exactly as wide as the near end, nothing tapers, narrows or converges, and no end face or side wall is visible. If one end is narrower than the other the camera was tilted and the image is wrong however good it looks. ⚠️ THIS SECTION IS REPEATED END TO END TO MAKE A LONGER QUAY, so BOTH SHORT ENDS MUST BE PLAIN AND IDENTICAL: square-cut, undecorated, with no bollard, no ladder, no marking and no feature of any kind within a hand's width of either end, and the deck surface running straight off both edges so two copies butt together invisibly. Everything interesting lives in the middle. THE DECK is poured concrete, a broad flat grey surface divided by straight EXPANSION JOINTS running across the width at even intervals, with patches where the concrete has been repaired in a slightly different tone and dark oil staining near the edge. Along the SEAWARD long edge — the top edge of the picture — runs a heavy dark COPING BAND, and hanging just outside it a row of FENDER TIMBERS: thick vertical baulks seen end-on from above as a line of short dark rectangles at even spacing. BOLLARDS: three heavy cast-iron mooring bollards spaced along the seaward edge, each a squat dark circle with a wider foot flange, far bigger than a pier bollard. Between them, two flush mooring RINGS set into the coping. COLOUR: weathered concrete around #9A968E, from #7B776F in the joints and stains to #B4B0A6 on clean slabs. The coping and fenders are dark creosoted timber near #46403A, the bollards a rusted cast iron near #5B4A40. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: The freight side's substrate, and NOT cove-pier resized. A pier is a timber finger reaching OUT on piles; a quay is a solid edge the land is built up to, with a hard vertical face. Different structure, different material, different silhouette at race scale — a broad pale concrete band against a narrow dark timber one. SIZE: 200 units = 21.7m. Lay three or four for a 65-87m berth, which is what the 720-unit (78m) cargo ship actually needs; one 700-unit monolith would be the largest sprite in the game and could only make one length of quay. ⚠️ THE TILING REQUIREMENT IS UNIQUE TO THIS ASSET IN THE WHOLE LIBRARY and is why the ends are specified so hard. Every other prop is placed as a discrete object; this one is designed to butt against copies of itself, so a bollard or a ladder near an end would repeat at a countable interval — the same failure the texture class guards against with 'no feature deliberately centred', arriving here on a prop. Check the ends on delivery by laying two copies side by side before anything else. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 2 ACCEPTED, AND THE TILING IS FIXED — which was the hard part and the whole reason this asset was risky. Measured end-to-end difference fell from 47.9 luma in round 1 to 21.1, and butted the join now reads as another slab joint rather than as a seam; round 1 produced a double dark line because the house-style contour ran round all four sides. THE FURNITURE ALSO CAME BACK — three bollards, two mooring rings and the fender row — which round 1 lost entirely. THE CAUSE OF THAT LOSS IS THE REUSABLE LESSON: round 1 led with a blanket prohibition ('no bollard, no ladder, no marking and no feature of any kind within a hand's width of either end'), and read as a global instruction rather than a positional one it deleted the furniture everywhere. Round 2 leads with the furniture as required and states the end rule as a constraint on WHERE those items sit. State what you want first; constrain its position second. ⚠️ ONE DEVIATION ACCEPTED AND IT IS A REAL ONE: the deck came back COOL BLUE-GREY at hue 199 deg and L* ~33 against a spec of warm weathered concrete #9A968E (hue ~36 deg, L* ~62) — much darker and much cooler than asked. Accepted because it happens to serve the design rather than fight it: at L* 33 it separates hard from the shipped coastalrock ground (#a19481, L* 60), so it reads as BUILT rather than as a natural ledge, and a cool dark working quay against the town's warm shingle-and-hydrangea shore is exactly the two-waterfront contrast the freight side was added to create. If a warm concrete is wanted later, reroll COLOUR ONLY and keep everything else — the tiling took two rounds to get and is the expensive part. ROUND 3 REPLACES ROUND 2 ON DISK, better on both counts that were wrong. COLOUR came back WARM at hue 42 deg — the weathered concrete the subject always asked for — against round 2's cool blue-grey 199 deg. TILING improved again: end-to-end difference 47.9 (r1) -> 21.1 (r2) -> 11.8 (r3), and the furniture is all present. Tones 29, the cleanest of the waterfront set. ⚠️ THE JOIN STILL SHOWS A LINE, AND THE METRIC I USED HIDES IT — worth recording because it is a flaw in the TEST, not just the art. Measuring 'do the two ends match' rewards a sprite whose ends both carry the house contour: they match perfectly and butting them DOUBLES the dark line. The right test is 'does the end have a contour at all'. Accepted anyway because the quay's own expansion joints drop 44 luma, so a doubled contour lands in the same range and reads as a heavy joint rather than a foreign seam — and this asset legitimately has vertical joints every few metres. A truly seamless quay needs the outline suppressed on the two short ends, which fights the house style; the standing alternative is to make the deck a bay-concrete TEXTURE and the furniture separate props, exactly as bay-lane does for lanes. DELIVERED OPAQUE ON WHITE and cut here with a border-flood key on the near-white AND unsaturated test, which kept 0 enclosed pale slabs — the bayou-oak method, and the reason a plain luminance threshold was not used.

They are what a ferry noses between. Along both long edges, a run of heavy FENDER TIMBERS seen end-on as short dark rectangles, and four BOLLARDS on the apron. A small square TICKET SHELTER stands on the landward third, off to one side of the vehicle lane: a plain flat-roofed box, its roof a pale grey panel with a dark rim. COLOUR: timber decking around #8B7B63, asphalt near #4E4A46 with #D8D3C4 lane paint, the steel ramp a cool grey-blue near #6E747C, dolphins and fenders creosote near #46403A. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. The ramp, the dolphins and the fender rows all arrived: steel-grey reads 39% of the sprite against 59% timber, the plank grain runs ACROSS the apron (horizontal gradient 5.34 vs vertical 2.29), and the mooring dolphins came back as clusters of small circles — piles seen correctly END-ON, which the pier's own piling heads did not manage. assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SMALL FLOATING MARINA, shot straight down from directly overhead — the slotted dock system a yacht club keeps its small craft in. THE OBJECT RUNS UP THE FRAME, long axis vertical, and its FRONT faces the TOP — the engine treats sprite-up as zero heading and rotates from there. THE SHAPE IS A COMB. One long MAIN WALKWAY runs up the frame, and off ONE side of it — the right — six narrow FINGER DOCKS project at right angles, parallel to each other and EVENLY SPACED along its length, with an open SLIP of water between each pair. All six fingers are the same length and the same width; the walkway is about twice as wide as a finger. This is a manufactured object and its regularity is correct: the fingers must be genuinely parallel and genuinely evenly spaced, not scattered. IT FLOATS, SO IT IS FLAT AND LOW. There are no piles, no legs and no height anywhere: what you see is DECKING, pale timber planks laid across the short axis of every walkway and finger. A dark RUBBING STRIP runs round the whole outline — walkway edges, finger sides, finger ends — as one continuous band, and it is the strongest line in the picture. ON THE DECK: a pair of small dark CLEATS at the outer end of each finger and two more along the walkway, each a flat double-ended horn; one small square DOCK BOX standing at the head of the walkway at the bottom of the frame, a plain low lid with a dark rim; and short lengths of chain running off two corners to the edge of the picture. THE SLIPS ARE EMPTY. No boat, no yacht, no dinghy, no mast, no mooring line strung across a slip — the gaps between the fingers are open transparent background and nothing is drawn in them. COLOUR: pale weathered decking around #C9BCA4, #A79879 in the plank shadows, #DCD2BC on newer boards; rubbing strip near-black #33302B; cleats galvanised grey #7E8288. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: The single most placement-efficient asset in the venue: one drop gives six berths and a whole yacht-club frontage that would otherwise be a dozen hand-aligned props. SIZE: 240 units = 26m, a small club marina; fingers off ONE side only so that two placed back to back make a double, which is more flexible than baking both sides in. THE ONE CASE WHERE A COMPOSED GROUP BEATS SCATTERED PARTS, against art-pipeline 3b's default. That rule exists because image models return symmetric rosettes when asked for 'seven of X' and a rosette reads as a snowflake at race scale — but a marina IS a regular repeating array, so the failure mode the rule guards against is here the correct answer. allowSymmetry true is mandatory for the same reason: 'evenly spaced' and 'symmetrical arrangement' are exactly what is being asked for. CONTACT NONE, unlike the rest of the waterfront set, and it is the cargo-ship argument: a circle fits a slotted comb worse than it fits anything else here — sized to the outline it seals six slips of open water, sized smaller it stops nothing. A hidden shape per finger is available if a placement ever needs teeth. EMPTY SLIPS, per bayou-dock: the bay already has five hulls that can be parked in them, and a boat baked into the sprite can be placed exactly once. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED, AND THE REGULARITY IS MEASURED RATHER THAN EYEBALLED: six fingers, pitch 244/235/236/237/238 px — a 9px spread across five gaps, i.e. genuinely evenly spaced — all parallel, all the same length, slips open and empty. That is exactly what allowSymmetry was turned on for, and it vindicates the departure from art-pipeline 3b: the rule bans composed groups because models return rosettes, but a marina IS a regular array, so the attractor the rule guards against was the correct answer here. Delivered running UP the frame with the fingers to the right, so `world` 240 fits the long axis and the comb comes out 26m x 15m. Highest resolution of any bay prop at 0.94x, because the sprite is nearly all content.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SHIP-TO-SHORE CARGO CRANE standing on a quay, shot straight down from directly overhead. ⚠️ THE PICTURE IS A WIDE HORIZONTAL STRIP, three times wider than it is tall, and the crane fills it end to end. THE BOOM RUNS LEFT-TO-RIGHT ACROSS THE FRAME — it points out over the water to the RIGHT, and the landward machinery and rails sit at the LEFT. Generate on a wide canvas. This matters more than it sounds: a crane drawn from the SIDE is a tall thing and cannot fit a wide strip, so the frame itself is what forces the correct view. ⚠️ A CRANE IS A TALL THING AND THIS PICTURE SHOWS NONE OF THAT HEIGHT. Every reference image of a cargo crane is taken from the ground or the sea, looking UP at a tower; this is the opposite, and it is the whole difficulty. From directly overhead there is NO TOWER, NO MAST, NO VERTICAL LATTICE and NO SILHOUETTE AGAINST THE SKY. A leg is not a column — it is a small SQUARE where it lands. The machinery house is not a box with faces — it is a flat RECTANGLE, its roof. Nothing tapers, nothing narrows toward any end, nothing recedes, and no part is drawn smaller for being further away, because every part is the SAME distance from the lens. ⚠️ THE SUREST TELL OF A WRONG PICTURE IS A LATTICE THAT NARROWS: a boom seen from above is the SAME WIDTH for its whole length, from the machinery house right out to its blunt tip. If the steelwork tapers, you have drawn a tower from the side. WHAT YOU SEE, from the right of the frame leftward: (1) THE BOOM, a long narrow steel LATTICE reaching out over the water to the RIGHT, of CONSTANT WIDTH end to end — drawn as two parallel main rails with a regular zig-zag of cross-bracing between them, the pattern unbroken along its whole length, ending in a blunt square head; (2) THE MACHINERY HOUSE where the boom meets the frame, a solid rectangular box with a flat panelled roof, the one closed mass in the picture; (3) THE PORTAL FRAME behind it, a broad open square of girders; (4) FOUR LEGS at the corners of that square, each seen END-ON as a small solid square where it lands, with a dark shadow beside it; and (5) TWO RAILS running TOP-TO-BOTTOM across the LEFT end of the frame, beneath the legs, a pair of straight parallel lines with sleepers between them, reaching a little way past the crane on both sides. A SPREADER hangs beneath the boom about two thirds of the way out: a plain rectangular frame, seen as a smaller oblong outline lying on the boom's line, with four corner blocks. COLOUR: painted industrial steel in a dull weathered RED-BROWN around #8E4536, from #6B3327 in shadow to #A9604F on lit surfaces, with the machinery house roof a cool grey #6E747C and the rails bare rust #7A5344. ⚠️ IT MUST NOT BE THE SUSPENSION BRIDGE'S ORANGE: that span is international orange #C0362C and this is browner, duller and darker, so the two never read as the same painted structure. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in.
assets.note: The freight side's identity, and the only LANDMARK in the waterfront set — role landmark rather than hazard because it stands ON the quay rather than reaching into the channel, which is exactly the line art-pipeline 2 draws ('a landmark never reads as an obstacle in the water'). SIZE: 230 units = 25m, a small ship-to-shore crane, tall in life and modest in plan. ⚠️ THE BOOM OVERHANGS THE WATER AND STRICTLY WANTS TO BE A SPLIT PAIR. It stands ~30m up, so a boat can pass beneath it — which by the plane rules makes the boom `canopy` and the legs `surface`, exactly the trunk/crown split the bayou trees carry. It ships as ONE `surface` sprite anyway, because in practice the berth beneath a working crane is occupied by the ship it is unloading, and paying for a split pair to serve a placement nobody will author is the wrong trade. This is the same coupling recorded on the shore trees: anyone re-planing this to `canopy` is changing what it occludes, and should split it first. THE LATTICE IS THE RISK. A generator asked for a crane from above will reach for a solid beam; the boom's identity is that it is OPEN steelwork, and the truss bridge's subject already proved the fix — describe it as a repeating zig-zag between two rails rather than as a 'lattice'. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ ROUND 1 CAME BACK AS A FRONT ELEVATION and the reroll changes the FRAME, not the wording, because the wording was already explicit. The delivery had the rails correct — two parallel lines with cross-ties, a true plan — and everything above them in side view: a lattice that NARROWS toward the top like a tower in perspective, portal legs showing their full vertical length, a machinery house drawn as a 3D box with faces, and no horizontal boom at all. Subject aspect 0.93, i.e. essentially square, which is the shape of a crane ELEVATION. THE FIX IS A WIDE FRAME AND IT IS A SHARPER VERSION OF THE WALL'S LESSON. The wall proved the frame sets the proportion; this goes further — a crane seen from the SIDE is a tall object and physically cannot fill a 3:1 wide strip, so the frame does not merely bias the proportion, it makes the wrong VIEW impossible. gen is now 3072x1024 with the boom running left-to-right and the frame's shape stated in the subject's first line. A NEW TELL WAS ADDED because it is the one thing that cannot be faked: a boom seen from above is the SAME WIDTH for its whole length, so a lattice that tapers is a tower drawn from the side. ⚠️ THIS BREAKS THE 'FRONT FACES THE TOP' CONVENTION deliberately — the boom points right at heading 0 rather than up — and the trade is worth it: a designer sets `heading` per placement anyway, and no heading can rescue a sprite drawn in elevation. Note it when registering the kind. bake set to 2 preemptively: at world 230 the profile's 4x would ask 920px of a master holding 881, which is the upscale the ferry hit.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A BLOCK OF SHIPPING CONTAINERS standing on a quay, shot straight down from directly overhead. A CONTAINER SEEN FROM ABOVE IS SIMPLY A RECTANGLE — this is the easiest subject in the venue and the only thing to get wrong is the camera. No side, no end, no door, no corrugated flank running away from you: you see the flat ROOF of each box and nothing else. THE BLOCK IS A TIGHT GRID: two rows of three or four containers, laid side by side with their long axes running UP the frame, packed with only a hand's width of gap between neighbours and the rows squared off against each other. Every container is the same size and they line up cleanly — this is a stacking yard and its regularity is correct. ON EACH ROOF: fine CORRUGATION ribs running ACROSS the short axis, evenly spaced the whole length; a small dark CORNER CASTING at each of the four corners; and on two or three of them a faint rectangular patch where the paint has been repaired. Two containers are STACKED — drawn as the same rectangle a touch larger with a hard dark shadow cast onto the box beside it, which is the only cue that they are two high. COLOUR IS THE WHOLE CHARM AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE IN THE TOWN THAT CARRIES SATURATION: give the block a mixed set — one rust red around #9B4032, one faded maritime blue around #35566E, one weathered sea green around #3D6B57, one dull grey around #7D8188, one bleached white-grey around #C4C1B8. Each container is ONE flat colour with a slightly darker tone in the corrugation shadows, all of them chalky and sun-faded, none of them glossy or new. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number. NO TEXT OF ANY KIND: no shipping line name, no lettering, no serial number, no logo, no placard.
assets.note: The cheapest readable asset in the venue by a wide margin, and the reason is worth stating: a container from directly overhead IS a rectangle, so this subject has no foreshortening trap, no vertical part to collapse to a dot, and no side-view prior to fight. Every other asset in this venue has spent its longest clause on the camera; this one does not need to. SIZE: 115 units = 12.5m, a block of six to eight boxes. IT IS ALSO THE VENUE'S COLOUR RELIEF. The whole town is grey, slate and cedar and the freight side is concrete and rusted steel; a mixed block of containers is the one place saturated colour belongs on this shore, and it reads at race scale when nothing else at 115 units would. allowSymmetry true because a stacking yard is a manufactured grid — 'evenly spaced' and 'tiled pattern' are precisely what is wanted. Part of Lighthouse Cove's WATERFRONT SET. Role and contact follow bayou-dock's argument, which transfers unchanged: a `landmark` never reads as an obstacle in the water, and a structure reaching into the channel is the whole reason to place one — so these are `hazard`, and the art must telegraph solid. PLANE FOLLOWS PHYSICS, not object class: a structure standing above the water is `surface` (over land and water, under the boats), a thing floating ON the water is `float` (after every mark the water makes, so no wake ripples across it, and behind the land so a bank covers it). ⚠️ THE CIRCLE-COLLIDER LIMIT APPLIES TO EVERY LONG PIECE HERE. compile emits a circle per contact prop, which fits a 4:1 wharf no better than it fits a cargo ship — sized to the width it leaves most of the structure sailable-through, sized to the length it is an invisible wall. The established answer is the river's: draw these as props and lay ONE HIDDEN HARD SHAPE along the face, the way the river's 82 banks sit behind one continuous drawn shore. Register contact per the table but expect a placement to override it to none wherever a hidden shape is doing the real work. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF — every piece here except the piling is directional. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED, AND IT WAS THE ONLY SUBJECT IN THE VENUE WITH NO CAMERA PROBLEM — exactly as the note predicted. A container from above IS a rectangle: no foreshortening trap, no vertical part to collapse, no side-view prior to fight, and the delivery came back a clean plan first try with corrugation ribs running across each box, corner castings at four corners, and a few stacked two high with hard shadows. Colour split rust 24% / green 22% / white-grey 20% / blue 18%, which is the mixed set asked for and the only saturated thing on the freight shore. ⚠️ WORLD RAISED 115 -> 225 AND THAT IS A SPEC CORRECTION, NOT A DELIVERY FAULT. The slot assumed a block two rows deep with the boxes' long axes running UP the frame — 12.2m long, hence 115. The delivery laid them the other way, four boxes end to end across the frame, which is 4 x 6.1 = 24.4m and needs world 224 for life size. At 115 each box would have drawn 3m long, obviously wrong beside a 78m cargo ship. Checked against the containers already painted on cove-cargo-ship's deck at race scale: the two now agree, which is the only scale test that matters for a freight yard. bake 3 rather than 4 because 225 x 4 = 900px would have asked more than the 881px the master holds — the ferry's lesson applied before ingest rather than after. Tones 154, the highest in the venue, and accepted for the same reason as the dinghy: at 225 units each box is ~56px, the ribs go sub-pixel, and what survives is a grid of flat coloured rectangles, which IS the asset.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A SMALL HARBOUR CAFE, shot straight down from directly overhead. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE: no wall, no window, no door, no shopfront and no gable end seen face-on. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. A SMALL RECTANGULAR BUILDING about 4:3 in plan. ⚠️ IT HAS A RIDGE AND THE RIDGE MUST READ: one straight line running left-to-right across the middle of the long axis, with the two slopes either side of it as FLAT PLANES AT CLEARLY DIFFERENT TONES and a hard edge between them. That tonal step is the only thing that says ROOF rather than RECTANGLE, and a roof drawn as one uniform plane of shingles has failed. The roof overhangs the walls, so the outline is the roof's own edge with a thin darker line of eaves shadow all round. Its two long edges run parallel, nothing tapers, and no end wall is visible. ALONG THE LOWER LONG EDGE — the street side, at the bottom of the frame — an AWNING projects beyond the eaves: a straight strip of canvas in a deep harbour GREEN around #2E5E3A, about a sixth as deep as the building, its outer edge cut into a row of even scallops, with a hard shadow beneath its outer lip. It runs the full width. ON THE ROOF: one squat brick CHIMNEY on the ridge, pointing at the camera and therefore a small rectangle with a darker flue inside it, never a tower with sides, casting one short hard shadow onto the slope beside it. One round metal VENT COWL on the upper slope, a small dark circle with a pale rim. WEATHERED CEDAR SHINGLE SEEN FROM TEN METRES: shingles do not resolve individually, so the surface reads as faint COURSES running parallel to the ridge with a gentle mottling where some have weathered lighter. Never shingle by shingle, never a crisp grid. COLOUR: a warm weathered grey around #9C968B, from #7B766C in the shaded slope to #B4AEA3 on the lit one, eaves in clean white trim around #F5F5F3. NO TERRACE, NO TABLES, NO PARASOLS AND NO FURNITURE OF ANY KIND — the building alone. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no paving, no terrace floor, no kerb, no lawn, no path, no cast shadow on the ground. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies what it sits on. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no text, no lettering, no logo.
assets.note: The one building in the town that is not grey, and the only one with a CIRCLE in it. A parasol seen from directly overhead is a circle with radiating seams — trivially readable, no foreshortening trap, and the only non-rectangular shape on the whole shore, so this asset reads as 'somewhere people go' at a size where nothing else could. SIZE 108 units = 11.7m for building plus terrace, kept off 100 (dormered cottage) and 129 (captain's house). THE TERRACE FURNITURE IS DRAWN INTO THE SPRITE and that follows cove-shanty's lobster pots rather than breaking the no-ground rule: objects may stand beside the building on transparent background; what may not be drawn is the GROUND they stand on. If the delivery paves the terrace, that is the failure. Part of Lighthouse Cove's SHOP SET — the town's only commercial buildings, and the design problem is that FROM ABOVE A SHOP AND A HOUSE ARE BOTH A ROOF. Everything that identifies a shop at street level — the window, the door, the sign, the goods — is invisible in plan, so the distinction has to be carried by roof furniture, and only three cues really work: a FALSE-FRONT PARAPET standing proud of the roof along the street edge, an AWNING projecting beyond the eaves, and (for the row) PARTY WALLS cutting one roof into bays. All three are used deliberately across the set. AWNING COLOURS ARE THE VENUE'S REGISTERED ACCENTS, deep red and deep green, taken from venue-art.md's palette registry ('red/green channel buoys') rather than invented — it makes the shops belong to this harbour instead of to a generic high street. No confusion risk with the buoys themselves: those are 28 units and float in the water, these are attached to buildings on land. These are also the only saturated colour anywhere in the town, which is the point: the other eight buildings are grey, slate and cedar. allowSymmetry TRUE on all three, for the cottages' three reasons at once — a gable roof is symmetric about its ridge, party walls and awning stripes are 'evenly spaced', and shingle courses are a 'tiled pattern', all of which ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE would otherwise forbid. Role ambient, plane surface, contact none — they stand on land the fleet cannot reach. Sizes deliberately avoid 129 so they do not twin the captain's house in the picker or the size ladder. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF and set `heading °`: a shop's awning faces the street. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⚠️ ROUND 1 SPLIT INTO TWO ASSETS, and the delivery is why. The parasols came back beautifully — green and cream wedge circles with radiating seams, exactly as specified, and the only non-rectangular shape on the whole shore — but they ATE THE BUILDING. Measured: the shop was 24% of the sprite height and the terrace 76%, and because fillTo scales the LONG axis to `world`, a 108-unit café would have drawn its building at about 26 units, smaller than the fish shanty at 55. At race scale it read as four umbrellas with a shed attached rather than as a café. THE FIX IS THE PILING'S FIX: a fixed cluster baked into one sprite locks a proportion and an arrangement, where a single placeable object lets the designer set both. So the parasols left as cove-parasol and this slot became the building alone at world 88, which puts it between the shanty (55) and the plain cottage (80) where a small café belongs. A RIDGE CLAUSE WAS ADDED, because the delivered roof had none: the 42-luma step measured on it sat at the awning/roof edge 12% down, not mid-roof, so the roof was one uniform plane of shingles. That is the failure the shared roof fragment exists to prevent and it slipped through on the one building whose subject had the fragment abbreviated. ROUND 2 ACCEPTED — the split worked. Building alone, no terrace furniture, ridge present at 36% down with a 35-luma step (round 1's roof had none, which is what the restored ridge clause was for), green scalloped awning along the street edge, chimney and round vent cowl. Ratio 1.07 against the 1.33 asked, squarer than specced and harmless. Delivered OPAQUE on white; cut with the border-flood key on near-white AND unsaturated, which KEPT 11,159 enclosed pale pixels — the shingle highlights — that a plain luminance threshold would have punched holes in. That is the bayou-oak method earning its place again.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF ONE CAFE PARASOL, shot straight down from directly overhead — the canvas umbrella over a harbour terrace table. A PARASOL SEEN FROM DIRECTLY ABOVE IS A CIRCLE, and its whole height runs into the camera and disappears. NO POLE IS VISIBLE AS A POLE — no shaft, no stem, no length of anything standing up — and no part of the underside shows. If you can see a pole, the camera was not overhead. IT IS A SHALLOW CONE OF CANVAS: an eight-sided disc, very slightly polygonal at the rim rather than a perfect circle, with eight straight SEAMS running from the rim in to a small dark cap at the exact centre. The eight panels alternate WARM CREAM around #EFE7D6 and deep harbour GREEN around #2E5E3A, and because the cone falls away from its centre the panels on one side are a step darker than those on the other — two flat tones of each colour, split down one axis, never a smooth radial blend. AT THE CENTRE, the FINIAL CAP: a small dark rounded disc where the eight seams meet, and nothing projecting from it. At the rim, a narrow scalloped VALANCE hangs a little way down all round, seen almost edge-on from above as a thin darker band just inside the outline, its lower edge cut into even shallow scallops. BENEATH AND JUST PEEPING OUT from under one side of the canvas, the pale timber rim of the round TABLE it stands over, and two small dark curved marks where chair backs show past the canvas edge. They are small — the canvas hides most of them, which is what proves it is above them. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no paving, no terrace floor, no kerb, no lawn, no path, no cast shadow on the ground. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies what it sits on. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no text, no lettering, no logo.
assets.note: Split out of cove-cafe after round 1, and the more useful half. A parasol from directly overhead is a CIRCLE with radiating seams — no foreshortening trap, no vertical part to collapse, and the only non-rectangular shape on the whole shore, so it reads at a size where nothing else would. It is also the town's only saturated colour outside the shop awnings. SIZE IS HONEST, UNUSUALLY: a real café parasol is 2.2-2.6m, so world 24 = 2.6m needs no exaggeration at all — the opposite of cove-piling, which had to be drawn 3.3x life size to be visible. SINGLE, NOT A CLUSTER, for the reason the piling established and the café delivery proved: a baked group locks its arrangement AND its proportion, and cove-cafe round 1 lost its building to exactly that. As a single object it can be scattered outside the café, ranked along the shop row, or dropped on the marina. PLACE WITH prop-spin ON — a parasol has no front, and rotating the green/cream wedges is free variety that stops a terrace of four reading as one stamp repeated. planRound TRUE and allowSymmetry TRUE: it genuinely IS a circle with eight evenly spaced panels, so the roundness test is the right tilt check and the radial-symmetry negatives would fight the subject — the mark and the lighthouse precedent. Role ambient, plane surface, contact none. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED WITH TWO RECORDED WARNINGS, and the interesting one is a REVERSAL of the piling's finding. Ingest flagged NOT ORTHOGRAPHIC at 1.17x (canopy alone 1.22x, implying a 31-degree camera) plus a grey underside band at 5.9% of the sprite — the canopy is drawn as a tilted 3D object rather than a flat plan. ⚠️ THE SAME OBJECT CAME BACK FLAT WHEN IT WAS FURNITURE: cove-cafe round 1 and cove-yacht-club both delivered parasols as clean flat octagons with radiating seams, drawn small as part of a bigger subject. Drawn ALONE and large, the generator reached for 3D shading and perspective. That is the exact inverse of cove-piling, where the standalone disc was correct and the same pile drawn twelve times as pier furniture came back as cylinders with sides. THE LESSON IS NOT 'alone is better' OR 'furniture is better' — it is that a subject's SIZE IN THE FRAME changes which prior the generator reaches for, and neither case can be assumed. ACCEPTED because at world 24 the aspect error is 24x21px and the underside band is about 1px: invisible, exactly as the lighthouse finial (1.4px) and the piling skirt (0.2px) were. Second warning: the master is 590px against the profile's 1024, so it bakes from 590 rather than upscaling — fine at 24 units (0.16x resolution) but regenerate larger if this is ever wanted bigger.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A GENERAL STORE, shot straight down from directly overhead. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE: no wall, no window, no door, no shopfront, no gable end seen face-on. If any wall is visible the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong. THE BUILDING IS A PLAIN RECTANGLE about 3:2 in plan, larger and squarer than a cottage, under a SHALLOW roof — two slopes meeting at a centred ridge running the long way, but a low-pitched one, so the two slopes read as broad flat planes with only a modest tone step between them at the ridge. Its two long edges run PARALLEL for their whole length, the far end is exactly as wide as the near end, nothing tapers, narrows or converges, and no end face or side wall is visible. If one end is narrower than the other the camera was tilted and the image is wrong however good it looks. THE FALSE FRONT IS WHAT MAKES IT A SHOP, and it is the whole reason this building is not a house. Along the LOWER long edge — the street side, at the bottom of the frame — a PARAPET stands proud of the roof: a straight raised band running the full width of the building, with its own narrow flat TOP surface catching the light and a hard dark SHADOW cast from it back across the roof slope behind. It is the boarded square front the roof hides behind, seen edge-on from above, and it must read as standing UP off the roof rather than painted onto it. BEYOND THE PARAPET, projecting out past the building's edge, an AWNING: a straight strip of canvas in a deep harbour RED around #8C3A2E, about a sixth as deep as the building, its outer edge cut into a row of even scallops, with a hard shadow beneath its outer lip. It runs the full width. ON THE ROOF, and little else: two squat brick CHIMNEYS on the ridge, each pointing at the camera and therefore a small rectangle with a darker flue inside it, never a tower with sides; and two round metal VENT COWLS on the upper slope, small dark circles with a pale rim. COLOUR: the roof is weathered grey cedar shingle around #9C968B, #7B766C in the shaded slope and #B4AEA3 on the lit one, with faint courses running parallel to the ridge. The parapet's top and the eaves are clean white trim around #F5F5F3. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: The standalone shop — a corner store or dockside chandlery, where cove-shop-row is a main street.
