If the delivery paints a stripe along the roof edge instead of casting a shadow from a raised band, it has failed on the one thing that separates this from a low-pitched cottage. THE SHALLOW PITCH IS THE SECOND CUE, and it is quieter but real: every house in this town has a steep Cape roof with a strong tone step at the ridge, and a commercial building reads flatter. Part of Lighthouse Cove's SHOP SET — the town's only commercial buildings, and the design problem is that FROM ABOVE A SHOP AND A HOUSE ARE BOTH A ROOF. Everything that identifies a shop at street level — the window, the door, the sign, the goods — is invisible in plan, so the distinction has to be carried by roof furniture, and only three cues really work: a FALSE-FRONT PARAPET standing proud of the roof along the street edge, an AWNING projecting beyond the eaves, and (for the row) PARTY WALLS cutting one roof into bays. All three are used deliberately across the set. AWNING COLOURS ARE THE VENUE'S REGISTERED ACCENTS, deep red and deep green, taken from venue-art.md's palette registry ('red/green channel buoys') rather than invented — it makes the shops belong to this harbour instead of to a generic high street. No confusion risk with the buoys themselves: those are 28 units and float in the water, these are attached to buildings on land. These are also the only saturated colour anywhere in the town, which is the point: the other eight buildings are grey, slate and cedar. allowSymmetry TRUE on all three, for the cottages' three reasons at once — a gable roof is symmetric about its ridge, party walls and awning stripes are 'evenly spaced', and shingle courses are a 'tiled pattern', all of which ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE would otherwise forbid. Role ambient, plane surface, contact none — they stand on land the fleet cannot reach. Sizes deliberately avoid 129 so they do not twin the captain's house in the picker or the size ladder. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF and set `heading °`: a shop's awning faces the street. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED WITH ONE CUE WEAK. The red awning, two chimneys and a 47-luma ridge all arrived, and at true race scale the awning strip alone separates it from a cottage. THE FALSE-FRONT PARAPET DID NOT FULLY LAND: it came back as a flat white band rather than a raised element casting a shadow back across the roof, so the cue the note called 'the asset' is doing less work than planned and the awning is carrying the building. Accepted rather than rerolled because at 124 units a parapet is about 4px and the awning is 20 — the weak cue was always going to be the quiet one. If this is ever regenerated, the fix is to specify the SHADOW rather than the band: it is the shadow that proves something stands up, which is the same thing the chimney and dormer clauses rely on.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A TERRACE OF THREE ATTACHED SHOPS — a short stretch of harbour main street — shot straight down from directly overhead. YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE ROOF AND AT NOTHING ELSE: no wall, no window, no door, no shopfront, no gable end seen face-on. IT IS ONE CONTINUOUS BUILDING, NOT THREE. A single long roof runs the whole length, about two and a half times as long as it is deep, with one straight ridge running the full length down its middle. Its two long edges run PARALLEL for their whole length, the far end is exactly as wide as the near end, nothing tapers, narrows or converges, and no end face or side wall is visible. If one end is narrower than the other the camera was tilted and the image is wrong however good it looks. WHAT DIVIDES IT INTO SHOPS IS TWO PARTY WALLS: two straight lines crossing the roof at right angles to the ridge, at even thirds along its length, each one a narrow raised band of masonry standing slightly proud of the shingles with a hard shadow on one side. They run from the front edge clean over the ridge to the back edge. The three bays between them are the same width as each other. ALONG THE FRONT EDGE — the lower long edge of the picture — EACH BAY HAS ITS OWN AWNING, projecting past the eaves as a straight strip of scalloped canvas with a hard shadow beneath its outer lip. THE THREE ARE DIFFERENT COLOURS and that is the life of the picture: deep harbour RED around #8C3A2E, warm CREAM around #E8DFC8, and deep harbour GREEN around #2E5E3A, in that order along the street. Each awning stops cleanly at its own party wall and does not run into its neighbour. Behind each awning a low PARAPET band stands proud of the roof edge for that bay's width. ON THE ROOF: a squat brick CHIMNEY standing on the ridge at each party wall, pointing at the camera and therefore a small rectangle with a darker flue inside, never a tower with sides. Faint shingle courses run parallel to the ridge the whole length. COLOUR: weathered grey cedar shingle around #9C968B, #7B766C shaded and #B4AEA3 lit, party walls and parapets in a paler stone around #B8B2A6, eaves in clean white trim #F5F5F3. NO GROUND AND NO WATER IS DRAWN: no shoreline, no waterline, no foam, no ripple, no reflection, no wet stain, no sand, no grass, no paving, no cast shadow on anything outside the object itself. It stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies whatever it sits on or in. NOTHING ALIVE AND NOTHING MODERN: no person, no bird, no car, no forklift, no text, no lettering, no signage with writing, no logo, no number.
assets.note: A whole main street in one placement, and the reason it is one asset rather than three: three separate shop sprites would have to be aligned by hand to sit shoulder to shoulder, and any drift in heading or spacing would read instantly as a mistake at race scale. An attached terrace is also historically right for a harbour main street, so this is not a shortcut. SIZE 200 units = 21.7m for three bays, about 7.2m each, which is a narrow old shopfront and correct. THE THREE AWNING COLOURS ARE THE ASSET. At 200 units the party walls are a couple of pixels and the shingle courses are texture; what actually reads from the water is three coloured strips in a row along the shore, which is exactly what a main street looks like from a boat. If the delivery returns one awning colour across all three bays, it has lost the thing that makes it a street rather than a long shed. ⚠️ THIS IS THE ASSET allowSymmetry MATTERS MOST FOR: 'evenly spaced' and 'symmetrical arrangement' are both banned by ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE and both are exactly what three equal bays under one roof require. Part of Lighthouse Cove's SHOP SET — the town's only commercial buildings, and the design problem is that FROM ABOVE A SHOP AND A HOUSE ARE BOTH A ROOF. Everything that identifies a shop at street level — the window, the door, the sign, the goods — is invisible in plan, so the distinction has to be carried by roof furniture, and only three cues really work: a FALSE-FRONT PARAPET standing proud of the roof along the street edge, an AWNING projecting beyond the eaves, and (for the row) PARTY WALLS cutting one roof into bays. All three are used deliberately across the set. AWNING COLOURS ARE THE VENUE'S REGISTERED ACCENTS, deep red and deep green, taken from venue-art.md's palette registry ('red/green channel buoys') rather than invented — it makes the shops belong to this harbour instead of to a generic high street. No confusion risk with the buoys themselves: those are 28 units and float in the water, these are attached to buildings on land. These are also the only saturated colour anywhere in the town, which is the point: the other eight buildings are grey, slate and cedar. allowSymmetry TRUE on all three, for the cottages' three reasons at once — a gable roof is symmetric about its ridge, party walls and awning stripes are 'evenly spaced', and shingle courses are a 'tiled pattern', all of which ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE would otherwise forbid. Role ambient, plane surface, contact none — they stand on land the fleet cannot reach. Sizes deliberately avoid 129 so they do not twin the captain's house in the picker or the size ladder. PLACE WITH prop-spin OFF and set `heading °`: a shop's awning faces the street. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ROUND 1 ACCEPTED AND IT IS THE BEST OF THE SHOP SET. The three awning colours all arrived and measure distinct along the bottom edge — red 31%, green 31%, cream 22% of that band — with the party walls reading as raised bands casting shadows, a chimney per bay, and a 98-luma ridge step. At TRUE race scale it does exactly what the note predicted: three coloured strips in a row along the shore, which is what a main street looks like from a boat. Ratio came back 2.06 against the 2.5 asked, which is the canvas again (the 1024x2048 gen was set but the delivery arrived 2816x1536); it costs nothing here because three bays under one roof read regardless.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A VERTICAL AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A LIGHTHOUSE, shot straight down from a drone hovering directly over the lantern — the picture a survey flight makes of a light station. THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY OF THIS SUBJECT IS THAT A LIGHTHOUSE IS A TALL THING AND YOU CANNOT SEE ITS HEIGHT. Every picture of one ever taken looks UP at a tower; here the entire height runs straight into the camera and disappears, and what is left is a set of CONCENTRIC RINGS seen from above. NO WALL IS VISIBLE ANYWHERE — no length of tower, no curved white side running away from you, no door, no window, no gallery seen from beneath, and nothing at all that tells you the building is tall. If any part of the tower's flank appears, the camera was not overhead and the image is wrong however good it looks. A classic NEW ENGLAND HARBOUR LIGHT: a short white masonry tower under a black lantern, the kind standing on Nantucket, the Vineyard and the outer Cape. Build it from the outside inward as FIVE RINGS, all sharing one centre. (1) THE BASE PLINTH, outermost and widest: a clean white circular apron of masonry with a crisp outer edge, and it is the disc that fills the frame. (2) THE TOWER. It tapers as it rises, so from overhead its wall reads ONLY as a narrow white annulus stepped in from the plinth — a ring, never a cylinder — divided from the plinth by a single fine shadow line where one steps under the other. (3) THE GALLERY DECK: a flat circular walkway ringing the lantern, stepped in again from the tower's edge, its floor a pale grey-white ring. Around its outer rim runs a BLACK IRON RAILING, drawn as it truly appears from above — one thin dark unbroken circle for the handrail, and just inside it a ring of short evenly spaced dark TICKS, one per baluster, each pointing at the centre. The balusters are seen END-ON and foreshorten to almost nothing, so they are ticks and never uprights. (4) THE LANTERN ROOF, the dark heart of the picture and its strongest shape. From above you see the ROOF and not the glass, because the roof overhangs the lantern and hides it: a shallow POLYGONAL DOME of eight sides in a deep green-black, with a crisp seam running from the centre out to each of the eight corners so the facets read as separate planes at slightly different tones. (5) THE VENTILATOR BALL AND FINIAL, dead centre: a small dark rounded ball with a fine lightning rod standing straight up out of it. THE ROD POINTS AT THE CAMERA, so it foreshortens to a DOT — a tiny dark point at the exact middle of the ball — and is never a line, a spike, or a mast lying across the frame. COLOUR, TAKEN FROM THE VENUE'S OWN CARD. The masonry is a clean warm-neutral chalk white around #F9F9F6, going no darker than #F2F1EC where one ring steps under another. The lantern roof, the railing and the ball are a deep GREEN-BLACK around #182F2B — dark, and unmistakably a COLOUR rather than a neutral: never pure black, never a blue-grey. No third hue appears anywhere on the building. NO LIGHT IS SHINING. It is broad daylight: no beam, no ray, no lens flare, no glow, no halo, no bloom, no lit window and no light spilling onto anything. A lighthouse beam travels sideways and out to sea, so from directly overhead it would not be visible even at night. NO STRIPES: this tower is plain white, with no red or black bands, no spiral barber-pole stripe, no chequer and no daymark pattern of any kind — a spiral seen from overhead reads as a bullseye, which is exactly the wrong picture. NO GROUND IS DRAWN: no headland, no grass, no rock, no path, no fence, no keeper's house, no cast shadow and no water. The lighthouse stands alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the bluff it is built on
assets.note: THE VENUE'S NAMESAKE, and the last of Lighthouse Cove's landmark set (the two bridges are the others). Drawn as the TOWER ALONE: venues.md lists the harbourmaster's house as its own asset, and art-pipeline 3b's one-object rule says a light station with its keeper's cottage is two things composed, not one generation. SIZE IS HONEST AND SITS AT THE TOP OF THE REAL RANGE. world 84 / 9.2 units per m = 9.1m across the base plinth. Real New England towers measure about 4m at the base (Brant Point) to 7m (Highland), and a masonry apron adds a metre or two, so this is a substantial light station rather than an exaggeration — and the scale block asks for any exaggeration to be declared, so it is worth saying there is none. ⚠️ THE CONSEQUENCE IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IS CORRECT: at 84 the lighthouse is NARROWER than cove-oak-black at 96. A big oak's crown really is wider than a light tower's base, and the venue's namesake being smaller in plan than a tree is what an aerial photograph of a headland actually looks like. Do not 'fix' it by inflating the tower; if it needs to read bigger, that is a placement decision (put it alone on a point) rather than a scale one. allowSymmetry TRUE, AND IT IS REQUIRED RATHER THAN PERMITTED — the same call as `mark` and the two channel buoys. ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE forbids 'radial symmetry', 'ring formation', 'circular arrangement' and 'evenly spaced', and this subject asks for concentric rings and a ring of evenly spaced balusters, so leaving the flag off would make the prompt argue with itself and the generator would resolve it by dropping one half at random. A lighthouse in plan is genuinely radial; the mandala risk it normally guards against does not apply to an object that IS a bullseye. planRound true: round in plan, so the outline is the acceptance test ingest measures. THE SUBJECT IS ORGANISED AS NUMBERED CONCENTRIC RINGS FROM THE OUTSIDE IN, which is buoy-channel-red's device and the right one here for the same reason: it converts 'draw a tall thing from above' into a list of flat shapes with an order, which is a thing a generator can actually execute. FOUR FAILURE MODES ARE NAMED, each because it is what the training data is full of. (1) THE SIDE VIEW is the big one and it is the red cedar's problem made worse — a lighthouse's identity IS its height, and the plan view deletes exactly that, so the clause states the geometry, gives the correct answer (concentric rings) and names the tell (any flank visible = wrong camera). (2) THE BEAM: generators reach for a light beam, glow or flare on anything called a lighthouse. From overhead a beam is invisible because it shines sideways, and this venue is broad daylight anyway. (3) THE FINIAL: a lightning rod is vertical, so it points AT the camera and collapses to a dot — the same foreshortening the bayou moss clause turned on, and the same failure available (a rod drawn lying across the frame is proof of a tilted camera). (4) STRIPES: half the lighthouses in reference imagery are banded or spiralled, and a spiral seen from overhead becomes a bullseye that would fight the real concentric structure. COLOURS MEASURED OFF assets/images/venues/bay.png with sky masked out by hue rather than by hand-picked boxes (a first pass sampled straight rectangles and returned #23699 5-ish blues — it was reading the sky between the railing balusters). Masonry #F9F9F6 across 7371 px, lantern and roof #182F2B across 3827. The green-black is real and worth holding: it is what the card has, and visual-style.md 267 asks for blue-black, green-black or warm charcoal rather than pure black. anchor `footprint` — the origin is the centre of the base plinth, which for a concentric subject is also the alpha bbox centre, so ingest's seed should land right for once; verify on the contact sheet anyway. WHAT TO CHECK ON DELIVERY, in order: no wall or window anywhere (a material failure, not a rendering one); the finial as a dot rather than a line; aspect under the 1.12 gate; then the ring COUNT — five distinct concentric bands, because the likeliest quiet failure is a generator collapsing plinth and tower into one disc. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6: slot, then art, then the kind. DELIVERED AND INGESTED 2026-08-10, first roll, clearing every gate and setting the bay's best orthography: aspect 1.001 against the 1.12 ingest gate. The five concentric rings all arrived and all read; the roof centre sits 0.2% of the radius off the disc centre, so it is genuinely concentric rather than nearly so; tones needed to cover 90% of the sprite came in at 45, inside the venue band and between the shipped oak (40) and tugboat (46); masonry #EDEBE5 and lantern #1E2B27 against a spec of #F9F9F6 / #182F2B, with the roof measurably a GREEN-black (g > r and g > b) as visual-style 267 asks. No baked ground shadow: zero dark semi-transparent px. ⚠️ ONE KNOWN DEFECT, ACCEPTED AND NOT TO BE REDISCOVERED: THE FINIAL IS DRAWN IN ELEVATION. The ventilator ball carries a short cylindrical post with a rounded cap, a highlight down one side and its own shadow falling on the ball — a side view of a rod, which is exactly what the subject's clause forbids ('the rod points at the camera, so it foreshortens to a DOT'). It is the one part of the image that is not a true nadir view, and the pattern is worth noting: the vertical-foreshortening rule was obeyed on the RAILING BALUSTERS, where it is hardest and where there are sixty of them, and missed on the single object small enough that it does not feel 'tall'. ACCEPTED because the rod measures ~24px in a 1421px sprite = 1.4px at world 84 — sub-pixel at display size, invisible in play, and touching no ingest gate. Rerolling would have risked four things this delivery got right to fix one nobody can see. Fix it if this is ever regenerated. PROCESSING: pre-cut with real alpha and BLACK under it, and the colour bleed was essential here rather than optional — against a premultiplied resize the black cost +66.6 luma at the edge, the largest halo measured in this venue's whole batch (oak +11.5, cedar +29.8, pine +50.5). A NEAR-WHITE SUBJECT IS THE WORST CASE for this defect, because the edge blend runs the full distance from the subject to black. Beware the wrong test: comparing edge luma to BODY luma said 1.01x and looked clean, which is meaningless on a subject whose body averages a white plinth with a black roof together — only the premultiplied comparison is diagnostic. Bled, cropped to the alpha bbox, padded to 86% content, ingested. Registered as `bay-cove-lighthouse`, world 84, surface, contact none.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TREE, shot straight down from well above it the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. YOU SEE FOLIAGE AND NOTHING ELSE. The crown is CLOSED right across the frame, centre included: no trunk, no dark hub, no limb, no branch, no twig and no bark shows anywhere in this picture, and least of all in the middle — the centre of the crown is more leaf, exactly like the rest of it. This tree is scenery standing on a headland; nothing passes beneath it and nothing needs to read its structure, so it is drawn as ONE CONTINUOUS MASS OF LEAF seen from above, and a branch showing through is a mistake rather than a detail. A BLACK OAK on a New England headland — Nantucket, the Vineyard, the outer Cape — and it is the BIGGEST AND HEAVIEST crown of the cove's three trees: a broad irregular dome built from chunky billowing broadleaf-mass blobs, each blob one two-tone rounded mound and never individual leaves. The blobs pack tight and overlap, so the whole surface reads as a rolling quilt of clustered leaf-mass. THE GREEN IS BRIGHT NEW ENGLAND SUMMER AND IT IS HIGH IN CHROMA. Build the entire tree from this set, sampled from Lighthouse Cove's own art: a vivid lit green near #789C00 on the tops that catch the sun, a strong mid green near #547800, a full-bodied green near #24540C, and a deep COOL shade near #0C3C18 that leans toward blue-green. Every one of those is a confident, saturated colour. THERE IS NO OLIVE, NO KHAKI, NO MUSTARD, NO OCHRE, NO TAN, NO BRONZE, NO ARMY DRAB AND NO DUSTY, GREYED-DOWN OR MUTED GREEN ANYWHERE IN THIS TREE. A drab tree belongs in a swamp; this one grows in hard bright sea light on an open coast. Where the crown turns into shadow it goes DEEPER AND COOLER, never browner and never duller, and if any green is in doubt push it toward the BLUE side of green rather than the yellow side. SALT PRUNES THIS TREE AND THAT IS ITS SIGNATURE. It grew in the wind coming off the water, so the crown is SHEARED FLAT ACROSS THE TOP — a level table of foliage, not a dome rising to a peak — and it is LOPSIDED: fuller and heavier on the sheltered side, thinner and more ragged on the exposed side. The outline is deeply lobed, with two or three bays biting well in between the clusters, and it is never a clean circle. A FEW SMALL POCKETS OF DEEP SHADE sit down between the blob clusters, painted in the coolest darkest green of the set with a hard edge rather than a soft gradient into them. They are shadow between one leaf mass and the next, they are small, and NOTHING IS VISIBLE INSIDE THEM. SUMMER FOLIAGE, NOT AUTUMN. New England says fall colour and this is the wrong season for it: no scarlet, no orange, no yellow, no rust, no bare twigs. The tree is in full green leaf. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — a dry headland is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the tree is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the bluff it stands on
assets.note: FIRST OF THE COVE'S THREE SHORE TREES, drawn to make Lighthouse Cove read as Nantucket / Martha's Vineyard / outer Cape Cod rather than as generic green headland. The set is black oak (Quercus velutina) + pitch pine (Pinus rigida) + eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana), the actual coastal-plain association of those islands, and this is the canopy species of it. SIZE IS HONEST, NOT EXAGGERATED, worth recording because the scale block asks for exaggeration to be declared: an open-grown coastal black oak spreads about 10.5m, and 10.5m x 9.2 units/m = 96u. No fudge. That sets the family's size ladder at 96 / 72 / 42 — 1.33x and 1.71x apart, far enough that the three are told apart by size alone before any colour arrives. ROLE ambient, NOT landmark: Lighthouse Cove's identity is carried by the lighthouse, the bridges and the traffic, and a shore tree is decoration behind all of it. THE THREE ARE SEPARATED ON SILHOUETTE FIRST AND COLOUR SECOND, because art-pipeline 2 requires the distinction to survive with colour removed: this one is a BROAD CLOSED DOME with a flat sheared top, the pine is a LOOSE CLUSTER OF SEPARATE BRISTLED TUFTS with a deeply notched rim, the cedar is a SMALL TIGHT ROSETTE. REVISED 2026-08-10, TWICE OVER, AND BOTH REVISIONS CAME FROM DELIVERED ART. (1) THE PALETTE WAS THE SWAMP'S, AND THE PROMPT ASKED FOR IT. The first oak and pine came back army-drab khaki. Measured: delivered oak hue 67 deg at saturation 0.41, delivered pine hue 50 deg — a YELLOW, not a green — at saturation 0.27, against the bay venue card's own foliage at hue 95 deg (band 72-144) and saturation 0.82 (band 0.62-0.99). So the primary error is CHROMA, 2-3x too grey, with a secondary rotation toward yellow; and the cause was the wording, which said 'olive shadow', 'warm bronze', 'dull yellow-olive', 'dusty' and 'grey-green' — every one of them a Gatorgrass Bayou word, whose registered palette is literally 'olive/yellow-green everything'. The rewrite deletes all of them, names four hexes sampled off assets/images/venues/bay.png, refuses the drab family by name, and gives a tiebreaker direction (push toward blue, not yellow) because that is the axis the error ran along. A PROP SUBJECT MAY NAME ITS OWN COLOUR THIS HARD WITHOUT BREAKING art-pipeline 3c: the venue clause forbids tinting an object TOWARD the venue's hue, and this is not that — a coastal oak in July really is a bright saturated green, so this corrects a wrong local colour rather than imposing a venue one. (2) NO TRUNK, NO LIMBS, NO HUB — the whole see-through-to-the-structure apparatus was inherited from the bayou trees and does not belong here. It exists there because a swamp tree is split into a `surface` trunk and a `canopy` crown so a boat can sail between them, and the visible limb hub is what makes the split legible. These are onshore scenery with no collision and nothing passing beneath, so the structure buys nothing and costs the one thing that matters at 96px: a clean unbroken foliage silhouette. Subject now demands a closed crown, centre included, and names trunk/limb/branch/twig/bark as errors. ANCHOR STAYS trunk-base even with no trunk drawn — the stem's position is implied at the crown centre, and ingest's bbox-centre seed is the honest estimate of it once nothing marks the spot. KEYED `cove-*`, NOT `bay-*`, deliberately: paths.py leaves the bay's keys unstripped because its assets share no common prefix, so `cove-oak-black` ships to props/bay/cove-oak-black.png and the PROP_KINDS id is `bay-cove-oak-black`, matching the ferries. A `bay-oak-black` key would land at props/bay/bay-oak-black.png and need the id `bay-bay-oak-black`. Head-noun-first follows the lagoon corals, so a white oak later is `cove-oak-white`. planRound true: a crown seen from straight above is round, and it is the only acceptance test a tilted camera cannot fake. NO allowSymmetry ON ANY OF THE THREE — the mandala attractor is worst on the conifers, but an oak from overhead reaches for a perfect disc too, and the first bayou-oak delivery came back a near-perfect circle. NO punchHoles AND NO minHoles, the swamp-oak lesson applied ahead of time: the openings floor exists because a CANOPY-plane sprite draws over the fleet, where a painted gap hides a boat as well as a leaf does. These are `surface`-plane land trees, so see-through buys nothing and keying dark pixels out of the crown is pure loss. Anyone re-planing them to `canopy` has to restore both first. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6: slot, then art, then the kind.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TREE, shot straight down from well above it the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. YOU SEE FOLIAGE AND NOTHING ELSE: no trunk, no dark hub, no limb, no branch, no twig and no bark anywhere in this picture, and least of all in the middle. This tree is scenery standing on a headland; nothing passes beneath it and nothing needs to read its structure, so where the foliage parts you see SHADOW INSIDE THE CROWN and never a branch. A PITCH PINE, the tree of the Cape Cod sand plains, and it is the RAGGED one: not a smooth dome but a LOOSE CLUSTER OF SEPARATE NEEDLE TUFTS, packed close and overlapping toward the middle and breaking apart into individual tufts around the rim. Each tuft is ONE chunky rounded pom of clustered needle-mass in two flat tones with a BRISTLED, SPIKY RIM — the needles are stiff and stand in threes, so the edge of every tuft is a hard ragged fringe rather than a soft one, and never drawn needle by needle. Fifteen to twenty-five tufts in the whole crown at plainly UNEVEN sizes, some big, some small, no two alike. THE TUFTS CLUMP; THEY DO NOT RING, and this is the single most important thing about the drawing. Do NOT put one tuft in the middle and arrange the rest around it: this crown has no centre, no ring and no spokes. Build it instead from TWO OR THREE CLUMPS of three to six tufts each, packed so tightly inside a clump that they merge into one larger lumpy mass, with the clumps at plainly different sizes. Between the clumps sits deep hard-edged shadow inside the crown, never a branch. COUNT NOTHING AND REPEAT NOTHING: walk around the edge of this crown, and if the same tuft spacing comes back four, five or six times on the way round, it has been drawn as a FLOWER and it is wrong however good it looks. No petals, no ring of blooms, no star, no wheel. Even is the one thing a real pitch pine never is. AND YET IT IS STILL ONE COMPACT TREE, which is the other half of the same rule and the easier half to lose. THE CROWN IS A SINGLE CONNECTED MASS: every tuft touches or overlaps a neighbour, and NOT ONE of them floats off on its own with clear space all the way round it. It is also COMPACT AND ROUGHLY ROUND TAKEN AS A WHOLE — draw the smallest circle that contains the tree, and the foliage should fill about seven-tenths of it, so the crown reads as one full round head with a ragged edge. Do NOT let the clumps drift apart into an L, a crescent, a diagonal streak, or two bushes with a gap between them, and do NOT leave a whole quadrant of that circle empty. THE UNEVENNESS BELONGS TO THE RIM AND TO THE SIZE OF THE TUFTS, NEVER TO THE OVERALL SHAPE: the outline is lumpy and bitten into, single tufts stand proud of it, and two or three notches cut in from the edge with one of them deeper than the rest where the wind took a limb — but it is still the outline of one round crown. A CONIFER GREEN — COOL, DEEP AND FULLY SATURATED, DARKER AND BLUER THAN A BROADLEAF AND NEVER YELLOWER. Build the whole tree from this set, weighted toward its dark end: a bright lit needle tone near #4C8A18 on the tops that catch the sun, a full-bodied green near #24540C through the mass, and a deep COOL shade near #0C3C18 in the shadow between tufts, with the deepest pockets darker still. NO NEEDLE IN THIS TREE IS MUSTARD, KHAKI, OLIVE DRAB, OCHRE, TAN, DUSTY OR GREYED-DOWN YELLOW-GREEN. A pine the colour of dry grass or army canvas is wrong: this is a rich, cool, saturated evergreen in bright coastal sun, and if any green is in doubt push it toward the BLUE side of green rather than the yellow side. SMALL CONES nestle in among the tufts, two or three at a time, short and egg-shaped and prickly in a warm mid brown, half-buried in the needle-mass rather than sitting on anything — sparse enough to read as an accent, and the ONLY warm thing in the picture: the cones may be brown, and nothing else may be. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — a dry sand plain is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the tree is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the bank it stands on
assets.note: The cove's signature tree — if one species has to say Cape Cod, this is it — and the middle of the three on every axis. SIZE IS HONEST: a wind-shaped coastal pitch pine spreads about 7.8m, and 7.8m x 9.2 units/m = 72u. See cove-oak-black for the family's shared reasoning: size ladder, ambient role, `cove-*` key derivation, planRound, anchor, and why punchHoles/minHoles are deliberately absent on all three. THIS ONE TOOK THE WORST OF THE 2026-08-10 COLOUR FAILURE and it is the reason the clause is written as hard as it is. The delivery measured hue 50 deg at saturation 0.27 — that is not a desaturated green, it is a YELLOW, sitting a full 45 deg off the bay card's foliage median of 95 deg and at a third of its chroma. It read as dry grass. The subject had asked for a 'dull yellow-olive' top over a 'deep grey-green' shade, which is a fair description of a Gatorgrass Bayou pine and the wrong tree entirely for a coast whose card is built on saturated grass-green. Fixed by naming hexes, weighting the set dark rather than yellow, refusing the drab family by name, and stating the tiebreaker direction. THE SPECIES REWRITE MATTERS AS MUCH AS THE COLOUR ONE. The old subject built this pine's whole identity on OPENNESS — 'the limb structure shows straight through it all the way in to the hub', tufts only at branch ends, cones sitting on bare limbs. That identity is unavailable now that these are trunkless onshore scenery, so it moves to where it can still live at 72px: the tuft CLUSTER as the unit, hard shadow rather than branch in the gaps, and a deeply notched asymmetric OUTLINE with a sector cut away. That is a better home for it anyway — silhouette survives reduction and interior branchwork does not, and art-pipeline 2's colour-removed test is a test of exactly this. THIS IS ALSO THE ONE THE ARRANGEMENT NEGATIVES ARE REALLY FOR: ask any generator for a conifer from directly overhead and it returns a snowflake. No allowSymmetry, so the mandala/rosette/snowflake negatives all apply, and the subject spends its longest clause refusing evenness. WHAT TO CHECK FIRST ON DELIVERY, in order: saturation (sample the lit tufts — under 0.55 is a reject), then hue (over 80 deg or it is drifting yellow again), then that no branch is visible, then the rosette test below. ROUND 2, 2026-08-10: COLOUR FIXED, ROSETTE NOT. The second delivery cleared colour outright — hue 117 deg at saturation 0.73, up from 50 deg / 0.27, comfortably inside the card band — and cleared orthography at aspect 1.007, and carried no stem: its nine brown blobs all measure elongation under 1.3, so they are cones. It failed on ARRANGEMENT. It came back a five-petal flower. THE TEST THAT CAUGHT IT, AND IT IS WORTH REUSING ON ANY RADIAL SUBJECT: resample the crown into polar coordinates, take mean brightness as a function of angle, and read the power spectrum of that profile. Ignore n=1 — that is lopsidedness from directional lighting, which every one of these correctly has, and treating it as repetition marks all three as mandalas and is simply wrong. Only n>=2 counts. This delivery put 71% of its n>=2 angular power into a single 5-fold harmonic, against 33% (4-fold) on the oak and 17% (8-fold) on the cedar — four times more repetitive than its neighbours, and visible once measured as a ring of tufts around a hub. THE LESSON IS THAT PROHIBITION DID NOT WORK. ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE already carried `rosette`, `ring formation`, `evenly spaced` and `compass rose`, and the subject already said in capitals that the tree is not a star, a wheel or a rosette. All of it was applied and none of it bit, because 'do not arrange evenly' does not tell a generator what to do INSTEAD, and radial-from-a-hub is its default answer for any crown. So the clause was rewritten from a prohibition into a CONSTRUCTION — two or three off-centre clumps of merged tufts, one part of the frame crowded and another bare, no centre and no ring — and the failure is now named in the terms the metric measures ('if the same spacing comes back five times on the way round it is a flower'). Same pattern that fixed the bayou moss: state the geometry, give the correct answer, name the failure. ROUND 3, 2026-08-10: THE ROSETTE FIX WORKED AND OVERSHOT, WHICH IS ITS OWN LESSON. The 5-fold harmonic fell from 71% to 27% — better than the accepted oak's 33% — so the clump-not-ring construction did exactly what it was written to do. The delivery still failed, on a defect the previous two rounds had never shown: it came back as an L-shaped sprawl in THREE disconnected pieces, two tufts floating free with clear space around them, filling 59% of its own bounding box against 71% for both accepted trees. THE PROMPT CAUSED IT, and the guilty words are identifiable: 'shoved OFF-CENTRE so they crowd toward one part of the frame and leave another part nearly bare' and 'AT LEAST ONE WHOLE SECTOR IS CUT AWAY'. Read literally — which is how they are read — those instruct a crown that occupies part of its frame and leaves the rest empty. Both are now gone: the sector becomes two or three rim notches with one deeper, and the frame-crowding clause is replaced by its opposite. THE REAL LESSON IS ABOUT WHAT A REWRITE DELETES. Rounds 1 and 2 got 'one compact connected crown' for free, because a rosette and a dome are both compact — so the constraint was never stated, and the moment the arrangement language changed there was nothing holding it. When a clause is rewritten to kill a defect, check what the OLD wording had been quietly guaranteeing. Two invariants are now stated outright and both are measurable on delivery: single connected mass (no floating tuft), and roughly seven-tenths fill of the smallest enclosing circle. ADD THOSE TO THE DELIVERY CHECKLIST, after saturation and hue and before the rosette test — they are cheaper to measure and this round proves they are not implied. ACCEPTED ROUND 4, 2026-08-10, clearing all four gates at once and hitting the two new invariants almost exactly: aspect 1.072 against the 1.12 orthography gate; saturation 0.72 and hue 143 deg inside the card band; ONE connected piece filling 70% of its smallest enclosing circle against the ~70% the subject asks for; and the 5-fold rosette down to 23.6% of n>=2 angular power, below the shipped oak's 33%. FOUR ROUNDS, AND EACH FAILED ON A DIFFERENT AXIS — colour, then arrangement, then compactness, the last of them caused by the fix for the one before it. The subject now carries a clause against all three, which is why it is the longest in the family and why none of them should be trimmed as redundant: every one is load-bearing against a defect that actually shipped. Registered as `bay-cove-pine-pitch`, world 72, surface, contact none.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TREE, shot straight down from well above it the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. YOU SEE FOLIAGE AND NOTHING ELSE: no trunk, no stem, no limb, no branch, no twig and no bark anywhere in this picture, and least of all in the middle. AN EASTERN RED CEDAR — the juniper standing in every old sheep field and stone-walled pasture on Nantucket and the Vineyard — AND IT IS A NARROW SPIRE, which is the whole difficulty of this picture. Every picture of this tree ever taken is a tall thin column seen from the side, and FROM DIRECTLY ABOVE IT IS NOT TALL AT ALL: all of that height goes straight into the camera and disappears, and a spire seen from overhead is a SMALL, TIGHT, DENSE ROUND TUFT. Draw the tuft, not the spire. It is by far the SMALLEST and TIGHTEST crown of the cove's three trees — a compact closed rosette where the black oak is a broad dome and the pitch pine is a ragged cluster of bristled poms. WHAT YOU SEE IS THE VIEW LOOKING STRAIGHT DOWN A CONE. The centre is the TIP of the tree, its leading shoot: the nearest point to the camera and the brightest, a small pale crest of FOLIAGE at the middle — foliage, never a stem and never a hub. From there the foliage steps DOWN and OUTWARD, so the crown reads as a bright small core inside a distinctly darker outer skirt — TWO FLAT STEPS OF VALUE with a clean hard edge between them, never a soft radial blend and never a glow. One or two SECOND LEADERS stand beside the main one, each its own small pale crest, so the centre is a little lumpy and off-balance rather than one perfect point. THE FOLIAGE IS SCALE-LIKE, NOT NEEDLED: short flattened SPRAYS, each a small tapering fan of tight overlapping scale-leaves, drawn as chunky two-tone fronds and never leaf by leaf. They lie close and overlap heavily, so the crown is CLOSED — no gap anywhere in it, and nothing but foliage from the rim right through to the centre. THE COOLEST, BLUEST GREEN OF THE THREE, AND STILL FULLY SATURATED. A sea-green evergreen: a lit tone near #2E9E38 on the crest, a body green near #24540C pushed toward blue, and a deep shade near #0C3C18 in the outer skirt, with the outermost sprays a shade cooler again. IT IS COOL BECAUSE IT LEANS TOWARD BLUE, NEVER BECAUSE IT IS GREYED DOWN — no sage, no dust, no khaki, no olive, no washed-out or muted pastel green anywhere in it, and nothing bronze or purple. Set beside the pitch pine it must read plainly BLUER; set beside the black oak, bluer and darker. A SCATTER OF PALE BERRIES — small round juniper cones in a frosted powder blue, almost white-blue — clustered a few at a time on the outer sprays. Sparse: a dozen or so visible, an accent and not a covering, and the palest coolest note in the crown. THE OUTLINE IS LUMPY, NOT STRUCK WITH A COMPASS: a rough circle broken by the individual sprays, with small notches and bumps all round it where one frond reaches past its neighbours and another falls short. The sprays are unevenly spaced and unevenly long everywhere. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — a dry field is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the tree is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the ground it stands on
assets.note: The understory scale of the cove's three trees, and the one that does the most for the New England read per pixel — a red cedar in a field is the Nantucket/Vineyard postcard. SIZE IS HONEST: an open-grown coastal Juniperus virginiana spreads about 4.6m, and 4.6m x 9.2 units/m = 42u. Small — a shade under lagoon-palm-young at 38, which is the shipped precedent that a 40-ish px plant reads — and it is the correct number rather than a compromise, because the whole point of this species is that it is narrow. See cove-oak-black for the family's shared reasoning on role, key derivation, planRound, anchor and the absent punchHoles/minHoles. NOT YET GENERATED WHEN THE OTHER TWO CAME BACK DRAB, and it was heading the same way: the first wording asked for 'a cold grey-green', 'the greyest' and 'a dusty bronze-purple cast', which is the same instruction that produced hue 50 deg at saturation 0.27 on the pine. The species truth is real — a juniper IS glaucous — but GREY IS THE WORD THAT BUYS DRAB, and the bay card holds no foliage below saturation 0.62. The rewrite gets the same read by moving along the HUE axis instead of the chroma axis: cool because it leans blue, at full chroma, with the glaucous note carried entirely by the frosted berries. That is a general lesson for this library and not just for this asset — when a subject wants 'muted', say which direction it is muted TOWARD, or a generator will simply desaturate. THE SUBJECT'S LONGEST CLAUSE IS ABOUT A CAMERA, NOT A TREE, and that is the specific risk here: a columnar species is the hardest case for the nadir view, because a spire's identity IS its height and the plan view deletes exactly that. Every reference image is side-on, so the generator has almost nothing to sample and will hand back a Christmas tree in three-quarter view. The clause names the geometry, names the correct answer and names the failure — the pattern that worked on the bayou moss. WATCH THE SIZE ON DELIVERY, not just the aspect: the second failure mode is a correct plan view of the WRONG TREE, a wide spreading juniper instead of a narrow one, and ingest cannot catch it because fillTo normalises content to the frame and a too-broad crown looks fine at 1024. Judge it on the contact sheet beside the oak and the pine, where 42u against 96u is the thing being checked. THE LIT-CORE/DARK-SKIRT STEP IS THE ONE PLACE A RADIAL VALUE CHANGE IS CORRECT IN THIS LIBRARY — you really are looking down a cone — so it is specified as two hard steps to stay inside the base style's no-gradients rule rather than being softened into the glow the phrasing would otherwise invite. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE SHRUB, shot straight down from well above it the way a survey frames a single plant. YOU SEE FOLIAGE AND NOTHING ELSE: no trunk, no stem, no limb, no branch, no twig and no bark anywhere in this picture, and least of all in the middle. This plant is scenery standing on a headland; nothing passes beneath it and nothing needs to read its structure, so it is drawn as ONE CONTINUOUS MASS OF LEAF seen from above, and where the mass parts you see hard-edged SHADOW INSIDE THE PLANT and never a branch. A SCRUB OAK — the bear oak that covers the sand plains of Cape Cod and the islands — AND IT IS A SHRUB, NOT A SMALL TREE. It is wind-pressed and ground-hugging: a LOW WIDE CUSHION of leaf sprawling out from the middle in three or four broad LOBES with shallow bays between them, the widest and least tidy of the cove's four shrubs. The rim is bitten and irregular the whole way round — clumps of leaf standing proud of it, short notches cut in between — and it is never a clean circle. AND YET IT IS ONE COMPACT CONNECTED CUSHION, which is the other half of that rule and the easier half to lose. Every clump touches or overlaps a neighbour and NOT ONE of them floats off on its own with clear space all the way round it. Draw the smallest circle that contains the plant and the foliage fills about seven-tenths of it. Do not let the lobes drift apart into a Y, a crescent, a diagonal streak or two separate bushes with a gap between them, and do not leave a whole quadrant of that circle empty. THE LEAF IS SMALL, STIFF AND LEATHERY, and the grain of the surface is what tells this apart from the black oak standing over it: build the whole plant from MANY SMALL CHUNKY LEAF CLUSTERS rather than from the big billowing blobs of a grown oak — each cluster a rounded two-tone patch of a few leaves together, never a single leaf drawn on its own. The surface reads as a coarse pebbled quilt. NO CENTRE AND NO RING. Do not put one clump in the middle and arrange the rest around it, and do not space the lobes evenly: walk round the rim, and if the same spacing comes back four, five or six times on the way round it has been drawn as a FLOWER and it is wrong however good it looks. No petals, no wheel, no star, no rosette. Build it instead from two or three merged clumps at plainly different sizes, one heavier than the rest. THE GREEN IS BRIGHT NEW ENGLAND SUMMER AND IT IS HIGH IN CHROMA. Build the plant from this set, sampled from Lighthouse Cove's own art: a vivid lit green near #789C00 on the tops that catch the sun, a strong mid green near #547800, a full-bodied green near #24540C, and a deep COOL shade near #0C3C18 that leans toward blue-green. A FEW LEAVES ARE TURNED OVER by the wind and show their paler undersides — a sparse scatter of small flat patches in a light green near #A6C82E, pale but still a confident saturated green, and the only light note in the plant. THERE IS NO OLIVE, NO KHAKI, NO MUSTARD, NO OCHRE, NO TAN, NO BRONZE, NO ARMY DRAB AND NO DUSTY, GREYED-DOWN OR MUTED GREEN ANYWHERE IN THIS PLANT. A drab shrub belongs in a swamp; this one grows in hard bright sea light on an open coast. Where it turns into shadow it goes DEEPER AND COOLER, never browner and never duller, and if any green is in doubt push it toward the BLUE side of green rather than the yellow side. SUMMER FOLIAGE, NOT AUTUMN. Scrub oak is famous for turning rust and scarlet, and this is the wrong season for it: no red, no orange, no yellow, no rust, no bare twigs, no fallen leaves. The plant is in full green leaf. NO ACORNS and no flowers — nothing on this plant is small enough to see from here. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — dry sand and thin turf is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the plant is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the bluff it stands on
assets.note: FIRST OF LIGHTHOUSE COVE'S FOUR SHORE SHRUBS — the understory layer beneath the three trees — and this note carries the family's shared reasoning the way cove-oak-black carries the trees'. THE SET IS scrub oak (Quercus ilicifolia) + northern bayberry (Morella pensylvanica) + beach plum (Prunus maritima) + bigleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla): the first three are the real sandplain shrub association of Nantucket, the Vineyard and the outer Cape, and the fourth is the islands' cultivated signature. SIZE IS HONEST, NOT EXAGGERATED, worth recording because the scale block asks for exaggeration to be declared: an open-grown wind-pressed bear oak spreads about 3.9m, and 3.9m x 9.2 units/m = 36u. The band is 36 / 28 / 22 / 18 and it sits deliberately BELOW the tree band, whose smallest member is the red cedar at 42 — a shrub layer that overlapped the trees would make the whole headland one undifferentiated size. ⚠️ SIZE IS NOT THE SEPARATOR IN THIS BAND, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN DECISION WORTH RECORDING. The trees are 96 / 72 / 42, 1.33x and 1.71x apart, and cove-oak-black is right that this lets them be told apart by size before any colour arrives. Four shrubs cannot have that: honest spreads for these four species all fall between 1.8m and 4.0m, so any four points in that range land 1.2-1.3x apart and no ladder fixes it. So the shrub band separates on RIM TEXTURE first and COLOUR second, and every subject is written around its own: this one is the widest and most deeply bitten outline over a coarse pebbled surface, the bayberry is the smoothest and darkest closed cushion, the beach plum is the loosest and bluest with purple fruit, and the hydrangea has a rim scalloped by big single leaves. All four still pass art-pipeline 2's colour-removed test on rim texture alone. THE FEATURE FLOOR IS THE OTHER THING THIS BAND HAS TO LIVE WITH, and it is arithmetic rather than taste. prompt.py's own floor is 4 screen px, and at world 36 / 28 / 22 / 18 against a 1024 master that is 11-22% of the plant's own width — which lands at ABOUT 0.43m on every one of the four. NOTHING UNDER ROUGHLY HALF A METRE RESOLVES ANYWHERE IN THIS BAND: an acorn (1.5cm), a bayberry berry (0.5cm) and a beach plum (2cm) are all invisible at race scale, and drawing them big enough to count individually would put half-metre acorns on a four-metre bush. So the acorns are simply deleted here, and on the bayberry and the plum the fruit is specified as DENSE CLUSTERS that merge into one patch of colour rather than as countable objects — a patch survives reduction where a berry does not. The hydrangea is the instructive exception: its flower heads are individually below the floor too, but they cover a third to a half of the crown, so they read as MASS. That is also why the hydrangea can be the smallest of the four and still the most legible — colour survives reduction better than shape does. COLOUR IS THE TREES' PALETTE, ON PURPOSE. Every green in the band is one of the four hexes cove-oak-black had measured off assets/images/venues/bay.png (#789C00 / #547800 / #24540C / #0C3C18) plus the pine's and cedar's lit tones; this is one plant community in one afternoon's light, and a shrub carrying its own green would read as a different afternoon. What varies between the four is WEIGHTING — the bayberry sits at the dark end, the plum leans blue, and this one takes the black oak's set unchanged because it is an oak. EVERY SUBJECT IN THIS BAND CARRIES THE DRAB REFUSAL VERBATIM, because it cost four rounds on the pitch pine and the failure is one wrong adjective away at all times: a low coastal shrub is exactly the subject a generator wants to render in sage, dusty grey-green or army drab. See cove-pine-pitch for the measurements. THIS ONE'S OWN RISKS, in the order to check them on delivery: (1) it comes back as a SMALL TREE with a trunk and a lollipop crown, because the word oak does that — the subject spends its second clause insisting it is a low wide cushion; (2) AUTUMN COLOUR, since bear oak is photographed in October far more than in July and rust-red foliage is a straight reject; (3) the drab palette; (4) the pine's compactness failure, since a lobed sprawling outline is very close to the wording that produced an L-shaped three-piece delivery there. Both invariants the pine ended with are stated outright in the subject and both are measurable: ONE connected mass with no floating clump, and about seven-tenths fill of the smallest enclosing circle. SHARED WITH THE TREES AND NOT REPEATED IN THE OTHER THREE NOTES: role ambient, because the cove's identity is the lighthouse, the bridges and the traffic and a shrub is decoration behind all of it; `cove-*` keys rather than `bay-*`, because paths.py leaves the bay's keys unstripped, so this ships to props/bay/cove-oak-scrub.png and the PROP_KINDS id is `bay-cove-oak-scrub`; head-noun-first naming after the lagoon corals and the cove's own trees, which is why it is cove-oak-scrub beside cove-oak-black and cove-plum-beach; plane `surface` on all four and never `canopy`, since nothing sails under a headland; planRound true, the only acceptance test a tilted camera cannot fake; NO allowSymmetry on any of the four, since the mandala attractor is worst on a round cushion seen from straight above; and NO punchHoles and NO minHoles, because the openings floor exists for canopy-plane sprites that draw over the fleet, and keying dark pixels out of a land shrub is pure loss. A THICKET IS PLACED, NOT DRAWN: real bear oak grows in continuous stands, but art-pipeline 3b puts repeated copies of one object in compose.py rather than in a generation, and for a shrub the cheaper answer again is to place four or five of these close together in the venue's prop list. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6: slot, then art, then the kind. ACCEPTED FIRST ROUND, 2026-08-10, clearing all four gates and the only member of the band to do so: aspect 1.021 against the 1.12 orthography gate; lit foliage at hue 73.2 deg and saturation 0.965, inside the card band on both axes and the highest chroma in the band; ONE connected mass filling 0.768 of its smallest enclosing circle against the ~0.70 the subject asks for; and 32.0% of n>=2 angular power in a 3-fold harmonic, just under the shipped black oak's 33%. Delivered 2048px square, downsampled to the 1024 master, visible at 31x30px. Registered as `bay-cove-oak-scrub`, world 36, surface, contact none. ⚠️ THE FILL INVARIANT IS NOT UNIVERSAL, AND THIS BAND IS WHERE THAT BECAME CLEAR — the same mistake ORTHO_ROUND's comment in prompt.py records about asserting the roundness test on everything. The ~0.70 figure comes from cove-pine-pitch, whose crown is RAGGED, and it binds on the ragged members here (this one at 0.768, the beach plum at 0.536 and correctly failing). It does NOT bind on the members whose own subjects ask for a closed cushion: the bayberry landed at 0.946 and the two hydrangeas at 0.852 and 0.864, and all three are right. Applied blanket-wise the gate would have marked three good deliveries as failures. Read the fill target off the SUBJECT's own shape clause, not off the band. ONE PIPELINE NOTE FOR THE NEXT BATCH: three of the five arrived in LANDSCAPE frames (2816x1536 and 1408x768) and ingest.py hard-fails a non-square master, so they were padded to square and re-centred on the content bbox before ingest — padding only, no resample, and fillTo re-crops to content anyway so nothing was lost. Worth asking the generator for a square frame up front.

A NORTHERN BAYBERRY — the dense aromatic shrub that fills the back of every dune and every hollow on Cape Cod and the islands — AND IT IS THE TIGHTEST, DENSEST, SMOOTHEST PLANT ON THIS HEADLAND. Where the scrub oak sprawls in lobes and the pitch pine breaks into tufts, this one is a single CLOSED ROUNDED CUSHION packed so tight that no gap shows anywhere in it: one full, heavy, evenly filled mound of leaf from the rim right through to the middle. Its outline is nearly round and only FINELY scalloped — small shallow bumps and dents where one leaf cluster stands a little past its neighbours, and nothing deeper than that. This is the plant whose silhouette is QUIET, and that quietness is what identifies it. NO CENTRE, NO HUB AND NO RADIAL STRUCTURE, and this is the one place the drawing could go wrong: nothing points outward from the middle, no spray fans out, and no leaf cluster is arranged around anything. The surface is the SAME all over — the middle of the plant looks exactly like its edge, neither lighter nor busier. It is not a rosette, not a flower, not a wheel and not a compass rose. The eastern red cedar on this same shore IS a rosette, with a bright pale core and sprays radiating out of it, and these two must never be mistaken for each other at a distance. THE LEAF IS NARROW, LEATHERY AND GLOSSY, carried in tight whorls, so the surface is a fine even pebbling of small two-tone leaf clusters — the FINEST grain of the cove's shrubs, finer than the scrub oak's and far finer than the hydrangea's coarse blades. Never draw a single leaf on its own. A HANDFUL OF SHALLOW HARD-EDGED SHADOW POCKETS sit down between clusters, small and dark, with NOTHING VISIBLE INSIDE THEM. IT IS THE DARKEST GREEN ON THIS SHORE AND IT IS STILL FULLY SATURATED. Build the plant from this set, weighted hard toward its dark end: a lit green near #4C8A18 only where the sun strikes the top of the mound, a full-bodied green near #24540C through most of the mass, and a deep COOL shade near #0C3C18 in the hollows, with the deepest pockets darker still. It reads DARK because it is deep and cool, NEVER because it is greyed down. THERE IS NO OLIVE, NO KHAKI, NO MUSTARD, NO OCHRE, NO TAN, NO BRONZE, NO ARMY DRAB AND NO DUSTY, GREYED-DOWN OR MUTED GREEN ANYWHERE IN THIS PLANT. A drab shrub belongs in a swamp; this one grows in hard bright sea light on an open coast. Where it turns into shadow it goes DEEPER AND COOLER, never browner and never duller, and if any green is in doubt push it toward the BLUE side of green rather than the yellow side. THE BERRIES ARE THE ONE PALE THING IN THE PICTURE. Tight knots of small waxy grey-blue berries — the bayberry wax that gets made into candles — sit low among the leaves in DENSE CLUSTERS and never scattered singly: three or four clusters visible in the whole plant, each one a small solid patch of frosted pale blue-white near #BFD3CE. They are the ONLY low-chroma colour in this picture and the foliage borrows NOTHING from them — the leaves do not go grey, dusty, pale or washed-out to match. Keep the clusters inside the crown, with green all round the rim. NO FLOWERS, no red, no orange, no autumn colour and no bare twigs. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — dry sand behind a dune is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the plant is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the ground it stands on
assets.note: The dune-back filler of the cove's four shrubs and the one a designer will place most of — bayberry is what actually covers the ground between the pines on those islands, so it is the band's workhorse rather than its set piece. SIZE IS HONEST: a mature open-grown Morella pensylvanica spreads about 3.0m, and 3.0m x 9.2 units/m = 28u. See cove-oak-scrub for the family's shared reasoning: the band's placement below the trees, why size is not the separator here, the half-metre feature floor, the shared palette and the drab refusal, key derivation, plane, planRound, and why punchHoles/minHoles are deliberately absent on all four. ITS JOB IN THE SET IS TO BE THE QUIET ONE, and that is harder to ask for than it sounds. Three of the four shrubs are defined by something happening — at the rim, in the fruit, in the flower — and this one is defined by NOTHING happening: the smoothest outline and the most evenly filled surface on the headland. That is a real read at 28px, and it is exactly what a generator will not volunteer, because it reaches for interest. The subject therefore spends its shape clause asking for a closed even cushion and naming the alternatives it refuses. ⚠️ THE CONFUSION TO WATCH FOR IS WITH THE RED CEDAR, and it is a size-plus-shape collision rather than a colour one: 28u against the cedar's 42u is only 1.5x, both are dark, both are compact, and both are round in plan. What separates them is STRUCTURE. The cedar is an explicit ROSETTE with a bright pale core and sprays stepping down and outward from it, because you are looking straight down a cone at its leading shoot; the bayberry has no centre at all and nothing radial anywhere. The subject says so in capitals and names the cedar's read as the failure. Judge it on the contact sheet with the two side by side, and if a delivery comes back with a pale middle it has drawn the wrong plant. THE BERRIES ARE THE ONE PLACE THIS FAMILY LETS A LOW-CHROMA COLOUR IN, and it is the cedar's precedent applied exactly: the glaucous note is carried entirely by the fruit while the foliage stays fully saturated. #BFD3CE is a genuinely desaturated pale blue-white and that is correct for bayberry wax — but it is stated as the ONLY low-chroma thing in the picture, with the foliage explicitly forbidden from borrowing it, because a subject that names a grey anywhere is how the pitch pine ended up at saturation 0.27. WHAT TO CHECK ON DELIVERY, in order: saturation of the lit foliage (under 0.55 is a reject), then that the middle of the plant is not lighter than its edge (that is a cedar, not a bayberry), then the single connected mass and the seven-tenths fill of the smallest enclosing circle, then the rosette power-spectrum test cove-pine-pitch describes — a smooth even cushion is the strongest mandala attractor in the band, and it is the one asset here whose correct answer looks most like the wrong one. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ACCEPTED FIRST ROUND WITH ONE DEFECT RECORDED, 2026-08-10. Cleared orthography at aspect 1.011, colour at hue 90.3 deg / saturation 0.789 (comfortably inside the card band, and the berries did NOT drag the foliage down, which was the specific risk), and compactness as ONE connected mass. Its fill of the smallest enclosing circle is 0.946 — near a solid disc, and CORRECT here rather than a failure, because this subject is the one in the band that asks for a closed evenly filled cushion; see cove-oak-scrub for why the ~0.70 figure does not transfer. The quietness read exactly as intended on the contact sheet: a clean solid dark-green disc at 28px and 56px, unmistakable against the cedar. ⚠️ IT FAILED THE ROSETTE TEST, AT 45.0% OF n>=2 ANGULAR POWER IN A 4-FOLD HARMONIC — worse than every shipped asset in the venue (oak 33%, pine 23.6%, cedar 17%). The cause is visible once measured and invisible before: the four pale berry clusters came back at even 90-degree spacing round the crown. THE PROMPT CAUSED IT BY OMISSION, which is the cove-pine-pitch round-3 lesson arriving in a new place. The berry clause specified count (three or four), density (dense clusters, not scattered), colour and that they sit inside the rim — and said NOTHING about where they go, because the foliage clause above it had already refused radial structure and that felt like enough. It was not: the refusal was scoped to the LEAF and the berries are a separate object, so nothing was holding them. When a clause forbids an arrangement, check every other element the picture contains. THE FIX FOR A REROLL, written as a construction rather than a prohibition per the pine: two clusters close together on one side, one alone across from them, none in the middle, at plainly different sizes. It ships as-is because the defect only resolves at 4x — at the 28px it actually occupies the berries are sub-pixel and the disc reads clean — but it is the first thing to fix if this is ever regenerated. Delivered 1408x768, padded to 854px square; that is under the 1024 target and irrelevant at a 112px bake. Registered as `bay-cove-bayberry-northern`, world 28, surface, contact none.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE SHRUB, shot straight down from well above it the way a survey frames a single plant. A BEACH PLUM IN LATE SUMMER, HEAVY WITH FRUIT — the low wild plum that grows in the sand behind every outer-Cape beach. IT IS NOT IN FLOWER. Every photograph of this shrub is taken in May when it is buried under white blossom, and that is the wrong month: there is NO white blossom, NO white petal, NO pink bud and no flower of any kind in this picture. This plant is in leaf and in fruit. IT IS THE LOOSEST AND MOST IRREGULAR of the cove's shrubs, and it is still ONE PLANT: a low straggling spread of leaf, heavier on one side than the other, built from five or six leaf clumps at plainly different sizes pushed up against each other into a single lumpy CONNECTED mass. The outline is deeply irregular — long shallow bays and blunt promontories, one side reaching further than the other. Build it from a lit green near #2E9E38 on the tops that catch the sun, a body green near #24540C pushed toward blue, and a deep shade near #0C3C18 in the hollows. Set beside the scrub oak it must read plainly BLUER and a little darker. NO SAGE, NO DUST, NO KHAKI, NO OLIVE, NO ARMY DRAB, no washed-out or muted pastel green, and nothing brown or bronze in the leaf. THE FRUIT IS THE WHOLE POINT AND IT IS THE ONLY COLOUR HERE THAT IS NOT GREEN. Small round plums in a deep dusky PURPLE near #4E2F73, each carrying a pale waxy bloom on the face turned to the sun in a soft lilac near #7E6EA8. THEY HANG IN DENSE BUNCHES, NOT SCATTERED SINGLY: four or five tight clusters of six to ten plums pressed shoulder to shoulder, so each cluster reads as ONE SOLID PATCH of purple rather than as separate berries. Place the clusters unevenly — two on one side, one on the other, none in the middle — and keep them inside the crown with green all round the rim. Purple appears NOWHERE else: no purple leaf, no purple shadow, no purple cast over the foliage. SUMMER FRUIT, NOT AUTUMN FOLIAGE: no red leaf, no orange, no yellow, no rust, no bare twig and no fallen leaf. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection.
