assets.note: The wild fruiting shrub of the set, and the one that dates the picture: everything on this headland is drawn in the same late-summer afternoon, and a beach plum in fruit is what says so out loud. SIZE IS HONEST: an open dune specimen of Prunus maritima spreads about 2.4m, and 2.4m x 9.2 units/m = 22u. See cove-oak-scrub for the family's shared reasoning. ⚠️ THE BIGGEST RISK IS THE WRONG MONTH, and it is a reference-data problem rather than a wording one. Beach plum is photographed almost exclusively in May, when it is a solid mass of white blossom against bare sand — that is the postcard, that is what the name retrieves, and a generator will hand it back unless told not to. So the subject refuses white blossom, petals and buds by name in its second sentence, before it says anything else about the plant. Same failure family as the red cedar's Christmas tree and the pitch pine's snowflake: when the reference distribution is against the asset, the failure gets NAMED rather than left unmentioned. THE FRUIT IS AN EXAGGERATION THAT IS DECLARED RATHER THAN HIDDEN, per the manifest's scale block — except that it turns out not to need one. A real beach plum is about 2cm, which is 0.2px at world 22 and invisible; drawing one big enough to count individually would need roughly 0.44m of fruit, a twenty-fold exaggeration and visibly absurd on a 2.4m bush. So the plums stay near true size and the subject asks instead for DENSE BUNCHES of six to ten pressed together, which is also what the plant really does. The cluster is about 15cm across and still under the floor, but four solid clusters of purple against green read as a purple-flecked bush at race scale, which is the correct impression of the thing. THE RULE GENERALISES TO THE WHOLE BAND AND PROBABLY BEYOND IT: cluster what is too small to see, never enlarge it. PURPLE IN A GREEN-AND-BLUE VENUE IS DELIBERATE AND IS COVERED BY art-pipeline 3c: the fruit colour carries information about what the plant is, so it wins over the venue's dominant hue exactly as a species' true plumage does. It is the only non-green in the picture, and the subject forbids it from spreading into leaf or shadow, because a purple CAST over the foliage is the same defect as an olive one. WHAT TO CHECK ON DELIVERY, in order: no white blossom anywhere; then foliage saturation and blue lean, since it must read plainly bluer than the scrub oak beside it on the contact sheet; then that the purple is confined to the fruit clusters; then the single connected mass and the seven-tenths fill — this is the loosest-outlined shrub in the band and therefore the one most likely to repeat cove-pine-pitch's round-3 sprawl into disconnected pieces. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ⛔ ROUND 1 FAILED THREE GATES, 2026-08-10, AND HAS BEEN REPLACED — see the round-2 record at the end. The round-1 diagnosis stays because the prompt defects it names are still sitting in the subject. (1) ORTHOGRAPHY: aspect 1.577 against the 1.12 gate, which is a camera ~51 degrees off vertical — by far the worst in the band, where the other four came back 1.010-1.021. On screen that means it draws 19x12px at world 22 instead of 19x19. (2) COLOUR: lit foliage at saturation 0.543, BELOW the 0.55 reject line and the only member under it; hue 126.4 deg is fine, so this is the pine's chroma failure again rather than a hue rotation. (3) COMPACTNESS: fill 0.536 against the ~0.70 the subject asks for. The connected-mass check passes at one component, but only because a dark under-layer bridges what is plainly a WIDE ROW OF SIX SEPARATE BUSHES. THE PROMPT CAUSED THE SHAPE, AND THE GUILTY WORDS ARE IDENTIFIABLE — the same diagnosis cove-pine-pitch's round 3 reached, in the same trap, one asset later. The subject leads with `IT IS THE LOOSEST AND MOST IRREGULAR of the cove's shrubs` and then asks for `five or six leaf clumps at plainly different sizes pushed up against each other`. Read literally, which is how it is read, that is an instruction to draw five or six bushes in a row. The compactness invariant WAS stated immediately afterward and it lost, which is the finding worth carrying: an invariant stated as a constraint does not survive a CONSTRUCTION that contradicts it, because the construction tells the generator what to draw and the constraint only tells it what to check. Rewrite the clump count downward (three or four), make the clumps OVERLAP rather than abut, and lead with the compact round head before introducing the ragged edge. THE DESATURATION HAS ITS OWN CAUSE and it is the word MATTE, which the subject uses of the leaf: matte is a chroma word wearing a finish word's clothes, and it sits next to `cool`, `slightly folded` and `leans toward blue` with nothing pushing back. The cedar solved the same problem by moving along hue at full chroma and naming the berries as the only low-chroma thing; this subject named the hue move but left `matte` in. Delete it. Registered as `bay-cove-plum-beach`, world 22, surface, contact none. ROUND 2, 2026-08-10: THE SHAPE FAILURE IS FIXED, THE COLOUR IS NOT, AND THE ARRANGEMENT WENT BACKWARDS. Two candidates were measured against the same gates and the SQUARE FOUR-CLUMP one was taken. Aspect 1.577 -> 1.026, so the 51-degree camera tilt is gone outright; fill 0.536 -> 0.755, against the ~0.70 the subject asks for; and the row of six separate bushes is gone — this is one compact head. It now draws 19x18px at world 22 where round 1 drew 19x12, and on the contact sheet it reads at 22px as a small dense shrub flecked with purple, which is the impression the asset exists to give. THE REJECTED CANDIDATE was the wide five-clump one: aspect 1.146, still over the 1.12 gate at ~29 degrees off vertical, fill 0.622, and 53.2% of n>=2 angular power in a 3-fold harmonic. Better than round 1 on every axis and still the worse of the two. ⚠️ COLOUR STILL SHORT, AND THE CAUSE IS STILL IN THE PROMPT. Lit foliage came back at saturation 0.571 — above the 0.55 reject line, so no longer a reject, but under the card band's 0.62 floor. Sampled directly, the brightest decile of leaf measures #46933E at hue 114.4 deg and saturation 0.576, against the #2E9E38 (hue 125 deg, saturation 0.709) the subject names. Hue is fine; chroma is 0.13 short and value is low. The word MATTE is still in the leaf clause and is still the most likely cause — see the round-1 diagnosis above. Deleting it is the cheapest single move available on this asset. ⚠️ AND THE ARRANGEMENT GOT WORSE, NOT BETTER: 32.6% -> 45.6% of n>=2 angular power, now a 2-fold, with a visible dark hub in the middle and four clumps ringed round it each carrying one berry cluster. So both the clumps AND the berries repeat — the same defect the bayberry shipped with, arriving here by a different route. THE REAL LESSON IS THE ONE cove-pine-pitch ALREADY WROTE DOWN, AND THIS IS ITS THIRD CONFIRMATION: each round fails on a different axis, and the new failure is caused by the fix for the old one. Round 1 sprawled; making it compact gave it a centre and a ring, which is what compact-and-radial looks like. So DO NOT CHASE THE ARRANGEMENT NUMBER ON ITS OWN — a reroll aimed at it alone risks bringing the sprawl straight back, exactly as the pine's round-3 rosette fix brought back a three-piece L. If there is a round 3, change colour and arrangement TOGETHER (delete `matte`; ask for three clumps with one clearly dominant and no gap at the centre) and re-measure COMPACTNESS explicitly, because that is the invariant this round is quietly holding and the next rewrite is most likely to drop. IT SHIPS AS IT STANDS: the two defects that mattered at race scale are fixed, and the hub and the 4-fold clumps only resolve at 2x and 4x. anchorPx was cleared before ingest so it re-seeded off the new art, at [0.4995, 0.5]. ROUND 3, 2026-08-10, TAKEN BUT A LATERAL MOVE, AND THE FLAT LINE IS THE FINDING. Aspect 1.048, fill 0.781, rosette 42.1% in a 4-fold, lit foliage saturation 0.572 with the brightest decile at #4BA847. Against round 2 that is better on fill (0.755 -> 0.781) and arrangement (45.6% -> 42.1%), marginally worse on aspect (1.026 -> 1.048, both far inside the 1.12 gate), and FLAT on chroma. It was taken for one thing only: the leaf VALUE went 0.576 -> 0.659, which is a visible lift out of murk even though the saturation did not move. ⚠️ STOP ROLLING THIS ASSET. Three deliveries now measure saturation 0.543, 0.571 and 0.572 — a flat line across three independent generations, which is as clean a demonstration as this library has that the constraint is the PROMPT and not the roll. The subject still says the leaf is MATTE, sitting next to `cool` and `leans toward blue` with nothing pushing back, and the card's floor is 0.62. The arrangement is the same story from the other side: 2-fold at 45.6% became 4-fold at 42.1%, i.e. the ring moved rather than went away, because the subject asks for a compact head and never says how the clumps or the berry clusters are distributed. A fourth roll against this wording will land in the same place. THE TWO EDITS THAT WOULD ACTUALLY MOVE IT, and they must go in together per the round-2 lesson: delete `matte` from the leaf clause and name the lit tone as a confident saturated green; and replace the clump count with a construction — three clumps, one clearly dominant, no gap at the centre, and berry clusters placed two-on-one-side/one-opposite rather than one per clump. Re-measure COMPACTNESS explicitly on whatever comes back, because that is the invariant these three rounds have been holding for free and it is the one a rewrite will drop.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE SHRUB, shot straight down from well above it the way a survey frames a single plant. YOU SEE FOLIAGE AND NOTHING ELSE: no trunk, no stem, no limb, no branch, no twig and no bark anywhere in this picture, and least of all in the middle. This plant is scenery standing on a headland; nothing passes beneath it and nothing needs to read its structure, so it is drawn as ONE CONTINUOUS MASS OF LEAF seen from above, and where the mass parts you see hard-edged SHADOW INSIDE THE PLANT and never a branch. A BLUE HYDRANGEA IN FULL BLOOM — the big mophead hydrangea that grows against every grey-shingled house on Nantucket and the Vineyard, and the one cultivated plant on this shore. THIS IS THE WHOLE SHRUB SEEN FROM ABOVE, NOT A CLOSE-UP OF A FLOWER. Almost every picture of this plant is one flower head filling the frame, and that is the wrong picture: here the flower heads are ONE PART of a round leafy bush, and there are MANY of them — twelve to twenty separate heads spread across the top of the shrub, each one small against the whole plant. THE SHRUB IS A ROUND, FULL, CLOSED CUSHION: a compact rounded mound of leaf with the flower heads sitting on top of it. Draw the smallest circle that contains the plant and it fills about seven-tenths of it, in ONE connected mass with nothing floating free. Its outline is SCALLOPED BY BIG LEAVES — the rim is made of large broad leaf blades, so it is bumpy in big soft curves rather than finely bitten. That coarse rim is what identifies this plant at a distance: every other shrub on this shore has a rim made of small elements and this one has a rim made of big ones. THE LEAF IS THE COARSEST ON THE HEADLAND: large, broad, blunt-tipped ovals with a strong midrib, carried in opposite pairs, and several of them read as individual blades rather than as clusters. THE LEAF GREEN IS FRESH, BRIGHT AND HIGH IN CHROMA — a lit green near #789C00 on the blades that catch the sun, a mid green near #547800, a body green near #24540C, and a deep cool shade near #0C3C18 beneath the flower heads. THERE IS NO OLIVE, NO KHAKI, NO MUSTARD, NO OCHRE, NO TAN, NO BRONZE, NO ARMY DRAB AND NO DUSTY, GREYED-DOWN OR MUTED GREEN ANYWHERE IN THIS PLANT. A drab shrub belongs in a swamp; this one grows in hard bright sea light on an open coast. Where it turns into shadow it goes DEEPER AND COOLER, never browner and never duller, and if any green is in doubt push it toward the BLUE side of green rather than the yellow side. THE FLOWERS ARE THE IDENTITY AND THEY ARE BLUE. Each head is a rounded dome of many small four-petalled florets packed shoulder to shoulder into one soft ball, drawn as a chunky two-tone mass and never floret by floret. THE BLUE IS A CLEAR CORNFLOWER-PERIWINKLE: a lit face near #7FA6DE, a body near #5480C4 and a shaded underside near #35548F. A few heads sit a shade paler and greener where they are still opening. NONE OF THEM IS PINK, MAGENTA, RED, ROSE, LILAC-PINK OR PURPLE — blue is the only direction this flower goes. THE HEADS CLUSTER, THEY DO NOT RING. Do not put one head in the middle and arrange the rest around it, and do not space them evenly: gather them into TWO OR THREE LOOSE GROUPS of three to six heads that touch and overlap, at plainly different sizes, with leaf showing between the groups. Walk round the plant, and if the same spacing comes back four, five or six times on the way round it has been drawn as a flower ARRANGEMENT and it is wrong however good it looks. No wreath, no ring, no bouquet, no posy, no rosette, no compass rose. BETWEEN A THIRD AND A HALF OF THE TOP OF THIS SHRUB IS BLUE, so at a glance the plant reads as a green bush wearing a big blue crown. But GREEN LEAF RUNS ALL THE WAY ROUND THE RIM: the flower heads sit INSIDE the leaf and never at the silhouette edge, so the outline of this plant is a leaf outline. NO GARDEN AROUND IT: no fence, no picket, no shingle wall, no house, no path, no gravel, no lawn, no border, no pot, no trellis and no other plant. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — a dooryard on sandy soil is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the plant is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the ground it stands on
assets.note: The islands' cultivated signature and the only planted thing on this shore — a blue mophead against grey shingle IS the Nantucket photograph, and this asset does more for the venue's sense of place per pixel than anything else in the band. SIZE IS HONEST: an established coastal Hydrangea macrophylla spreads about 1.9m, and 1.9m x 9.2 units/m = 18u. That makes it the SMALLEST world-prop in the library, under bayou-cypress-knee at 26 — AND IT IS THE ONE ASSET THAT CAN AFFORD TO BE, because its identity is a colour rather than a shape, and colour survives reduction where rim texture does not. See cove-oak-scrub for the family's shared reasoning and for the feature-floor arithmetic this asset is the exception to. ⚠️ IT IS A GARDEN PLANT, AND THAT IS A PLACEMENT CONSTRAINT RATHER THAN A DETAIL. The other three go anywhere on a wild bluff; this one belongs against the harbourmaster's house, along the village shore and by the lighthouse keeper's garden, in ONES AND SHORT ROWS. A hydrangea scattered across an open headland reads as a mistake to anyone who knows those islands, and at 18u a row of three or four along a shoreline is the shape the eye actually recognises anyway. Recorded here because the prop placement system art-pipeline 6 is waiting on has nowhere else to carry it yet. BLUE, NOT PINK, IS A DECISION AND NOT A DEFAULT. The same species is pink in alkaline soil and blue in acid; the islands are acid, blue is the signature, and one committed colour reads far better at 18px than a mixed shrub, which would simply go muddy. The pink variant now exists as `cove-hydrangea-pink`, which is the reason this key carries the COLOUR where the other three carry a species modifier: Hydrangea macrophylla has no sibling in this flora, so the species name would distinguish nothing, and the colour is what the asset is for. ⚠️ IF THIS IS GENERATED ON THE MAGENTA CHROMA KEY, check the flower edges after dekey.py — the BACKGROUNDS clause tells the model that no part of the subject may be magenta or pink, which argues with a flowering shrub even when the flower is committed blue. White or transparent is the safer background for this one asset. THREE FAILURE MODES, ALL OF THEM FROM THE REFERENCE DISTRIBUTION RATHER THAN FROM THE STYLE. (1) THE CLOSE-UP: nearly every hydrangea image is a single flower head filling the frame, so the subject's second clause insists this is a whole bush carrying twelve to twenty small heads. (2) THE SETTING: those same images almost all include a picket fence, a shingled wall or a garden bed, and the class add-on's no-scenery clause has never before had to fight a subject that implies one this strongly, so fence, picket, shingle, house, path, gravel, lawn, border, pot and trellis are refused by name. (3) THE WREATH: a round bush wearing a dozen round flower heads is the most direct invitation to a rosette anywhere in this library, worse than the pitch pine's, so the arrangement clause is written the way cove-pine-pitch's round-2 lesson requires — a CONSTRUCTION (two or three loose overlapping groups at plainly different sizes) rather than a prohibition, with the failure named in the terms the polar power-spectrum test measures. ONE MORE CLAUSE THAT IS DOING TWO JOBS: green leaf runs all the way round the rim and the flower heads sit inside it, so the silhouette of this plant is a LEAF silhouette and the blue never touches the outline. That is botanically right — mopheads sit on top of a skirt of foliage — and it is also what protects art-pipeline 8's 3:1 contrast floor on the contact sheet, since a mass of #5480C4 read against Glacier Sound is the one colour in this band at real risk of losing that check. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ACCEPTED FIRST ROUND WITH ONE DEFECT RECORDED, 2026-08-10. Cleared orthography at aspect 1.010 — the best in the band — colour at hue 78.9 deg / saturation 0.939, and compactness as ONE connected mass at 0.852 fill, which is right for a closed cushion (see cove-oak-scrub on why the ~0.70 figure does not bind here). All three predicted reference-distribution failures were AVOIDED: it is a whole bush and not a close-up, there is no fence or wall or bed anywhere in it, and the green leaf runs unbroken round the rim exactly as the clause asks, so the silhouette is a leaf silhouette. ⚠️ THE WREATH GOT HALFWAY IN: 44.9% of n>=2 angular power in a 4-FOLD harmonic, against a subject that explicitly asked for TWO OR THREE loose groups. Four groups is one more than the construction allowed, and four is the number that reads as a ring. The clause was right in form — it named a construction, gave the count, and named the failure in the metric's own terms — and the count is simply what got missed. Narrowing it to `exactly two groups, one clearly larger` is the cheap reroll fix; `two or three` leaves a generator free to round up, and it did. WHAT THE CONTACT SHEET ADDS THAT THE NUMBERS DO NOT: at the 18px it actually occupies the blue reads as a TINT on a green dot rather than as a blue crown, and only resolves into flower heads at 2x. That does not contradict this asset's premise — it is still far more legible than a rim texture would be at 18px, which is why it was sized here — but the honest claim is `a green shrub with a blue cast`, not `a blue shrub`. If more blue is wanted the lever is COVERAGE, not saturation: push the third-to-a-half up rather than brightening #5480C4, which would only cost the contrast the green rim is protecting. Delivered 2816x1536, padded to 1600px square. Registered as `bay-cove-hydrangea-blue`, world 18, surface, contact none.

assets.note: The blue hydrangea's sibling, and the pair is the point: a Nantucket dooryard is not one colour, it is blue and pink in the same bed, because the same plant goes blue in acid soil and pink where shell and lime got into the ground. Placing them alternately along the village shore is what the venue actually wants. SIZE IS THE SAME 18u for the same reason it was honest there — same species, same 1.9m spread, 1.9m x 9.2 units/m = 18. See cove-oak-scrub for the shrub band's shared reasoning and cove-hydrangea-blue for everything specific to this species: the close-up failure, the garden-setting failure, the wreath failure, the green-leaf-round-the-rim clause and why a cultivated plant is a placement constraint. ⚠️ IT IS NOT A HUE ROTATION OF THE BLUE ONE, and it must not be generated as though it were. Two masters identical in every way but colour would show up the moment a designer plants them together, which is the ONLY way they are meant to be planted — a repeated silhouette reads as a stamp exactly the way a texture's repeated feature does. So the subject varies the things that are free to vary within one species and holds the ones that identify it: the coarse big-leaf rim, the leaf palette and the flower coverage are word-for-word the blue's, while this plant carries FEWER AND LARGER heads (eight to fourteen against twelve to twenty), a LOPSIDED rather than an even cushion, and a two-groups-plus-outliers arrangement against the blue's two or three. Check the two masters side by side on the contact sheet before accepting either; if their outlines match, reroll this one. ⚠️⚠️ NEVER GENERATE THIS ASSET ON THE MAGENTA CHROMA KEY. The blue one carries this as a caution and here it is a hard rule, because the failure is a PROMPT CONTRADICTION rather than a keying accident. BACKGROUNDS['magenta'] in prompt.py ends with the sentence `no part of the subject may be magenta or pink`, so an assembled prompt for a pink-flowered shrub would tell the model to refuse the subject's own identity — and prompt.py's own portrait note records what a generator does with a self-contradicting prompt: it ignores one half at random. The keying arithmetic happens to be safe (dekey.py floods from the border with a tolerance summed across RGB, default 160, and #EA9BB0 sits 255 from (255,0,255)), so this is not about pixels being eaten. Generate on white or transparent. THE OTHER CONTRADICTION IS WITH THE VENUE CLAUSE, AND IT IS RESOLVED IN THE SUBJECT RATHER THAN FOUGHT. Every prop prompt for this venue carries `avoid hues that would look alien in it, like neon, HOT PINK or tropical green` — the one named refusal that this asset walks straight into. art-pipeline 3c settles who wins (a colour carrying real information beats the venue's commitment, and a pink hydrangea is genuinely pink), but winning an argument is worse than not having one, so the subject agrees with the clause instead: it asks for a soft warm garden rose at hue ~340 deg and refuses neon, fuchsia, magenta, shocking, candy and bubblegum pink by name. That is the general lesson — when a subject collides with a standing clause, look for the reading where both are true before invoking the override. ⚠️ SEPARATION FROM THE RED CHANNEL BUOY WAS CHECKED, since art-pipeline 2 forbids an ambient prop reading as a nav aid. buoy-channel-red is #BB3220 — hue 7 deg at saturation 0.83, a deep warm signal red — against this flower's hue 338-344 deg at saturation 0.34-0.63. Far apart in hue and much softer in chroma, and the two never share a surface: the buoy is in the water at 28u and this is on land at 18u. The subject still refuses scarlet, crimson and maroon by name, because the drift from rose toward red is a short one and buoy-channel-red's own subject already refuses pink from the other side. Nothing here needs the buoy's canonical coding protecting from it, but the check is worth recording so the next warm-coloured ambient prop does not have to redo it. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. ACCEPTED FIRST ROUND, 2026-08-10, and the cleaner half of the pair. Aspect 1.013; lit foliage hue 82.0 deg at saturation 0.930; ONE connected mass at 0.864 fill, right for a closed cushion; and 34.2% of n>=2 angular power in a 2-FOLD harmonic, which is the correct answer rather than a near-miss — 2-fold is lopsidedness, and this subject is the one in the band that ASKED to be lopsided, so the metric is reporting the instruction being followed. Compare the blue's 44.9% at 4-fold, which is a ring. THE COLOUR CAME BACK WHERE IT WAS AIMED, which matters because this asset was written against two standing clauses that both push the other way. It is a soft warm garden rose, not a hot pink: no fuchsia, no magenta, nothing fluorescent, and nothing that could be taken for the channel buoy's #BB3220 signal red. So the resolution the note argued for — agree with the venue clause by choosing a pink it does not refuse, rather than invoking art-pipeline 3c to override it — worked, and is worth reusing the next time a subject collides with a standing clause. THE PAIR-DIFFERENTIATION CHECK PASSES, which was this asset's whole reason for existing: set beside the blue it differs in arrangement (2-fold at 34.2% against 4-fold at 44.9%), in head count and head size, and in cushion symmetry, while sharing the coarse big-leaf rim and the leaf palette that identify the species. Planted alternately they will not read as one sprite stamped twice. Generated on transparent, never on the magenta key, per the note above. Delivered 2048px square. Registered as `bay-cove-hydrangea-pink`, world 18, surface, contact none.

assets.subject: A SINGLE MOON JELLYFISH, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating just under the surface — the round translucent bell filling the frame, tentacles beneath it. ⚠️ AUTHOR IT PALE AND NEARLY COLOURLESS. This one asset is deliberately NOT painted in its own local colour: the game tints it per jellyfish, so the blues, purples, oranges and pinks are added in code and must not be in the file. Paint the whole animal in WHITE and the faintest cool grey — the form carried entirely by VALUE, light against dark against nothing, with no hue anywhere. A colour baked in here multiplies against the tint and comes out muddy. THE BELL IS A CIRCLE, because that is what a dome is from straight above: as tall as it is wide, no oval, no tilt, no side of the animal, no horizon. Its edge is a soft scalloped rim, slightly irregular the way a live bell is, never a hard drawn circle and never a mechanical cog. Inside it, concentric rings of translucency — brightest as a fine bright line just inside the rim, softer toward the middle — so the bell reads as a lens of jelly rather than a flat disc. THE FOUR-LEAF CLOVER IS THE SIGNATURE and the proof of the camera: a moon jelly's four horseshoe gonads sit near the centre of the bell and show THROUGH it from above as four pale rounded loops arranged in a cross, a little brighter than the jelly around them. Nothing else reads as unmistakably 'jellyfish from directly above' at a glance. Radiating out from that centre, fine straight canals run to the rim — a few dozen hair-thin lines, evenly spaced, fading as they go. Beneath and just outside the rim, a dense FRINGE of very short fine tentacles all the way round, drawn as a soft feathered edge rather than individual strands, and four longer ruffled oral arms trailing from the centre, curling loosely under the bell and reaching a little past it — soft ribbons, not legs. NO GLOW IS PAINTED HERE. The engine adds the bioluminescence as a light of its own, so the file must contain no halo, no bloom, no outer aura and no soft light spilling off the animal — those would double with the engine's and fix the colour the tint is supposed to choose. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps, no gloss, no specular highlight, no gradient background. No water, no ripples, no caustics, no bubbles, no seabed, no other jellyfish, no cast shadow, no text and no numbers anywhere
assets.note: Glowtide Strait's first asset, and the venue's signature ambience — the card is full of them. ROLE ambient: pure decoration, and the roles table's bar applies, never confusable with a hazard at race scale. It clears that easily: a soft round bell against a venue whose hazards are angular dark karst. ⚠️ PAINTED WHITE ON PURPOSE, WHICH BREAKS THE LIBRARY'S OWN RULE. Every other prompt here carries the venue clause telling the generator to render a subject in its own correct local colour, and this subject overrides it in its second sentence. The reason is that ONE asset has to supply blues, purples, oranges and pinks: the engine tints it per instance through the same multiply-and-cache path `getTintedBoatPart` already uses for hulls, so a white master gives every hue for one generation and one review, where four coloured masters would be four of each. The cove cargo family took four reroll rounds apiece; that is the cost being avoided. THE GLOW IS THE ENGINE'S, NOT THE ART'S, and the subject bans it explicitly. A baked halo would double against the additive light drawn in drawNightGlow and would also lock the glow's colour, defeating the tint. Same division as the nav lights: the object is a dimmed physical thing, the light is emissive and added after the ambient wash. planRound TRUE, and it is the rare asset where that test is exactly right — a dome seen from straight above is a circle, so the outline is an honest tilt check and ingest will measure it. allowSymmetry TRUE for the opposite reason to the cruise ship's: a jellyfish IS radially symmetric, and ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE's ban on 'radial symmetry, mandala, rosette' would be the prompt arguing with the animal. SCALE IS STYLISED AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. At the bay's 9.2 px/m a world of 34 is a 3.7 m bell — a Nomura's jellyfish, not a moon jelly's 30 cm. A true-scale jelly would be three pixels. The venue card draws them big and legible and so does this; the same call the ferries' entries made about the size ladder beating fidelity. WHEN THE ART LANDS: register as a PROP with plane 'seabed' (the coral note has the argument — it draws under every surface layer and the water above is what sells the depth), contact none, and motion 'drift' so it rides the real current. Drift is free tidal movement and it earns its keep twice: on the one venue built around reading the stream, a field of jellyfish IS a current telltale.

assets.subject: A SMALL BLOOM JELLYFISH, seen from DIRECTLY OVERHEAD, floating just under the surface — a compact round bell filling the frame, tentacles beneath it. A DIFFERENT ANIMAL from the big moon jelly it shares the water with: busier, frillier and simpler in outline, so a drift of the two reads as a mixed bloom rather than one shape at two sizes. ⚠️ AUTHOR IT PALE AND NEARLY COLOURLESS, for the same reason as its sibling: the game tints it per jellyfish, so the colour is added in code and must not be in the file. White and the faintest cool grey only, the form carried entirely by VALUE. No hue anywhere. THE BELL IS A CIRCLE — as tall as it is wide, no oval, no tilt, no side of the animal. Its rim is finely ruffled, more frilled than the moon jelly's soft scallop. WHAT MAKES IT THE OTHER SPECIES: EIGHT radial canals instead of a four-leaf clover, spaced evenly like the spokes of a wheel and reaching most of the way from centre to rim, each a clean pale line a little brighter than the jelly. At the centre, a small dense knot of pale tissue rather than four loops. Between the canals the bell is almost clear. Around the whole rim, a fringe of FINE TENTACLES, longer and more visible than the moon jelly's — a soft feathered corona reaching out perhaps a third of the bell's own width, drawn as a mass with a few individual strands catching the eye, never as a ring of identical spikes and never as a hard star. NO GLOW IS PAINTED HERE. The engine adds the bioluminescence, so no halo, no bloom, no outer aura, no soft light spilling off the animal. Flat hard-edged shading in clear steps, no gloss, no specular highlight, no gradient background. No water, no ripples, no caustics, no bubbles, no seabed, no second jellyfish, no cast shadow, no text and no numbers anywhere
assets.note: The second jellyfish, and the reason there are two rather than one at two scales: a drift of a single silhouette repeated reads as wallpaper, and this venue puts a lot of them on screen at once. DISTINGUISHABLE AT A GLANCE on the axis that survives reduction — EIGHT spokes and a long feathered corona against the moon jelly's four-leaf clover and tight fringe. At world 22 against 34 the size difference helps, but it is not what tells them apart. Same three unusual manifest choices as [[glowtide-jelly]] and for the same reasons: painted WHITE because the engine tints per instance, planRound because a dome from overhead really is a circle, allowSymmetry because a jellyfish is radially symmetric and the arrangement negatives would otherwise argue with the animal. The glow is the engine's and the art must not bake one. AT 22u THE DETAIL BUDGET IS ABOUT 22 PIXELS ON SCREEN, so the eight spokes are the only interior detail asked for. The moon jelly can afford concentric rings and oral arms at 34u; this one cannot, and asking for them would deliver mush. WHEN THE ART LANDS: plane 'seabed', contact none, motion 'drift', as its sibling.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE PALM TREE, shot straight down from well above the crown the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. You are looking at the top of the whole tree and at nothing else: no length of trunk runs away from you, no bark surface shows, and the only part of the stem in this picture is the small circle of its top, glimpsed between the frond bases at the very middle. A COCONUT PALM standing on a South Pacific sand cay. ONE crown and ONE hub — this is a single rosette, and it is the only tree in this venue's set that is. Long feathered fronds radiate from the hub, and each frond is ONE chunky tapering blade of clustered leaflet-mass rather than a comb of separate leaflets: draw the leaflets as a coarse even sawtooth worked along the two edges of that blade, an EDGE TREATMENT and never a hundred individual strokes, with a soft rounded tip. Twelve to eighteen fronds in the whole crown. THE CROWN IS ALIVE, NOT GEOMETRIC, and this is the one place a palm seen from overhead goes wrong. The fronds sit at plainly UNEVEN lengths and at uneven angles: one or two droop shorter than their neighbours, one crosses over the frond beside it, and two or three older ones bend lower with their tips turned down and inward. There is no constant angle between fronds anywhere in this crown and no two fronds are the same length. Walk around the rim, and if the same spacing comes back four, five or six times on the way round, it has been drawn as a compass rose and it is wrong however good it looks. REAL DAYLIGHT SHOWS BETWEEN THE FRONDS. Around the outer half of the crown, leave clear hard-edged wedges of OPEN SPACE between neighbouring fronds, and let two or three of those wedges cut most of the way in toward the hub. Those gaps are TRANSPARENT BACKGROUND, not dark green paint — a gap painted mid-green is a gap that will not exist. The middle of the crown, where the frond bases pack together, stays closed. AT THE HUB, a tight cluster of three or four coconuts in a warm mid brown, half-buried in the frond bases, with the pale grey-brown top of the trunk just visible between them. The coconuts are the ONLY warm colour in the picture. THE GREEN IS BRIGHT TROPICAL SUN AND IT IS HIGH IN CHROMA. Build the whole tree from this set, sampled from this game's own accepted palm art: a bright lit green near #94C701 on the fronds that catch the sun, with the sunniest tips near #D8F113; a mid green near #6FA504; a full-bodied green near #478903; and a deep COOL shade near #114E13 in the shadow between fronds, going almost black near #002410 in the deepest pockets. Every one of those is a confident, saturated colour. THERE IS NO OLIVE, NO KHAKI, NO MUSTARD, NO OCHRE, NO TAN, NO BRONZE, NO ARMY DRAB AND NO DUSTY, GREYED-DOWN OR MUTED GREEN ANYWHERE IN THIS TREE. Where the crown turns into shadow it goes deeper and cooler, never browner and never duller, and if any green is in doubt push it toward the BLUE side of green rather than the yellow side. THE SILHOUETTE IS AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE. A crown seen from straight above is round, and one wider than it is tall means the camera was tilted. The unevenness belongs to the FRONDS, never to the overall proportion. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — a coral sand beach is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the tree is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the cay it stands on
assets.note: FIRST OF BLUEWATER BONANZA'S THREE TREES, the set that turns the venue's new sand cays from bare coralsand into a South Pacific archipelago. The three are told apart on SILHOUETTE FIRST, per art-pipeline 2's colour-removed test: this one is ONE ROSETTE OF LONG FEATHERED BLADES, the pandanus is SEVERAL SPIKY STRAP-ROSETTES CLUSTERED TOGETHER, and the tropical almond is a BROAD TIERED DOME. Size ladder 110 / 70 / 52 — 1.57x and 1.35x apart, wider than the cove family's 1.33x, so they are separable by size before any shape arrives. SIZE IS HONEST, NOT EXAGGERATED: an open-grown coconut palm carries a crown about 7.6m across, and 7.6m x 9.2 units/m = 70u. It is also exactly [[lagoon-palm]]'s number, which is the point — same species, same scale, so the two venues' palms are interchangeable and neither reads as the other's at the wrong size. ⚠️ THIS SLOT MAY NOT NEED A GENERATION AT ALL, and that should be decided before paying for one. lagoon-palm ships four accepted variants (palm, palm-leaning, palm-young, palm-dense), PROP_KINDS ids are global rather than venue-gated, and the editor's palette lists every kind — so Pearl Lagoon's palms can be planted on these cays today. A coconut palm on a Tuamotu motu and one on a Caribbean cay are the same tree, and reuse guarantees the style match that a fresh generation only hopes for. The case FOR drawing it anyway is bookkeeping rather than looks: an ocean-keyed asset puts the venue's palms in art/masters/ocean/ and on the ocean row of the manifest, where the next person looks. Draw it if the venue wants its own record; reuse lagoon-palm-leaning in particular if it does not — a palm leaning out over the water off a small cay is the single most South Pacific silhouette available and it already exists. PLANE canopy WHEN THE ART LANDS, following lagoon-palm and against the cove trees. Read the plane as a question about what is physically above what: a palm leans off a sand spit and a hull genuinely passes under its crown, where nothing sails under a headland. These cays are small — shape-2 measures 225x398u, about seven boat lengths — so a beach-edge palm really does overhang water a boat can reach. contact none: the tropicsand it stands on is already `hard`, so the land stops the hull before the tree would, and a collider here would never be tested. NO minHoles AND NO punchHoles, and that is a MEASURED decision rather than an omission. The swamp-oak note couples the openings floor to the canopy plane — a sprite drawn over the fleet hides a boat with a painted gap as well as with a painted leaf — and that argument is sound but the floor has never actually been held: measured on what ships, lagoon-palm (canopy plane) is 0.03% see-through, palm-dense 0.08%, cove-pine-pitch 0.05%, cove-oak-black 0.00%. Setting minHoles here would invent a gate no tree in the game has ever passed. Two things make it cost less than the note implies: canopyAlpha fades a crown to ZERO as the player's own boat goes under it, so your hull is never lost; and script.js states outright that a COMPETITOR vanishing under leaves is the venue working correctly. So the openings are asked for in the subject, where they buy a better-looking crown, and not enforced at ingest. If a delivery comes back a closed disc and it bothers you at race scale, sweep punchHoles on that delivery per the swamp-oak method — lowest luma that clears the floor, because every point above it is crown thrown away. allowSymmetry true, following lagoon-palm: a coconut crown is genuinely one radial rosette, and the arrangement negatives would otherwise argue with the tree. The unevenness clause is what keeps it off the mandala attractor instead. planRound true: a crown from straight above is round, and it is the only acceptance test a tilted camera cannot fake. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6: slot, then art, then the kind. DELIVERED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-14, pre-cut with real alpha, 2048px master. Ingested with NO WARNINGS: content 86%x85% of frame after fillTo, bake 280px for 70px display. EVERY GATE PASSED. Orthography: content aspect 1.012 against the 1.12 planRound gate — a true plan view, and the tightest of the three. Colour: green-only saturation 0.93 and hue 109, so the drab failure this library keeps having did not recur. Warm pixels 2.5%, which is the coconut cluster and nothing else. One connected mass, no floating fronds. NOT A MANDALA, despite carrying allowSymmetry and therefore being exempt from the arrangement negatives: the strongest angular harmonic is n=8 holding 25.8% of n>=2 power, BELOW the accepted cove oak's 33% and nowhere near the rejected cove pine's 71%. The uneven-frond-length clause did the work the flag would have let it skip. SEE-THROUGH 0.2%, which is modest in absolute terms and still better than every canopy tree already shipping (lagoon-palm 0.03%, palm-dense 0.08%, cove-pine 0.05%, cove-oak 0.00%). No minHoles was set and none is now needed. STANDS DARK ON ITS OWN GROUND, the constraint the whole family was designed around: crown mean L* 52.6 against tropicscrub's delivered body at 68.9, so the ground is +16.3 above it. Cove precedent is +26.0 / +37.2 / +32.2. Circle fill 65% against the ~70% the subject asks for — under, and correctly so for a feathered star whose fronds are separated by design. Registered `ocean-palm-coconut`, world 70, plane canopy, contact none. ⚠️ THE BLACK-UNDER-ALPHA HALO DID NOT HAPPEN, AND THE WAY THAT WAS ESTABLISHED IS THE REUSABLE PART. All three arrived pre-cut by a background remover with real alpha and near-black RGB under it (mean 0.4-1.0), which is the exact condition the bayou-oak note warns produces a dark fringe: ingest resizes RGBA with a plain PIL resize, which averages channel-by-channel without premultiplying, so black under the alpha gets mixed into every edge pixel. THE FIRST MEASUREMENT SAID IT WAS SEVERE and was wrong. Comparing a plain resize against a premultiplied one showed the rim 43-53 luma darker, and on a spiky subject the rim is a lot of the sprite (measured at display size: pandanus 20.6% of pixels, palm 11.0%, almond 3.8%). That comparison is not a halo test — un-premultiplying DIVIDES by alpha, which amplifies the bright antialiased edge the remover left, so the gap between the two methods is mostly that amplification. THE TEST THAT ACTUALLY ANSWERS IT is ordering: composite the master over the ground at full resolution and THEN downsample (exact by construction), against downsample-then-composite (what the engine does), and difference the two in the rim band. Measured over this venue's own tropicscrub body at both bake and display size, the mean error is under 0.5 luma on all three, worst single pixel 4-9. There is no halo to fix. A colour bleed was written, applied, measured to change nothing, and reverted — the pixels ship exactly as delivered, which is bayou-oak's 'geometry only' conclusion arrived at independently. USE THE ORDERING TEST, not plain-vs-premultiplied, on any future pre-cut delivery.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TREE, shot straight down from well above the crown the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. You see the top of the foliage and nothing else: no length of trunk, no bark, no branch and no limb runs away from you anywhere in this picture. A PANDANUS — screw pine, Pandanus tectorius, the tree that grows on every windward beach crest in the South Pacific, and the one that makes an island read as Pacific rather than as generic resort tropical. IT IS NOT ONE ROSETTE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DRAWING. A pandanus forks: the trunk divides, the branches divide again, and EVERY branch tip carries its own separate head of leaves. So from directly above you see THREE TO SIX SPIKY ROSETTES at plainly different sizes, packed close and overlapping into one crown — one obviously the largest, one or two small ones about half its width, the rest in between. DO NOT put one head in the middle and arrange the others around it: this crown has no centre, no ring and no spokes. Cluster the heads OFF to one side of each other, two of them touching and merging where they overlap, the group as a whole leaning. EACH ROSETTE IS BUILT OF LONG STIFF STRAP LEAVES spiralling out from its own small centre. A strap is ONE narrow blade of nearly even width for most of its length, tapering to a fine point — one flat chunky shape with a hard edge, never a bundle of separate grass blades. Ten to sixteen straps per head. They run STRAIGHT AND STIFF for their inner two thirds, and then the outer third BENDS OVER AND DROOPS, arching down and curling back so the tips hook away from the centre. That gives each head a spiky star with soft curling points rather than a flat asterisk, and it is the species' signature from above. The strap edges carry a fine even sawtooth, drawn as an edge treatment and never tooth by tooth. THE SPACE BETWEEN THE STRAPS IS OPEN AIR, not paint. This crown draws over the racing fleet, so the wedges between neighbouring straps are TRANSPARENT BACKGROUND, hard-edged and clean, widest at the rim and closing up toward each head's centre. A gap painted dark green is a gap that will not exist. AND YET IT IS STILL ONE COMPACT TREE. The heads form a SINGLE CONNECTED MASS: every rosette touches or overlaps a neighbour, and NOT ONE of them floats off on its own with clear space all the way round it. Draw the smallest circle that contains the tree and the foliage should fill about seven tenths of it. Do not let the heads drift apart into an L, a crescent or two bushes with a gap between them, and do not leave a whole quadrant of that circle empty. NO PROP ROOTS. This tree is famous for the stilt roots that hold it up on a beach crest, and FROM DIRECTLY ABOVE NONE OF THEM CAN BE SEEN — they stand under the crown, hidden by it. Drawing them is proof the camera was at the side. FRUIT ON ONE HEAD OR TWO, never on all of them: a single ROUND SEGMENTED FRUIT sitting in the middle of a rosette, a knobbly ball divided into flat polygonal facets like the skin of a pineapple, in a warm orange-brown. It is the ONLY warm colour in the picture. THE GREEN IS COOLER AND BLUER THAN A COCONUT PALM'S, AND EVERY BIT AS SATURATED. Build the whole tree from this set: a bright lit green near #3CB812 on the straps that catch the sun, a mid green near #0F850B, a full-bodied green near #075717, and a deep cool shade near #022E18 between the straps and under the overlapping heads. THERE IS NO OLIVE, NO KHAKI, NO MUSTARD, NO OCHRE, NO TAN, NO ARMY DRAB AND NO DUSTY, GREYED-DOWN GREEN HERE. Cool does not mean dull: if any green is in doubt push it toward BLUE, never toward grey and never toward yellow. THE SILHOUETTE IS AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE, taken as a whole. The unevenness belongs to the heads and to the rim, never to the overall proportion. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — a windward sand crest is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the tree is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the shore it stands on
assets.note: THE VENUE'S IDENTITY TREE. A coconut palm says 'tropical' and could be anywhere between Barbados and Bali; a pandanus says PACIFIC, and it is the cheapest thing on this list that makes Bluewater Bonanza's cays read as a place rather than as sand with palms on it. Same job cove-pine-pitch does for Lighthouse Cove. SIZE IS HONEST: a mature multi-headed Pandanus tectorius spreads about 5.7m, and 5.7m x 9.2 units/m = 52u. Smallest of the venue's three, 1.35x below the palm — see [[ocean-palm-coconut]] for the family's ladder and shared reasoning. THE MULTI-HEAD CONSTRUCTION IS THE WHOLE SLOT, and it is written as a CONSTRUCTION rather than as a prohibition on purpose. cove-pine-pitch spent four rounds proving that 'do not draw a rosette' does not work — ARRANGEMENT_NEGATIVE already carried rosette, ring formation, evenly spaced and compass rose, all of it applied, and the delivery still came back a five-petal flower, because radial-from-a-hub is a generator's default answer for any crown and refusing it leaves nothing in its place. So this subject says what to draw INSTEAD: three to six heads, uneven sizes, clustered off-centre, two of them merged. It also carries cove-pine-pitch's round-3 lesson pre-emptively — the fix for the rosette overshot into an L-shaped sprawl in three disconnected pieces, so 'single connected mass' and 'seven tenths of the smallest enclosing circle' are stated outright here rather than left as something the old wording had been quietly guaranteeing. Both are measurable on delivery and both are cheap. NO allowSymmetry, unlike the palm. Each individual head IS radial, but the tree is not, and the failure mode this asset has to survive is exactly the one the negatives exist for: asked for a spiky crown from directly overhead, every generator returns a snowflake. The palm can afford the flag because it genuinely is one rosette; this cannot. PROP ROOTS ARE NAMED AS AN ERROR because they are the single most likely wrong answer here. Every photograph of this tree is a side view showing the stilt roots, so a model asked for a pandanus will want to draw them, and from a true plan view they are invisible under the crown. Same foreshortening argument that fixed the bayou's spanish moss: state the physics, give the correct read, then name the failure so a generator can refuse it. COLOUR IS SPECIFIED AGAINST THE PALM, NOT AGAINST THE VENUE. Real pandanus foliage is a cooler, bluer green than a coconut palm's yellow-green, so naming it corrects a wrong local colour rather than imposing a venue one — art-pipeline 3c's distinction, the same one cove-oak-black relies on. The hexes were picked by rotating the measured lagoon-palm ladder (hue 67-147, saturation 0.78-1.00) about 35 degrees cooler at matched saturation, so the two families sit in the same chroma band and differ only in hue. THE DRAB REFUSAL IS LOAD-BEARING AND MUST NOT BE TRIMMED: the cove batch asked for 'grey-green' and got hue 50 at saturation 0.27, a yellow that read as dry grass, and 'cool' is one synonym away from that failure. Hence the explicit 'cool does not mean dull' tiebreaker. WHAT TO CHECK ON DELIVERY, in order: saturation of the lit straps (under 0.55 is a reject), hue (under 100 degrees and it is drifting back to the palm), no stilt roots, one connected piece at about 70% fill of its smallest enclosing circle, then the polar power spectrum for the rosette — ignore n=1, which is honest lopsidedness from directional light, and reject if any single n>=2 harmonic carries more than about a third of the angular power (the accepted cove oak sits at 33%, the rejected pine at 71%). PLANE canopy WHEN THE ART LANDS, contact none. It grows on the beach crest with its head out over the water, which is the plane comment's literal test. See [[ocean-palm-coconut]] for why minHoles is deliberately absent on both canopy trees. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6. DELIVERED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-14, pre-cut with real alpha, 2048px master, ingested with no warnings (bake 208px for 52px display). THE MULTI-HEAD CONSTRUCTION CAME BACK EXACTLY AS SPECIFIED — five heads at plainly uneven sizes, two large ones carrying fruit, clustered off-centre and overlapping, with the strap tips bending and curling as asked. No stilt roots, which was named as the likeliest wrong answer and did not appear. Aspect 1.017; one connected mass. ⚠️ THE ROSETTE METRIC READS 43.6% AT n=3 AND THAT IS NOT A FAILURE. It is above the accepted cove oak's 33%, and the check written above would reject on it. Read what n=3 MEANS here: this crown is built from a small number of discrete heads, so the angular profile genuinely has a low-order component — the metric is detecting the construction the subject demanded, not a ring of identical tufts around a hub. The cove pine's 71% at n=5 was a five-petal flower with nothing else in it; this has 56% of its angular power elsewhere. THE LESSON: the polar test assumes a crown that should be angularly featureless, and a deliberately multi-headed subject breaks that assumption. Judge it against the head count, or do not apply it. BEST SEE-THROUGH IN THE GAME BY A WIDE MARGIN: 3.9% interior alpha holes, against 0.03% for the shipped lagoon-palm and 0.00-0.08% for every other canopy tree. The openings floor the swamp-oak note wanted (6%) is still not met by anything, but this is 50x closer to it than the family's best, and it is the crown most worth having on the canopy plane. COLOUR SEPARATION FROM THE PALM HELD, which was the point of specifying it against the palm rather than against the venue: green-only hue 131 against the coconut palm's 109, so it is genuinely the cooler, bluer tree, and the check's 'under 100 and it is drifting back to the palm' was never in danger. Saturation 0.78, well past the 0.60 reject line, so 'cool' did not become 'drab'. Warm pixels 2.9% — the two fruit. Crown mean L* 43.6, so tropicscrub sits +25.3 above it. CIRCLE FILL 52% AGAINST THE ~70% ASKED, the one number that misses, and it is accepted on the same reasoning that makes the rosette metric inapplicable: a spiky multi-head crown cannot fill its own enclosing circle the way a tuft cluster does, because the gaps between straps are the subject. The invariant that actually mattered — ONE connected mass, no head floating free — is met. Registered `ocean-pandanus`, world 52, plane canopy, contact none. See [[ocean-palm-coconut]] for the shared halo finding.

assets.subject: THE PICTURE IS A DRONE PHOTOGRAPH OF THE TOP OF ONE TREE, shot straight down from well above the crown the way a forestry survey frames a single specimen. YOU SEE FOLIAGE AND NOTHING ELSE. The crown is CLOSED right across the frame, centre included: no trunk, no dark hub, no limb, no branch, no twig and no bark shows anywhere in this picture, and least of all in the middle. This tree stands inland on ground the fleet cannot reach and nothing passes beneath it, so it is drawn as ONE CONTINUOUS MASS OF LEAF seen from above, and where the mass parts you see hard-edged SHADOW INSIDE THE CROWN, never a branch. A TROPICAL ALMOND — Terminalia catappa, the broad shade tree behind every beach and village in the Pacific — and it is the BROADEST AND HEAVIEST crown of this venue's three trees, the one that gives a cay a middle. THE STOREYS ARE THE SUBJECT, and they are what makes this tree unmistakable from directly above. It grows in TIERS: its branches leave the trunk in flat horizontal whorls, one storey above the next, each storey reaching wider than the one over it. Seen from the air that reads as STEPPED RINGS OF FOLIAGE — a smaller, brighter cap of leaf at the top of the tree, a wider and distinctly darker ring of leaf around it, and a wider and darker ring again around that. THREE FLAT STEPS OF VALUE with a CLEAN HARD EDGE between them, cut by the band of shade where each storey overhangs the one below. No soft gradient anywhere between the steps. The steps are in the SHADING, not in the drawing: there is still no branch and no limb visible, only leaf-mass at three depths. AND IT IS NOT A BULLSEYE. Push the small bright cap plainly OFF-CENTRE, so every ring is eccentric and one side of each step is much wider than the other — this tree grew in the trade wind off the water and it is lopsided, fuller and heavier on the sheltered side. The outline is deeply lobed, with two or three bays biting well in between the clusters, and it is never a clean circle. If the rings come back concentric and even, it has been drawn as a target and it is wrong however good it looks. THE LEAF IS BIG AND IT SHOWS. Terminalia leaves are large broad PADDLES, widest near the rounded tip and narrowing to the stalk, and at this size a few of them must read individually: build the crown from chunky two-tone clusters, and let single paddle-shaped leaves break the rim here and there so the outline is scalloped by leaf shapes rather than by billowing blobs. This is the one tree in the venue's set whose individual leaf is legible, and it is a second axis of separation from the palm's blades and the pandanus's straps. OLD LEAVES TURN RED, AND THAT IS THE SPECIES, NOT THE SEASON. This tree sheds in flushes all year round in the tropics, so at any moment a few leaves anywhere in the crown are deep crimson near #943021 and warm bronze near #804117. SINGLE SCATTERED LEAVES ONLY: no more than about one leaf in ten, never a patch, never a whole branch turned, and none of them on the outer rim where they would break the silhouette. THIS IS NOT AN AUTUMN TREE — no scarlet mass, no orange canopy, no yellow, no rust wash, no bare twigs. The tree is in full green leaf and the red leaves are an accent a viewer notices second. THE GREEN IS A DEEP GLOSSY TROPICAL BROADLEAF, RICH AND FULLY SATURATED. Build the crown from this set: a lit green near #679E08 on the top storey where the sun lands, a mid green near #327303, a full-bodied green near #0F4C02 through the lower tiers, and a deep COOL shade near #022B0A in the bands between storeys and in the pockets between leaf clusters. THERE IS NO OLIVE, NO KHAKI, NO MUSTARD, NO OCHRE, NO TAN, NO ARMY DRAB AND NO DUSTY, GREYED-DOWN OR MUTED GREEN ANYWHERE IN THIS TREE. Where the crown turns into shadow it goes deeper and cooler, never browner and never duller, and if any green is in doubt push it toward the BLUE side of green rather than the yellow side. THE SILHOUETTE IS AS TALL AS IT IS WIDE. A crown seen from straight above is round; one wider than it is tall means the camera was tilted. The sprawl belongs to the LOBES and to the off-centre cap, never to the overall proportion. NO WATER ANYWHERE: no waterline, no wet stain, no reflection. And no ground is DRAWN either — dry ground behind a beach is where it grows, not something painted into the sprite; the tree is alone on a transparent background and the engine supplies the island it stands on
assets.note: THE VENUE'S BROAD-CANOPY TREE, and the one that gives a cay an interior. Palm and pandanus are both edge species, so a cay planted with those two alone is a rim of vegetation round a bare middle; this is what fills it. Placed farther inland and in the sheltered lee, per the brief. SIZE IS HONEST, NOT EXAGGERATED: an open-grown coastal Terminalia catappa spreads about 12m, and 12m x 9.2 units/m = 110u. That makes it the biggest of the three at 1.57x the palm, and it lands on the same number as swamp-oak, the game's other broad land tree — which is a coincidence worth keeping rather than nudging, since the two really are comparable crowns. See [[ocean-palm-coconut]] for the family's ladder and shared reasoning. ⚠️ PLANE surface, NOT canopy, AND IT IS THE ONE CHOICE IN THIS SET WORTH ARGUING. Its two siblings are canopy because a palm and a pandanus lean off a beach crest and a hull genuinely passes under them. Nothing sails under the middle of an island. On canopy this would draw OVER the fleet, so an inland almond would paint itself across a boat racing past the shore — occlusion with no object doing the occluding, the same bug the plane comment calls out for a lily pad on `surface`. Read the plane as a question about what is physically above what, never as a question about what kind of thing it is. That is also why this one is drawn as a CLOSED crown with no openings asked for, where the other two are asked for see-through: on `surface` nothing draws over a boat, so see-through buys nothing and a clean unbroken silhouette at 110px is worth more. Anyone who ever re-planes this to canopy has to add the openings requirement first — the same coupling swamp-oak carries. contact none, decided rather than deferred: it stands on tropicsand that is already `hard`, so the land stops a hull well before the tree does and the collider would never be tested. THE TIERED CONSTRUCTION IS THE SLOT'S REASON TO EXIST. A broad tropical dome from overhead is the most generic thing in this set and would come back as a green blob indistinguishable from cove-oak-black; Terminalia's pagoda whorls are a real, photographable structure that survives reduction, and stepped value rings read at 110px where interior branchwork does not. It is the same move cove-cedar-red makes at 42u — 'a bright small core inside a distinctly darker outer skirt, TWO FLAT STEPS OF VALUE' — one size up and with a third step. cove-cedar-red also shipped with NO allowSymmetry despite being a concentric subject, and this follows it: the arrangement negatives fight ANGULAR repetition, which is not what a tier is, and the off-centre cap plus the lobed rim are what keep it off the target/bullseye read. Reject a delivery whose rings come back concentric. THE RED LEAVES ARE INFORMATION, NOT DECORATION, which is what earns them under art-pipeline 3c — colour that carries information wins even where it appears nowhere else in the venue. Terminalia genuinely drops its leaves in crimson flushes year-round in the tropics, so this is species identity, not a season. It is also the riskiest clause here: cove-oak-black had to refuse autumn outright because New England summons it, and a generator that over-reads this one returns an orange canopy in a cobalt ocean. Hence the hard bound — one leaf in ten, singles never patches, none on the rim silhouette — and the explicit 'not an autumn tree' refusal alongside it. IF A DELIVERY COMES BACK WITH MORE THAN ABOUT A TENTH OF THE CROWN WARM, REJECT IT; do not accept it and plan to tune later, because there is no post-process that puts leaves back. WHAT TO CHECK ON DELIVERY, in order: warm-pixel fraction inside the crown (over ~12% is a reject), saturation of the lit tier (under 0.55 is a reject), no branch or trunk visible, three distinct value steps present, cap plainly off-centre, aspect under 1.12. NOT REGISTERED IN PROP_KINDS YET, by art-pipeline 6: slot, then art, then the kind. DELIVERED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-14, pre-cut with real alpha, 2048px master, ingested with no warnings (bake 440px for 110px display). THE PAGODA TIERS ARRIVED and they are what makes this legible at 110px: a small bright cap with two wider, darker rings stepping outward, hard-edged, no branch or trunk visible anywhere. Aspect 1.004, the truest plan view of the three. One connected mass. ⚠️ IT LOOKS LIKE A BULLSEYE AND MEASURES AS NOT ONE, which is worth recording because the eye and the usual metric both fail here. By eye the concentric tiers read as a target. The polar harmonic test says n=20 at 13.3%, the LEAST rosette-like sprite of the three — but that test cannot see this defect at all, because a bullseye is RADIAL structure and the polar test measures ANGULAR repetition. The test that answers it: take the centroid of the brightest decile of crown pixels and compare it to the crown's own centroid. Here the cap sits 12.7% of the radius off-centre, and the radial luma profile is not monotonic (6 of 9 steps decreasing, rising again at the rim where the outer leaves catch light). Not a target. ADD THE CAP-OFFSET TEST to any future tiered or concentric subject; the polar spectrum will pass a perfect bullseye without complaint. THE RED LEAVES STAYED INSIDE THEIR BOUND, which was the riskiest clause in the subject: warm pixels measure 3.5% against a stated reject line of ~12%, scattered as singles, with the crown otherwise in full green leaf. No autumn canopy. Green-only saturation 0.91, hue 107. Crown mean L* 32.1 — the darkest of the three, so tropicscrub sits +36.8 above it, right at the top of the cove's +26 to +37 range. Circle fill 77%, above the ~70% asked, correct for the family's dense one. PLANE surface AS DESIGNED, so it neither draws over the fleet nor fades under canopyAlpha — verified in the running game beside the two canopy species at matched camera distance, where the palms fade and this does not. Registered `ocean-almond-tropical`, world 110, contact none. See [[ocean-palm-coconut]] for the shared halo finding.

assets.subject: Bare uplifted coral limestone seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — MAKATEA, the old reef of Niue, Nauru and the raised Tuamotus: dead coral reef lifted clear of the sea and eaten by rain into a rough, porous, razor-sharp rock. Sun-bleached pale grey stone. THE PITTING IS THE SUBJECT. This surface is not a mosaic of humps and it is not a field of broken blocks: it is a rock EATEN AWAY FROM WITHIN. Across the whole frame, dense irregular SOLUTION HOLLOWS — rounded and lobed pits of plainly uneven size, from small dimples to pockets a hand's span across, packed close but never touching in a pattern, each one cut with a HARD sharp rim rather than a soft edge, and each one a clear step darker inside. Between the pits the stone stands up in narrow ribs and blades: the SHARPEST natural rock anywhere, thin lips and points and knife edges, a shade lighter along their crests where the sun catches them. Nothing here is rounded, worn smooth or softened. THE GHOST OF THE CORAL SHOWS THROUGH, and it is what makes this reef and not just rock. Here and there in the stone, the faint fossil pattern of the old reef itself: the pale ring of a coral head sectioned through, a few short branching stems of staghorn cut off flush with the surface, the honeycomb of a brain coral's ridges. Draw them as SOFT PALE GHOSTS INSIDE the stone, a shade lighter and cooler with no hard outline — they are the same rock, not objects sitting on it, and no more than five or six anywhere in the frame. A few deeper pockets go much darker, near the bottom of the range, where a pit runs down into shadow and old organic stain. Small, scattered, and never more than a handful. NOTHING LINES UP. No bedding direction, no parallel ribs, no grid of pits, no repeating spacing, no direction the eye can follow, and nothing in the frame agreeing with anything else. Spread the pitting at roughly the same density everywhere and keep every feature small — nothing may run more than about a third of the way across the frame. THE WHOLE IMAGE HOLDS A NARROW PALE GREY RANGE from #8F8E81 to #C4C3B6 around a mean of #ABA99B — a NEUTRAL, faintly warm bleached grey. Limestone is calcium carbonate and it is a cool stone: this is never the warm grey-tan of a New England glacial headland, never an orange or rust sandstone, never a cold blue mountain granite, and never a brown earth or mud. Hold the whole image inside a narrow value range. No water, no foam, no spray, no wet rock, no waterline, no tide line, no seaweed, no barnacles, no living coral, no shells, no sand, no soil, no moss, no lichen patches, no grass and no vegetation of any kind
assets.note: BLUEWATER BONANZA'S HARD GROUND, and its answer to basalt. The venue grew an archipelago and needed a rock that says REEF ISLAND rather than volcano: makatea is that rock, and drawing it is what stops the ocean's cays reading as generic tropical islands. Registered as the `coralrock` kind / `coralrock` look, label 'Coral Limestone'. TILE 128, NOT THE ROCK FAMILY'S 256, and it is the one number here most likely to be argued with. The shipped rocks sit at 256 because their features are metre-scale — bay-rock's note works it out exactly, a rounded whaleback wants 27.8 world metres of tile and halving it 'would make it a cobble field'. This material's features are NOT metre-scale: a solution pit runs 0.2 to 1 m, so at 256 the pitting lands at 2-9 px on screen and the whole identity of the tile dissolves into grey noise. At 128 the same pit is 4-18 px and reads. The risk that buys is a countable repeat — a cay rim is only a few hundred units, so 128 puts 2-5 repeats across it — which is why the subject spends its longest clause on 'nothing lines up'. If the repeat is visible at race scale the move is up to 192 or 256, and the pitting has to be redrawn coarser to survive it; retiling alone will not fix it (the bay-sand lesson: a smaller tile makes features smaller and never fewer). ALPHA 0.35 IS PRE-REGISTERED, NOT MEASURED — granite's and coastalrock's number, taken because this is a rock. ⚠️ EXPECT TO MEASURE IT DOWN. This is a hard-rimmed pitted surface with deep shadow in the pockets, so its luma sd will land well above bay-rock's 8.10, and the last two grounds to arrive both came off their pre-registered 0.5 for exactly this reason (marsh -> 0.40, scrub -> 0.40). The band to land inside is the set's on-screen sd 1.38-6.75, and a ground must LOSE the contrast fight with the boats and props drawn on it. Sweep it on delivery; do not ship the pre-registered value unmeasured. THE BODY IS THIS SPEC MEAN (#ABA99B) AND MUST BE RESET TO THE DELIVERED TILE'S OWN MEAN on ingest, the coralsand / bay-rock move — with base equal to tile mean the blend cannot move the colour, only the spread around it, so alpha stays a pure contrast knob and the mean-luma shift the arctic textures warn about cannot happen. Carry the spec's own stroke/veg/rock offsets onto the new body rather than leaving them (the bayou-mud precedent); they are already written that way in ISLAND_STYLES. COLOUR SEPARATION WAS SCORED IN COASTALROCK'S TWO TIERS. In-venue, which is what the player reads at speed, it is dE 22.4 from `coralsand` — the sand it shares every shoreline with — against the cove's accepted sand-vs-rock 23.9. Cross-venue it is 9.0 from `coastalrock` and 10.4 from `lane`, and that is accepted because neither can be in the same race; 19.2 was called fine there where 5.3 was not. The `lane` neighbour is the honest one: crushed shell IS pulverised coral limestone. NEUTRAL, NOT WARM, is the axis that separates it from coastalrock where value cannot — hue 53 / sat 0.09 against 44 / 0.19 — so a delivery that comes back beige has lost the distinction and should be rejected. WHAT TO CHECK ON DELIVERY, in order: seamless wrap on all four edges; mean and sd (mean within ~3 of #ABA99B, then reset the body to it); saturation under ~0.14 (over that and it is drifting to coastalrock's warm tan); pit rims HARD, not soft — this is the single likeliest failure, because every generator softens a rock; at least three fossil-coral ghosts present but under six; and no feature running more than a third of the frame. NO LAND_TEXTURES ROW YET — it is written out ready in the ISLAND_STYLES comment in script.js. The kind ships now and draws as a flat fill until this arrives, which getLandPattern gives for free. DELIVERED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-14, at 1254px (downsampled to the 1024 profile master by ingest; mean and sd unchanged across the resample). ALPHA MEASURED TO 0.20, well off the pre-registered 0.35, and the note above called it: this is the loudest master the pipeline has ever taken in at luma sd 21.79 (tile 128), against a previous worst of marsh's 16.39 and bay-rock's 8.14. 0.35 would have landed on-screen sd 7.63 — past every accepted ground including `grass` (6.66) — on a material that is meant to be a quiet rock. 0.20 lands 4.36, between the two shipped hard rocks (bay-rock 2.85, arctic granite 4.89). Dropping all the way to bay-rock's own 2.85 (alpha 0.13) was tried and rejected by eye: the tile goes flat and the solution pitting, which is this material's whole identity, disappears. ⚠️ THE MASTER DOES NOT WRAP, AND THE ALPHA IS WHAT SAVES IT. Measured at the 128px it draws at, edge-to-edge difference is 1.47x (horizontal) and 1.32x (vertical) the interior neighbour difference, where a seamless tile sits near 1.0 and its sibling ocean-scrub measures 1.11 / 0.87. A seam is a CONTRAST artefact, so the knob that quiets the tile quiets the seam with it — at 0.20 the mismatch is under 4 luma units and invisible in a 3x3 tiling. That makes the SEAM the binding constraint on this row rather than the contrast band: raising alpha brings the seam back before it brings the loudness back. Any future redraw should fix the wrap and would then be free to run louder. PERIODICITY IS EXCELLENT AND WAS THE ONE WORRY THAT DID NOT MATERIALISE: peak/mean 4.44 on the radially averaged power spectrum, the LEAST periodic tile in the whole set (shipped range 8.65-12.18), with only 15.8% of variance in its dominant band. The tile 128 gamble in the note above therefore paid off — no countable repeat, and the pitting resolves at race scale. ⚠️ COLOUR DRIFTED WARM AND THE DELIVERY CHECK MISSED IT, which is the transferable finding. Spec was NEUTRAL #ABA99B at hue 53; delivered is #A7A193 at hue 41.7 — coastalrock's own hue (44). The check written above says to reject if SATURATION goes over ~0.14, because that is how a neutral stone becomes a warm tan; delivered saturation is 0.12 and sailed straight through while the drift happened entirely on hue. WATCH HUE, OR WATCH BOTH. Accepted anyway, and the trade is recorded because it is not one-sided: in-venue separation from `coralsand`, the sand this shares every shoreline with and the only separation that matters in play, IMPROVED from 22.4 to 24.8 — now past the cove's accepted sand-vs-rock 23.9. What it cost is cross-venue picker separation from `coastalrock`, down from 9.0 to 6.1, close to the 5.3 that note calls a real collision. Those two can never be in the same race, so the labels carry it: 'Coral Limestone' against 'Coastal Rock'. Body reset to the delivered mean; stroke/veg/rock are the spec's own offsets carried onto it. Registered `coralrock`, tile 128, alpha 0.20.

assets.subject: A closed sward of coarse tropical island grass and low scrub seen from directly overhead from about ten metres up, in flat even light — the dry-season interior of a small South Pacific island, sun-dried and salt-pruned rather than lush rainforest. AT THIS HEIGHT INDIVIDUAL BLADES DO NOT RESOLVE, and that is the subject: the sward reads as a soft clumpy mottle, rounded tussock crowns a shade lighter where the grass mounds up and narrow sinks a shade darker between them, every clump blending into its neighbours with no hard edge and at roughly the same density everywhere. This grass is COARSER AND MORE TUSSOCKY than a temperate pasture — the clumps are bigger and stand more separately, with more of the darker sink showing between them. THROUGH THE SWARD, LOW SCRUB — broader, rounder, distinctly DARKER and slightly BLUER patches where beach naupaka and low salt-tolerant shrubs lie flat against the trade wind. Each is a soft-edged mound a little denser than the grass around it, scattered unevenly, covering perhaps a quarter of the frame. THEY ARE PATCHES OF A DIFFERENT PLANT, NOT BUSHES: no branch, no stem, no drawn outline, no cast shadow, and nothing tall enough to read as an object sitting on top of the ground. This is where the olive in this ground lives — in the scrub and in the sinks, never in the mean. A few broad drifts of paler, drier, straw-tinted grass move through at the largest scale, soft and wide, where the dry season and the salt have burned the sward back — drifts of tone only, never a shape with an edge. NOTHING LEANS ANY PARTICULAR WAY. No combed direction, no mowing stripes, no swirls, no rows, no terracing, nothing lining up with the frame or with itself, and no spacing that repeats anywhere in the image. THE WHOLE IMAGE HOLDS A NARROW SUN-BLEACHED RANGE from #93A527 to #C2D160 around a mean of #AABD31. IT IS SUN-BLEACHED, NOT SUN-GREYED, and that distinction is the whole colour brief. Bleached grass goes LIGHTER and YELLOWER; it does not go gritty or grey. So this is a bright, clean, confident yellow-green — dried by hard tropical sun, but every bit as alive. NOTHING HERE IS KHAKI, SAGE, GREYED-DOWN, DUSTY, MUTED OR ARMY-DRAB, and nothing is the cured tan-olive of a dead sward. If a green looks washed out or dirty it is wrong; take the fading upward into light, never sideways into grey. Hold the whole image inside a narrow value range. No visible soil, no sand, no coral rubble, no rock, no flowers, no palm fronds, no fallen leaves, no individual drawn blades, no fine hairline strokes, no paths, no tracks, no footprints, no fences, no water and no shoreline
assets.note: BLUEWATER BONANZA'S PLAIN LANDMASS FILL — the ground a cay's interior is made of, between the beach and the trees. It exists to close a gap the venue actually has: with only `tropicsand` and three tree props, an island is either bare beach or solid forest, and there is nothing in between to draw. Registered as the `tropicscrub` kind / `tropicscrub` look, label 'Tropic Scrub'. ⚠️ THE BODY WAS PICKED AGAINST THE TREES, NOT AGAINST THE OTHER SWARDS, and that is the constraint to preserve. This ground carries trees: true and is what ocean-palm-coconut, ocean-pandanus and ocean-almond-tropical stand on. Measured: the body sits at L* 73.0 against those three crowns' lit tones at 74.3 / 66.0 / 59.3 and their mid tones at 61.9 / 48.1 / 42.7, so every crown reads DARK against its own ground. Lighthouse Cove is the precedent and works the same way — ground L* 66.4 under crowns at 59.7 and 46.1. The obvious 'lusher tropical green' lands at L* 56, inside the crown range, and would dissolve three trees into their own lawn. Anyone re-tuning this colour re-checks those seven numbers first. TILE 128, with `grass`, `swampgrass` and `bay-scrub`: tussock crowns are centimetre-scale and land at true size there. No argument on this one — it is the whole sward family's number. ALPHA 0.40 IS PRE-REGISTERED from coastalscrub's MEASURED value rather than from the swards' original 0.5, because this is the same kind of material and coastalscrub is the one that had to move: its delivered mottle came back at luma sd 14.30, which at 0.5 would have made it the loudest ground in the game. Starting from the corrected number is the cheap version of that lesson. ⚠️ STILL MEASURE IT. This subject asks for coarser, more separated tussocks and a full quarter of the frame in a second darker plant, so it may well arrive busier than bay-scrub did. Land inside the set's on-screen sd band of 1.38-6.75, ideally between swampgrass (5.10) and grass (6.75) where bay-scrub sits at 5.72. BODY IS THIS SPEC MEAN AND MUST BE RESET TO THE DELIVERED MEAN on ingest, per [[ocean-coralrock]] and the coralsand / bay-rock move. A FOURTH SWARD, AND THE LIGHTEST AND YELLOWEST OF THEM: dE 18.8 from `coastalscrub`, 14.8 from `grass`, 36.2 from `swampgrass`. All three are cross-venue and so picker-only under coastalrock's two-tier rule; in-venue, which is what matters in play, it is 60.5 from the sand it sits behind and 60.8 from the limestone it sits against. SATURATION IS HELD AT 0.74 ON PURPOSE — above coastalscrub (0.62), below `grass` (0.83) — and the 'sun-bleached' is bought with VALUE. This is coastalscrub's hardest-won lesson applied ahead of time rather than re-learned: its first answer cut chroma to 0.54 to buy sun-fading, landed with the cured DEAD sward `swampgrass` (0.48) and read army-olive. Cutting saturation is how a ground leaves the family, not how it gets weathered. The subject therefore refuses the drab words by name and states the tiebreaker direction. WHAT TO CHECK ON DELIVERY, in order: seamless wrap on all four edges; saturation of the lit tussocks (under 0.60 is a reject — that is the failure this family keeps having); mean within ~3 of #AABD31, then reset the body to it; the scrub patches present and genuinely darker AND bluer than the grass, not just darker; no combed direction and no repeating spacing; no soil, rubble or fallen frond anywhere.
